about: Pages of the first hour as the narrator told them, each once (scripts/prose-census.ts --fixture). Re-recorded when the prose moves.

pages.label: Lead the horse while he heaves
pages.page: You take the horse by the bridle and lead it forward while the wagoner pushes on the wheel. The cart comes up out of the ditch and back onto the road. The cart stands square on the road again, its load roped down, the horse quiet. The wheel is out of the ditch, and the wagoner’s meal is on the road again because of you.

pages.label: Steal a sack of meal off the cart
pages.page: The sack comes off the tail of the cart without a sound. The wagoner, shoulder to the wheel, curses the wheel and does not turn round.

pages.label: Help him, for a share of the load
pages.page: ‘A share,’ says the wagoner, and looks at you a long moment. ‘A sack, then, and a coin. Be quick about it.’ You put your shoulder to the wheel with him, the horse pulls, and the cart comes up out of the ditch. He gives you a sack of meal and one coin. ‘You’ll go far,’ he says. He does not say it kindly. The cart stands square on the road again, its load roped down, the horse quiet.

pages.label: Walk on
pages.page: ‘No more could the last six,’ says the wagoner, and turns back to his wheel without looking at you.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You have been three years on the other side of the hills, hiring out with the droves. Your mother’s letter took a week to find you. Your father went out on the road with the cart, it said, and did not come home. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Millholm: low roofs against the sky, painted wagons among the houses, eel-traps stacked against the walls. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Look along the road between Mistshaw and Millholm for your father, who went out by it with the cart and did not come home.

pages.label: go(region__s2_approach_way,region__s2_green)
pages.page: Millholm is half houses and half wagons with their wheels taken off, painted saffron and rose and a deep blue. Cook-smoke drifts between them, smelling of cumin and charred onion. Beyond the roofs lies the Mistmere. Twice this month the Hall’s keeper has driven the town’s pigs off the verge of the old road. A notice is nailed to the clerk’s trestle by the well, under the shire-reeve’s mark: THE TALLY OF IRON AND GOLD IS TO BE MADE UP BY MIDWINTER. FOR THE WEIGHT OF IRON AND GOLD WANTING, SEE THE CLERK. A plank door in the wall, barred on the outside: the lord’s lockup. Above the roofs, to the east, two columns of smoke stand on the ridge: one thick and black from the digging, one thin and white from the old woman’s fire. An old woman is telling a story to a ring of children in a tongue you do not have, and they laugh together at the same places. Wellby is sitting at the side of the way mending a pot, with his wares spread on a blanket. Cora is tuning a fiddle on a bench, frowning at one string. Callie is touching up a painted backcloth of a castle with a small brush. Garret stands by the door with a cudgel at his belt, watching the street. The alehouse dog, a rough-coated hound, sits by the door of Corrin’s alehouse, thumping his tail on the step. A grey cat sits on a wall-top with her eyes half shut and her tail hanging down the stones. Your brother is sitting on a rail with your father’s old spear across his knees, watching the road. He is taller by a head than when you went away. A grey dog lies by the door of Corrin’s alehouse with her head on her paws, watching the road. She holds one forefoot off the ground. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. Asters grow in the gardens about the green in clumps, mauve with yellow eyes. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A faded Wapshott’s bill from the last round is peeling off the wall, the Colonel’s face half gone. Across it someone has chalked the round: Lowmouth, Mistshaw, Millholm, THREE DAYS EACH. Bask, a salter, selling from the house door, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Millholm, is here. The old woman in the doorway, the innkeeper’s mother, who has not been out of her chair since the harvest and who asks, every morning, whether the lamp has been lit, is here. So are Thessaly Brandt, Tibb Holt, Sim Tull, Granfer Tull and Robin. The grey dog barks twice, then comes to see who you are.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_r6)
pages.page: Callie looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__tull)
pages.page: A broad man in a smock with forearms the colour of the pit and a pot of ale in each hand gives you one of the pots before you have asked. ‘Sim Tull,’ he says. ‘Foreman of the marl, when there’s marl to dig.’ He drinks. ‘Come to the Marl Wake, when the circus is next here: there’s a greasy pole with a leg of mutton on top. Nobody’s had the mutton in four years. My granfer had it in his day; he never stops telling us.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__granfer)
pages.page: A tiny, bald, furious old man in a smock older than you are, sitting on a bench with his stick between his knees, looks you up and down. ‘In my day,’ he says, ‘we had the mutton every year. Every year. Now they slide down that pole like butter off a knife.’ He spits. ‘And some thief of a dealer had my best bantam off me at Michaelmas for a shilling and a lie.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_th_preacher)
pages.page: ‘You’re back, then,’ says Thessaly Brandt, as if you had been gone a week and not three years.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s4_reeve)
pages.page: Aldous Fenn looks you over, from your boots up. ‘You’ll be walking out to the Hall, I suppose. Everyone with boots does.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_merchant)
pages.page: Bask looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: listen(region__s1_u_store_lock)
pages.page: You put an ear to the corn-store padlock, and hold your breath. There is nothing to hear from it.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_tie_nan)
pages.page: A very old woman has been set in a chair in the lee of the door with a blanket to her chin and a rosary of dried peas. ‘Is it lit?’ she says, not to you. ‘It is lit, Mam,’ somebody says from inside. ‘Then I may sit,’ she says.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_r7)
pages.page: ‘You’re back, then,’ says Garret, as if you had been gone a week and not three years.

pages.label: listen(tollKeepers__lockup_bar)
pages.page: You put an ear to the lockup door, and hold your breath. There is nothing to hear from it.

pages.label: ask(region__s2_merchant,word11__h1_s2_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Black Keep: a walled keep on its rise in the fen east of Sedgebrook,’ says Bask. ‘A crier in the castellan’s colours has read a levy on the green: spears and grain, to be at the keep on the twelfth day, for the king’s muster,’ says Bask. Black Keep is the name of the walled keep on its rise they speak of.

pages.label: talk_to(howe__clerk)
pages.page: The shire-reeve’s clerk looks up from a writing-board and a stack of tallies. ‘You are not here to pay the levy,’ he says, ‘so you must be here about the torc. Everyone is.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_r1)
pages.page: Wellby looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: talk_to(drover__son)
pages.page: ‘There you are,’ says Tibb Holt, as if you had stepped out an hour ago; only the voice gives it away.

pages.label: ask(region__s2_merchant,word3__h3_s2_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Merespire: a lone tower in the fen east of Millholm,’ says Bask. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “wet spire”.’ ‘Behind Merespire, the tower where the green light burns at night, an old well runs down into the cellars,’ says Bask. ‘The builders used it.’ Merespire is the name of the lone tower they speak of.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_r2)
pages.page: ‘You’re back, then,’ says Cora, as if you had been gone a week and not three years.

pages.label: go(circus__tober_lane_c,circus__tober_c)
pages.page: A long field outside Millholm with an old stone cross at the top of it, worn to a stump, that someone has hung a horseshoe on. There is a ring of yellowed grass in the middle of the field, and a scatter of old sawdust, and deep ruts going out at the gate.

pages.label: go(circus__meadow_path_c,circus__meadow_c)
pages.page: Wet meadows in a loop of slow water, the grass long and silver, alders along the bank, and a line of pollard willows like men with their hair standing up.

pages.label: search(circus__meadow_c)
pages.page: You search the water-meadows below the town with care, a little at a time. Low in the long grass, where nobody would see it who was not looking for it, there is frost: a line of frost-ferns on the blades, like the breath on a window, running from the alders to the willows. In the middle of summer. It melts as you look at it. It is your woodcraft that makes it out.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__battleaxe)
pages.page: You set a battleaxe down.

pages.label: go(circus__meadow_path_c,circus__tober_c)
pages.page: A long field outside Millholm with an old stone cross at the top of it, worn to a stump, that someone has hung a horseshoe on.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__pole)
pages.page: You set a ten-foot pole down.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__torch)
pages.page: You set a torch down.

pages.label: wait_hour
pages.page: An hour passes.

pages.label: go(region__road_s2_s3,region__s2_s3_way)
pages.page: It is hot on the road, and you walk slower than you meant to. Partway, the road comes down to the river and goes over it by the bridge, and the water runs deep and quick under your feet. The bridge over the Deepwater is narrow and humped, with a cut stone at its crown too worn to read. An otter’s head breaks the water downstream and is gone. At a bend in the road a squat old milestone with a crowned wheel cut in its face, so worn that the crown is only a row of bumps, like knuckles. A goat with a broken tether is cropping the verge, with her whole attention. Lavinia, a messenger, overtakes you at a trot on the road to Sedgebrook, and calls back over her shoulder that she cannot stop. A man in a good grey coat sits at a trestle by a bar across the road, with a ledger and a strongbox. Two men in the lord’s livery lean on the bar across the road. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Sphagnum moss lies in the wet hollows, red and green, holding water like a sponge: it binds a wound better than linen. Comfrey grows rank by the water, hairy-leaved, its bells hanging: knitbone, the herb-wives call it. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Foxgloves stand tall at the wood’s edge, purple bells speckled inside: they heal, prepared rightly, and kill otherwise. A bay tree grows along the road, dark and glossy, clipped for its leaves. Banewort grows along the road, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Dragonwort grows along the road, a red spike among spearing leaves. Bloodroot grows along the road, broad-leaved, with white flowers low to the ground. Rosenoble grows along the road, a briar of deep red roses. Woodbine climbs along the road, its cream and yellow flowers sweet at dusk. A cinnamon tree grows along the road, its bark peeled in strips. Actaea grows along the road, its white flowers in feathery spikes. Ofbit grows along the road on thin stems, its flowers blue. The toll-reeve, the lord’s toll-reeve, is here. The customs-men are here. The bar stays down. ‘The lord’s toll,’ says the reeve, dipping his pen. ‘Three coin. Names?’ To go on along the road without paying is to run the lord’s toll, and his men will know you again.

pages.label: tollKeepers__pay_toll(party,region__s2_s3_way)
pages.page: The reeve writes you down, sands the ink, cuts a notch in a hazel tally and splits it, and hands you your half. ‘Good both ways till this day next week.’ Fenn lifts the bar.

pages.label: go(region__s2_lanes_way,region__s2_lanes)
pages.page: The lanes behind the houses run between yards and workshops: the ring of a hammer, a smell of bread or tallow, a door open on somebody’s work, a cat asleep on a sill. Eldon is cutting a mortise, a chisel in one hand and the mallet in the other, a pencil behind one ear.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_r5)
pages.page: Eldon looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: wait_watch
pages.page: Eldon goes away.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__candle)
pages.page: You set a candle down.

pages.label: go(region__s2_inn_door,region__s2_taproom)
pages.page: Corrin’s alehouse is a front room with a barrel on trestles by the hearth and two benches worn smooth. It smells of peat smoke and sour malt, and the ale is drawn into horn cups. Eel-men sit at the long table, smelling of the river. Everyone here is grumbling about the toll on the road: food is dearer for it, and there is less of it. ‘Ambrose there is looking for work,’ says Corrin. ‘Would go anywhere with anyone, for a few coins and their keep.’ Cora is arguing with the next table about the price of wool. Bree is arguing with the next table about the price of wool. Eldon is at the long table with a cup, telling a long story about a horse. Callie is at the long table with a cup, telling a long story about a horse. Lyle Goodbarrel, the pedlar, has his tray of ribbons and needles open on a bench. Your mother is at the hearth with her back to the room. Corrin, an alehouse-keeper, is here. Ambrose, a soldier, is here. Dannel Hobb, a boy of ten with a white streak in his hair, kept indoors, is here. So are Orabel Holt and the hedger.

pages.label: examine(region__gate_hollins_notice_s5)
pages.page: A notice in a clear, pinched hand, carried down by a carter and nailed up where travellers will see it: WANTED, A RATCATCHER, FOR HOLLINS, THE HOUSE BEING OVERRUN. TWO CROWNS THE DAY, AND TWOPENCE THE TAIL. APPLY AT THE MAT, BOOTSCRAPE, TEN UNTIL TWO. D. PYECROFT. Under it, in pencil, someone has written: north over the march, and mind the cat.

pages.label: search(region__s2_taproom)
pages.page: You search Corrin’s alehouse with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: talk_to(drover__hedger)
pages.page: ‘You’re back, then,’ says the hedger, as if you had been gone a week and not three years.

pages.label: ask(region__s2_traveller,word11__h2_s2_traveller)
pages.page: ‘The lord of Black Keep has not been seen in eleven days,’ says Ambrose. ‘His castellan signs for him.’

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You have the letter inside your coat, from the brothers of your order to the priest of Nodens at Lowmouth. It asks that Wenna, who reads the old script, be given a bed and shown the way to Mistlake. There is writing there that the order has heard of for a hundred years and never seen copied. Lowmouth is smaller than the brothers made it sound, after so many days on the road. The first person you ask points the way to the priest of Nodens, and you go in. The brothers want the old writing at Mistlake read and set down: who made the place, or how its makers ended. Their letter is for Eogan, priest of Nodens at Lowmouth, who will show you the way.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word9__h2_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘The well-head of Nodens at Lowmouth: Lowmouth’s first priest made it, and their name is cut on the back, worn almost away,’ says Eogan. ‘Fengate: the fallen walls in the fen north of Mistshaw,’ says Eogan. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “fen gate”.’ ‘Dogs will not go into the hollow beyond Fengate, and an old priest said the ground there hummed on feast days, a long low note that the monks of the old order tried to sing against, and could not,’ says Eogan. Fengate is the name of the fallen walls they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word10__h3_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘Black Barrow: a grassed mound in the fen east of Mistshaw,’ says Eogan. ‘An old woman keeps a fire on the ridge above Black Barrow, in sight of the king’s howe,’ says Eogan. ‘The priest says she is the last who still keeps the dead’s rest.’ Black Barrow is the name of the grassed mound east of Mistshaw they speak of.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_anselm)
pages.page: A lean young man in a grey habit looks up from the lamp he is trimming, unsmiling. ‘You are not here to pray,’ says Brother Anselm Tarr. ‘Good. I have run out of things to say to people who are.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_priest)
pages.page: Eogan takes in the road on your boots, and that you have come straight to him, and waits to hear what you have brought.

pages.label: go(region__s1_approach_way,region__s1_green)
pages.page: Boats lie drawn up keel to keel on the shingle at Lowmouth, and the houses come right down to them, nets hung on every fence. The air is salt and tar, and the shingle rattles back with every wave. The boat-sheds are short of oak this year: the Hall has chained the road-wood, and the good timber is behind it. At dusk every dog in the town turns its head toward the hill, and the geese go silent. A bear is asleep on the ground by the players’ wagon, with a thin man for a pillow, and a big old man in a faded crimson coat sits on the wagon’s tail-board, squinting up at the sky. The gangway is drawn in. A boat is coming in under half its sail, and a man waits on the quay with a coil of rope over his arm. Lambert is crying wares along the street: pots mended, knives ground. Moll is eating a heel of dry bread, slowly. Baldric has an apron with a pocket for every tool and is mending a hinge, tapping the pin home with a small hammer. Nicol is reckoning the week’s takings on a slate. The inn’s dog noses along the foot of the wall of the Lucky Phoenix, following a smell from stone to stone. A thin brown cat crouches at the foot of a wall, watching a hole in it without a blink. Amaranth grows in the gardens about the green, its dark red tassels hanging over the beds. Bamboo grows in the gardens about the green in a dense clump, its canes knocking together in the wind. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. A tall wagon, painted with a sun and a moon and the words GOSSE’S COMPANY in red letters gone pink, stands on the landing at Lowmouth with its shafts down. A chain runs from its back wheel to a post, and the chain has a padlock on it. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. The spring-head by the green has been running low for a year. The rope comes up with a hand’s depth of brown water in the bucket and a smell of wet stone, and the women who draw it do so in silence, to save breath. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Lowmouth, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. A drover’s boy of fourteen, seen on the hill the morning after the herd crossed it, is here. So are Absalom Gosse, Hepzibah Dimmock and Jem Pudding. Patience ambles to the end of her rope to see who you are, and goes through your hands for honey.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_tie_boy)
pages.page: A boy of fourteen or so sits on the well-curb with his bundle between his feet, done with arguing. ‘I was after the cattle,’ he says. ‘Nobody asks what I was after.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r8)
pages.page: Moll sighs before you have said a word. ‘Go on, then.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r10)
pages.page: Nicol looks you up and down. ‘Whatever it is, the answer’s probably no. Go on.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r7)
pages.page: Lambert looks at you a long moment before speaking.

pages.label: talk_to(players__pudding)
pages.page: A thin man with a face like a folded napkin is lying on his back on the ground with a bear’s head on his stomach. He raises one hand without moving anything else. ‘Mind her,’ he says. ‘She is asleep, and she is a duchess when she wakes.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r9)
pages.page: Baldric takes in the state of you: the road dust, the tiredness. ‘You’ve come a way. What do you need?’

pages.label: talk_to(players__hepzibah)
pages.page: A small grey woman sits on the tail-board with a book on her knee and a pencil in her hair, sewing a gold braid back onto a king’s cloak. She looks at you over her spectacles and goes on sewing.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_hesper)
pages.page: A girl in a leather apron, with soot to the elbows and a roll of paper under her arm, looks you up and down. ‘Can you carry? Can you keep quiet? Can you stand still while somebody takes a measurement?’

pages.label: talk_to(players__gosse)
pages.page: A big old man in a coat that was crimson once rises from the wagon’s tail-board with his hand on his heart, as if you were the Margrave. ‘A face from the world,’ he says, in a voice that would carry to the back of a field. ‘Absalom Gosse, of Gosse’s Company, at your service and very much at your mercy.’

pages.label: go(region__s1_sheds_way,region__s1_sheds)
pages.page: Long low sheds stand open to the water, with boats inside in every stage of being built or mended: ribs like a whale’s, an oar with a split blade. Shavings and tar lie thick underfoot, and an adze knocks at the back. Aldith is caulking a seam along the boat’s side with oakum and a mallet. A hull stands half planked in the nearest shed, its ribs bare at the stern.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r1)
pages.page: Aldith looks up, and puts her hands still, and waits for you to say what you want.

pages.label: search(region__s1_sheds)
pages.page: You search the boat-sheds with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: look_closely(region__s1_sheds_hull)
pages.page: You look closely at the hull half planked. A name is chalked on the stem, rubbed out, and chalked again: her builder has not settled what to call her.

pages.label: region__s1_r1_where
pages.page: ‘Willow? By the water, same as everywhere,’ says Aldith. ‘There’s a good stand on the road between Lowmouth and Mistshaw, and along the old bank in Elmholt. Strip the bark, not the wood.’

pages.label: go(region__s1_herbs_door,region__s1_green)
pages.page: Boats lie drawn up keel to keel on the shingle at Lowmouth, and the houses come right down to them, nets hung on every fence. The air is close and wet, and the flies are bad. The hay stands in cocks in the meadows, and swallows hunt low over the grass. Lambert is crying wares along the street: pots mended, knives ground. Moll is eating a heel of dry bread, slowly. Baldric has an apron with a pocket for every tool and is mending a hinge, tapping the pin home with a small hammer. Nicol is reckoning the week’s takings on a slate. The inn’s dog noses along the foot of the wall of the Lucky Phoenix, following a smell from stone to stone. A thin brown cat crouches at the foot of a wall, watching a hole in it without a blink. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. A tall wagon, painted with a sun and a moon and the words GOSSE’S COMPANY in red letters gone pink, stands on the landing at Lowmouth with its shafts down. A chain runs from its back wheel to a post, and the chain has a padlock on it. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. The spring-head by the green has been running low for a year. The rope comes up with a hand’s depth of brown water in the bucket and a smell of wet stone, and the women who draw it do so in silence, to save breath. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Lowmouth, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. A drover’s boy of fourteen, seen on the hill the morning after the herd crossed it, is here. So are Absalom Gosse, Hepzibah Dimmock and Jem Pudding.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_pit_path,region__s1_u_pit)
pages.page: A bowl of grey stone cut out of the hill long ago, ivy over its faces. At the bottom a square adit goes back into the rock behind a barred gate. A board on the gate says KEEP OUT in three hands. Low on the north face, where the ivy has pulled away, is a mark no quarryman cut. It is a wheel with no wing, its strokes worn soft.

pages.label: listen(region__s1_u_adit_lock)
pages.page: You put an ear to the padlock on the adit gate, and hold your breath. There is nothing to hear from it.

pages.label: search(region__s1_u_pit)
pages.page: You search the old quarry pit with care, a little at a time. You turn the spoil over, a stone at a time. Under the last of the broken face, a flint with a hole worn through it comes up into your hand. It is somebody’s luck, dropped and never found.

pages.label: wait_for_dark
pages.page: The light goes. It is dark.

pages.label: wait_for_light
pages.page: The sky greys, then lightens. It is morning. It is a long time since you slept. You are weary, and will fight the worse for it until you sleep.

pages.label: push(region__s1_u_adit_lock)
pages.page: You push at the padlock on the adit gate, then pull. It does not shift, either way.

pages.label: change_thing(region__s1_u_adit_lock_force)
pages.page: It holds, and holds, and then it does not, all at once, with a crack that anyone near will have heard. The adit gate’s padlock hangs open on its chain.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_bone_arch,region__s1_u_crypt)
pages.page: It is pitch dark. Without a light you can see nothing here, and do nothing that needs seeing.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_brood_way,region__s1_u_gallery)
pages.page: It is pitch dark. Without a light you can see nothing here, and do nothing that needs seeing. In the dark you can hear the spider in the old workings close by. The spider in the old workings stands its ground and watches you. It will not have you here for long. The spider in the old workings is watching you. In 10 minutes it will be on you.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_brood_way,region__s1_u_brood)
pages.page: White sacs the size of loaves hang from the roof in a cluster, and something in them moves. The spiders’ mother crouches over them, and will not let you near. The spiders’ mother, a spider the size of a pony, swollen and slow, crouched over the eggs at the back of the web, is here. The spiders’ mother will not let you come any nearer. The spiders’ mother is watching you. In 10 minutes it will be on you.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_drain_mouth,region__s1_u_drain)
pages.page: It is pitch dark. Without a light you can see nothing here, and do nothing that needs seeing. In the dark you can hear a great centipede close by. A great centipede stands its ground and watches you. It will not have you here for long. A great centipede is watching you. In 10 minutes it will be on you.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_drain_way,region__s1_u_warren)
pages.page: It is pitch dark. Without a light you can see nothing here, and do nothing that needs seeing. In the dark you can hear the rats under the corn-store close by. The rats under the corn-store stand their ground and watch you. They will not have you here for long. The rats under the corn-store are watching you. In 10 minutes they will be on you.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_trap,region__s1_u_store)
pages.page: Sacks are stacked to the rafters, and the place smells of mice. A sack of grain weighs down a trapdoor in the floor, and every wall is gnawed through at its foot.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You owe Mik fifty coin, for a cart of salt that went into the river at the ford last spring. The oxen went too. Mik has been patient, and wrote to say so. Patient until market day, ten days from now: not a day longer. Lowmouth has not changed. You come in off the road with your head down, past faces that knew you once. You go straight to Mik’s door: better it is done at once. 50 coin by market day, owed to Mik, salter at Lowmouth.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word9__h3_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Fengate: the fallen walls in the fen north of Mistshaw,’ says Mik. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “fen gate”.’ ‘At Fengate, where the brook goes under the road-wall, the arch is wide enough to crawl in, and the water that comes out of it is warmer than brook water has any right to be,’ says Mik. Fengate is the name of the fallen walls they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word1__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘A factor at the inn buys old bronze by the pound and asks no questions: bells, weir-metal, green fittings from the plough,’ says Mik.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word13__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘A company of the barefoot is walking the old road from town to town, chalking the milestones and calling out their numbers, and the Bench does not like it,’ says Mik.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word12__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘The head of the Chapter of the Standing Stone has had no word from one of its halls since the quarter-day, and has sent no one, for want of anyone who can be spared,’ says Mik.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word9__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘The old paved road bends once at Fengate, eight miles round a hill that has nothing in it to bend for,’ says Mik. ‘Carters leave a coin at the bend and do not stop. Some say the hill hums.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_merchant)
pages.page: Mik looks at your hands before your face, to see whether there is anything in them.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word10__h2_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Black Barrow: a grassed mound in the fen east of Mistshaw,’ says Mik. ‘The shire-reeve’s clerk is raising a levy and is short of iron and gold,’ says Mik. ‘He will pay by the weight for the torc of the king of the great howe on the ridge, or for any torc of the Barrow-Kin.’ Black Barrow is the name of the grassed mound east of Mistshaw they speak of.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r10)
pages.page: ‘Let me guess,’ says Nicol. ‘You want something.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r7)
pages.page: Lambert finishes what he was saying to someone else first.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_avenue,region__s1_manor_front)
pages.page: A house of the grey stone of the hill, long and gabled, its windows set in rows, smoke going up from three chimneys. The forecourt is raked gravel round a mounting-block. The steward keeps all this, and keeps it well. The front door stands open. The door in the garden wall is on the latch. Wystan Hale, the gamekeeper of the Hall, once a castellan’s spearman, who has been told to stand at the road-wood chain and let nobody cut, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_manor_keeper)
pages.page: Wystan Hale does not move from the end of the chain. ‘Not today,’ he says, not unkindly. ‘Tell the reeve it’s not today. Tell him it’s not been today for six years.’

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_gate,region__s1_manor_garden)
pages.page: A garden inside high walls, clipped hedges and gravel walks round a fountain. In the walls, here and there, a stone is cut with marks that were not made by the masons who laid it. The door in the garden wall is on the latch.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_steps,region__s1_manor_loggia)
pages.page: An open walk of columns along the garden side of the house, out of the wind. The country goes away below it to the river, and above the roofs of Lowmouth the hill stands up with its old stones on top.

pages.label: search(region__s1_manor_loggia)
pages.page: You search the loggia with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_arches,region__s1_manor_hall)
pages.page: The hall goes up the whole height of the house to a roof of dark beams. A fire is laid in a hearth carved with the arms of the house, and the long table under the windows is set for nobody. The front door stands open. The steward of the Hall, the steward who keeps the Hall while the family is away, a precise person with a ring of keys, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_manor_steward)
pages.page: ‘Yes?’ says the steward of the Hall, without hurry.

pages.label: search(region__s1_manor_hall)
pages.page: You search the great hall with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_libdoor,region__s1_manor_library)
pages.page: Books to the ceiling on three walls, a ladder on a rail, and a table under the window with the house’s papers squared on it. The press-door in the library is shut, and has been so long that the paint has joined it to the frame. It has a keyhole, a good one. A thick book bound in calf lies on the table, the house’s arms on the cover: its history, in a careful amateur’s hand.

pages.label: listen(region__s1_manor_press)
pages.page: You put an ear to the muniment-press door, and hold your breath. There is nothing to hear from it.

pages.label: search(region__s1_manor_library)
pages.page: You search the library with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: change_thing(region__s1_manor_book_read)
pages.page: They dressed limestone so true it needed no mortar, cast sluice-gates of bronze as tall as a house, and ran lead pipes through the hills for miles. They held that water remembers: a valley kept under water could not be taken, and still water, rightly read, showed what was coming. So the house’s historian says of the Water-Wardens, and that the dome on the hill was where they laid their dead, or meant to, and that the folk would not go near it even then. The history of the house begins long before the house, with the Water-Wardens on the hill, and goes on to the kingdom of Aergodríce and who held the land under it.

pages.label: light_item(region__party_1__torch)
pages.page: You light a torch.

pages.label: wait
pages.page: Time passes.

pages.label: take_item(region__s1_manor_box,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: Wenna gains 12 experience: found a silver music box.

pages.label: wait_for_light
pages.page: The sky greys, then lightens. It is morning.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You have come over the hills into Merscfaenn with your trade and not much else. There is work in any country for someone who will do what others will not. The place to hear of it is the inn. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Lowmouth: low roofs against the sky, masts at the landing, salt-houses black with tar. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Look at the boundary stones in the inn’s back garden: the innkeeper and the merchant are at odds over them.

pages.label: go(circus__tober_lane_a,circus__tober_a)
pages.page: A grazing field outside Lowmouth, sloping a little toward the road, with a five-barred gate and a lime tree. The big top stands in the middle of the field, striped red and dirty white, its king-pole flying a pennant that says WAPSHOTT’S in letters gone pink. Guy-ropes run out from it to stakes in every direction, so that walking anywhere is a kind of dance. Before the flap a painted front of boards announces THE GRAND PEREGRINE CIRCUS & HIPPODRAMA, PATRONIZED BY THE NOBILITY, and someone has written under it in chalk, WHICH NOBILITY. The big top’s king-pole stands up through the canvas, and the pennant snaps. Ada Thripp, the circus’s book-keeper, is here. Signor Cornelius Fipps, the circus’s bandmaster, is here. Gideon Lusk, the circus’s boss canvasman, is here. So are Nance Tibbet and Sidney Quirk. The field gate stands open and the grass inside it is already trodden into paths. A smell of horse and oranges and wet canvas, a dog asleep on a coil of rope, and a man somewhere out of sight shouting HEAVE in a voice like a gong. You have walked into a circus.

pages.label: talk_to(circus__fipps)
pages.page: A round man with a round face and a black wooden horn wound three times round his body is polishing the horn’s mouthpiece on his waistcoat. ‘Fipps,’ he says. ‘Signor Fipps, for the profession; Cornelius to my friends; Corny to the Colonel, who has no idea how much I mind. The band, sir: myself on the serpent, young Tom Gale on cornet, and Abel Rudd on the drum, who is deaf, which is a help.’ He pats the horn. ‘This is the serpent. She is very old and she has a crack, and there are three notes she will not play, and one of them is the one we need.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__quirk)
pages.page: A thin man with a paste-pot in one hand, a brush in the other and a roll of bills under each arm is pasting a bill to the wall at a speed that suggests he has been asked to stop. ‘Quirk!’ he says. ‘Advance agent, Wapshott’s. I go a day ahead and bill everything that holds still. Walls, barns, gates, a hearse, once, by mistake, though the family were very good about it.’ He looks at you with professional interest. ‘You’re nice and flat across the back. Hold still a moment.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__nance)
pages.page: An old woman in nine shawls, rings on every finger and two on one thumb, is sitting on the steps of a black wagon with SIBYL on it in gold, smoking a clay pipe. ‘Nance Tibbet,’ she says, ‘the Sibyl of the Seven Rivers, which the Colonel made up; I’m from a town with one river and that one’s mostly mud.’ She looks at your face the way a horse-coper looks at teeth. ‘You want to know something. Everybody who comes to the Sibyl wants to know something. It’s usually something they know already.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__lusk)
pages.page: A very large man with a beard like a hedge and hands like spades is splicing a rope with his teeth and one hand. He takes the rope out of his teeth. ‘Lusk,’ he says. That seems to be all. Then, after a while: ‘Canvas.’ Then, after another while, as if he had thought hard about whether you deserved it: ‘Mind the guys.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__ada)
pages.page: A young woman in a green bonnet with ink on her fingers sits in the hatch of the ticket wagon with a cash-box, a ledger and a pencil behind each ear. ‘Ada Thripp,’ she says. ‘I keep the books. Somebody has to; the Colonel thinks a ledger is a kind of hat.’ She looks you up and down as if pricing you. ‘If you have come to be paid, the answer is Thursday. If you have come to pay, you are the first this week and I could kiss you.’

pages.label: go(circus__back_a,circus__yard_a)
pages.page: Behind the big top is the backyard, where the circus lives: horse lines, a cookhouse fire with a kettle on a chain, washing on the guy-ropes, a heap of hay, a man asleep in a barrow. Through the gap in the canvas you can hear the ring. Honoria Bulstrode’s cookhouse fire burns under a black kettle and a pot the size of a font. Honoria Bulstrode is frying bacon by the hundredweight in a pan like a cartwheel, and the whole circus is queuing for it in its nightshirts, in order of precedence: the Colonel first, then Bucephalus, then everyone else. Mumchance, the circus’s old clown, is here. Honoria Bulstrode, the Ox of Abernant, strongwoman and cook, is here. Billie Ostrander, the circus’s horse-keeper, is here. ‘You’ve not eaten,’ Honoria says to Mumchance. ‘I’ve eaten,’ says Mumchance. ‘You’ve not eaten properly,’ says Honoria, and gives him a bowl, and he eats it, and neither of them says anything else, and it is the most married thing you have ever seen. Bucephalus looks at you down the length of his nose, decides you have no apples, and looks at the horizon instead.

pages.label: talk_to(circus__billie)
pages.page: A broad-shouldered woman in a man’s coat and gaiters, with a curry-comb in one hand and an apple in the other, is grooming an old grey horse who is pretending not to notice. ‘Wilhelmina Ostrander,’ she says. ‘Billie. I keep the horses: the four ponies and His Lordship here, Bucephalus, who keeps himself. My father was a drover. I’ve been kicked by everything with legs.’ She hands the horse the apple. ‘Don’t feed him. He’ll tell you he’s starving. He’s lying.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__mumchance)
pages.page: An old man sits on an upturned bucket in his shirtsleeves, painting his face white in a bit of mirror nailed to a wagon wheel. He has a long, lined, patient face, like a horse that has seen everything twice. He finishes the line of his mouth before he looks at you. ‘They call me Mumchance,’ he says, in a soft dry voice that you have to lean toward, ‘because in the ring I never say a word. Out here I say several.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__honoria)
pages.page: A woman as wide as a doorway, in a flowered apron, is lifting a cauldron off the fire one-handed and setting it on the grass as if it were a teacup. ‘Honoria Bulstrode,’ she says, wiping her hand to shake yours, which she does gently, like someone who has broken hands before by accident. ‘The Ox of Abernant on the bills; Mrs Bulstrode at the stove. Have you eaten? You haven’t. Sit there. No, there. The other one’s a goose.’

pages.label: go(circus__ring_curtain_a,circus__ring_a)
pages.page: Inside, the big top is brown and warm and smells of trodden grass, sawdust, horse and oranges. Benches rise on scaffolding round the ring, which is a low wall of painted boards forty-two feet across, because that is the size a horse likes to canter in. High up between the two king-poles a wire is strung, so fine you lose it against the canvas. The ring’s painted boards are scuffed with a hundred towns’ boots. Pip Gallant, the circus’s ring-girl and Mumchance’s apprentice, is here. Hal Quincey, a tumbler, one of the Brothers Quincey, is here. Dunstan Quincey, a tumbler, one of the Brothers Quincey, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(circus__hal)
pages.page: A square young man in tights and a striped jersey is doing handsprings across the sawdust, one after another, very fast, as if to get away from something. He lands in front of you. ‘Hal Quincey,’ he says. ‘The elder. By eleven minutes. The better, by more than that. If you’re looking for my brother, he’s the one over there pretending he can’t see me.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__pip)
pages.page: A girl of seventeen or so, all elbows, with a broom twice her height and sawdust in her hair, falls over the broom, rolls, comes up on her feet, and bows. ‘Meant that,’ she says. ‘Pip Gallant. I sweep the ring and hold the hoops and I’m going to be the greatest clown since Mumchance, only he says I have to learn to fall first, and I’ve been learning to fall for two years, and I can fall really well now, look.’ She falls over again.

pages.label: search(circus__ring_a)
pages.page: You search the big top with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: talk_to(circus__dunstan)
pages.page: A square young man in tights and a striped jersey, the image of the other one across the ring, is stretching his hamstrings with tremendous dignity. ‘Dunstan Quincey,’ he says. ‘Of the Brothers Quincey. There is, for the time being, only one Brother Quincey. Tell the other one that, if he asks. He won’t ask. He’s too proud. It’s the only thing he ever invented.’

pages.label: wait_watch
pages.page: It is rehearsal. The Brothers Quincey are tumbling, one at each end of the ring, not looking at each other. Pip is holding a hoop for nobody. Up on the wire the Sylph is walking very slowly back and forth, back and forth, in a grey practice dress, like somebody pacing a landing at night. Colonel Florian Wapshott and Mumchance and Mademoiselle Zéphyrine and Honoria Bulstrode and Bucephalus and Signor Cornelius Fipps come where you are.

pages.label: talk_to(circus__zephyrine)
pages.page: She is Mademoiselle Zéphyrine, the Sylph of the Wire. A slight woman with her hair scraped up in a silver net, her feet in soft kid slippers, is doing something to the inside of one ankle with a strip of linen, very slowly, as if the ankle were a violin. ‘I am Zéphyrine,’ she says, in an accent that comes from somewhere, though perhaps not from anywhere in particular. ‘The Sylph. Of the Wire.’ She looks at you with very still grey eyes. ‘You have come to look at me. Everyone does. It is permitted.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__wapshott)
pages.page: A big man in a crimson coat with frogging across the chest, a moustache dyed the black of a new boot, and a voice like a church organ with the stops out, takes your hand before you have offered it. ‘Colonel Florian Augustus Wapshott,’ he says, ‘Proprietor, Ringmaster, and Sole Patentee of the Grand Peregrine Circus and Hippodrama, at your service, and very much at your disposal, and if you are from the Rates, I am not here.’ He considers you. ‘You are not from the Rates. You have an honest face. I have one myself; I keep it for Sundays.’

pages.label: take_leave(circus__pip)
pages.page: ‘Come back and tell me how it goes!’ calls Pip Gallant after you.

pages.label: circus__give_rations
pages.page: Honoria takes them as if they were a bunch of violets. ‘That’s thirty dinners’ worth of soup,’ she says, which cannot be true, and somehow is.

pages.label: circus__wap_money
pages.page: ‘Splendidly,’ says the Colonel. ‘Brilliantly. The houses are full, the public is enraptured, and the money comes in like the tide.’ A pause. ‘And goes out like it. Ask Ada. No, don’t ask Ada; she will show you the book, and the book is a pessimist.’

pages.label: talk_to(circus__pip)
pages.page: ‘Hullo!’ says Pip, from somewhere she has just landed.

pages.label: circus__lend_colonel
pages.page: The Colonel takes the coins as a bishop takes a relic, and kisses one, and gives them to Ada, who was standing behind him and did not want him to see her face. ‘You will be repaid,’ he says, ‘TENFOLD.’ Ada writes down: ten.

pages.label: circus__pip_cant
pages.page: ‘Oh!’ Pip sits down on a bucket, delighted to be asked. ‘The tober’s the ground. The flatties are you lot, the town, no offence. A joey is a clown, after Joey Pell, who was the first one, at Dunmere, a hundred years ago, and could make a whole house cry by eating a string of sausages. A kinker’s a performer, a grafter’s a canvasman, the half is half an hour before the show, and the bunce is what’s left in the box after, which is never anything.’ She thinks. ‘And if you ever hear somebody shout Hey Rube, you drop what you’re holding and run toward it, whatever it is. That’s the oldest one. That’s for when the flatties come for the tober with sticks. It hasn’t happened since I’ve been here.’ She looks pleased and a little disappointed. ‘Mumchance says it happened at Wakeham.’

pages.label: circus__mum_silence
pages.page: ‘Because a laugh,’ says Mumchance, ‘is a thing the audience does, not a thing I do. If I talk, I tell them what is funny. If I don’t, they have to find it themselves, and what you find yourself you keep.’ He considers the white of his face in the mirror. ‘Also when I was young I had a voice like a gate and they threw things.’

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: The map is inside your shirt, where it has been since the night you won it. It is a square of greased hide with the hills drawn on it in soot. On it are Ironkeep out in the fen north-west of Mistshaw, and a cross at its door. The drover you won it from laughed when he lost it. In the morning he was dead in the straw, and nobody in the inn would say of what. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Lowmouth: low roofs against the sky, masts at the landing, salt-houses black with tar. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. The dead man’s map marks Ironkeep, out in the fen north-west of Mistshaw, with a cross at its door. Search there.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r1)
pages.page: Aldith hears you come, and finishes what she was doing before she looks round.

pages.label: take_leave(region__s1_r1)
pages.page: Aldith lifts a hand, once.

pages.label: light_item(region__party_1__candle)
pages.page: You light a candle.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r1)
pages.page: Aldith inclines her head, and says nothing.

pages.label: wait_watch
pages.page: Nothing comes, and nothing changes. The hours go by.

pages.label: douse_light(region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You put the light out, and what was left of it is spent.

pages.label: go(walk__gate_a,walk__camp_a)
pages.page: The Station arch stands open, with the old stone beyond it. A yard behind a stable, given over to the Walk: straw on the ground in rows, fire-rings of ash-wood, staves stacked in threes against the wall, and a line of washed heel-cloths drying on a rope. Whoever is in charge sits where the draught is least. A number is chalked above every door.

pages.label: go(walk__arch_a,walk__station_a)
pages.page: The Station arch stands open, with the old stone beyond it. The Station is a roofed rest beside an old milestone: three posts and a slate roof, a stone bench, and the milestone itself, a squat grey column with the Office’s wheel cut in the top and a number cut below it that was recut, in a newer hand, over an older number. Ash from a hundred small fires lies in the bench’s corners.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__ring)
pages.page: You set ring mail down.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__dead_mans_map)
pages.page: You set a dead man’s map down.

pages.label: take_item(region__party_1__battleaxe,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take a battleaxe.

pages.label: take_item(region__party_1__pole,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take a ten-foot pole.

pages.label: go(walk__arch_a,walk__station_a)
pages.page: The Station arch stands open, with the old stone beyond it.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: Her last letter is in your coat, read so often it has come apart at the folds. She was going out to Ironkeep, in the fen north-west of Mistshaw, with two men from Lowmouth who swore there was silver in it. She would write when she was rich. The two men came back at the end of the summer. She did not, and they will not say why. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Lowmouth: low roofs against the sky, masts at the landing, salt-houses black with tar. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Your sister went into Ironkeep, out in the fen north-west of Mistshaw, and did not come out. Search there for any sign of her.

pages.label: go(region__s1_shrine_door,region__s1_shrine)
pages.page: A well-head with a carved lip, the water close under it: the well-head of Nodens, Lord of Nature. A wreath of ivy hangs on it, cut fresh at each new moon. Offerings of salt lie before it. Under the lamp at the back, a young acolyte in a grey habit is copying the offering-book’s yearly sums onto a slate. A stair goes up inside the tower wall, worn hollow in the middle of every step, to where the bell hangs. A man lies on the shrine’s bier under a grey cloth, his boots still on. A wood-warden’s mark is tied at his belt. The offering-box by the lamp is shut, its lock whole, and light in the hand: the little bronze things that were left in it have gone, and the coppers have not. Eogan, the priest of Nodens, is here. Brother Anselm Tarr, the priest’s acolyte, who has read everything the shrine owns and wants to know what it leaves out, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_priest)
pages.page: Eogan grins before you have said anything at all. ‘You look like a person with a question.’

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word9__h2_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘Fengate: the fallen walls in the fen north of Mistshaw,’ says Eogan. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “fen gate”.’ ‘Dogs will not go into the hollow beyond Fengate, and an old priest said the ground there hummed on feast days, a long low note that the monks of the old order tried to sing against, and could not,’ says Eogan. Fengate is the name of the fallen walls they speak of.

pages.label: change_thing(region__s1_shrine_view_climb)
pages.page: From the top of the tower Lowmouth lies below you, its roofs and its yards, and the country round it as far as the light goes. To the east, not far off: the edge of Oakhurst by Lowmouth. To the north-west, not far off: the march-stone of Fencarr. To the north-east, some way off: a great long mound with a door of stone. The way to a great long mound with a door of stone: to the edge of Oakhurst by Lowmouth, and on to the holly hollow in Oakhurst, where the track to it starts. To the east, some way off: Ironkeep. To the south-east, some way off: the charcoal-burners’ clearing in Oakhurst. To the north-east, some way off: the holly hollow in Oakhurst. The way down is the stair you came up.

pages.label: take_leave(region__s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘Come back and tell me how it goes!’ calls Eogan after you.

pages.label: go(fellowship__door_a,region__s1_green)
pages.page: Boats lie drawn up keel to keel on the shingle at Lowmouth, and the houses come right down to them, nets hung on every fence. Lambert is crying wares along the street: pots mended, knives ground. Moll is eating a heel of dry bread, slowly. Baldric has an apron with a pocket for every tool and is mending a hinge, tapping the pin home with a small hammer. Nicol is reckoning the week’s takings on a slate. The inn’s dog noses along the foot of the wall of the Lucky Phoenix, following a smell from stone to stone. A thin brown cat crouches at the foot of a wall, watching a hole in it without a blink. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. A tall wagon, painted with a sun and a moon and the words GOSSE’S COMPANY in red letters gone pink, stands on the landing at Lowmouth with its shafts down. A chain runs from its back wheel to a post, and the chain has a padlock on it. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. The spring-head by the green has been running low for a year. The rope comes up with a hand’s depth of brown water in the bucket and a smell of wet stone, and the women who draw it do so in silence, to save breath. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Lowmouth, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. A drover’s boy of fourteen, seen on the hill the morning after the herd crossed it, is here. So are Absalom Gosse, Hepzibah Dimmock and Jem Pudding.

pages.label: go(region__gate_pentrice_road,region__gate_pentrice)
pages.page: It is hot on the road, and you walk slower than you meant to. An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. The road goes on into the vale of the Arle. Ahead, a minster tower over a river town, where one river falls into another.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_pentrice,region__t65)
pages.page: A long low field, buttercups to the knee, and the smell of hay on the air. To the north-east the land rises. Mistshaw is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw65_86,region__t86)
pages.page: You set out from open fields south-west of Mistshaw. The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. To the south-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw65_85,region__t85)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Pine wood, the ground soft with needles and the smell of resin heavy in the still air. To the south the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_tallow,region__t104)
pages.page: Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. To the east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw103_123,region__t103)
pages.page: Pine wood, the ground soft with needles and the smell of resin heavy in the still air. To the north-east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw83_102,region__t102)
pages.page: Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. Reed-beds whispering in the wind, and a bittern in them booming like a blown jar. To the north-east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_pellam,region__t83)
pages.page: A stand of tall trees with little under them, so that you can see a long way between the trunks, and nothing moving. To the east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw82_83,region__t82)
pages.page: The path goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it. A causey of old turves across the marsh, and on either side of it water that does not show how deep it is. To the east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw62_82,region__t62)
pages.page: Water stands on both sides, and the path between is soft enough to take the print of your boot and keep it. A causey of old turves across the marsh, and on either side of it water that does not show how deep it is. To the south-east the land rises. Lowmouth is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke. Tracks cross the ground here, heavy and fresh and all going the one way, north-east, and the same tracks older under them: something uses this way often.

pages.label: go(region__tw42_62,region__t42)
pages.page: Night comes on while you are still on the path, and you walk the last of it in the dark. Birch and rowan on a slope, the light coming white through the leaves. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight.

pages.label: go(region__tw22_42,region__t22)
pages.page: It is hot on the path, and you walk slower than you meant to. Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. Lowmouth is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw22_23,region__t23)
pages.page: Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. To the east the land rises. Lowmouth is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw23_24,region__t24)
pages.page: Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. To the east the land rises. Woundwort grows thick in a wet hollow under the trees, purple-flowered and rank-smelling: the herb the hedge-doctors bind on cuts.

pages.label: go(region__tw24_44,region__t44)
pages.page: Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tr44_s1_s4_way,region__s1_s4_way)
pages.page: The road between Lowmouth and Mistshaw goes through scattered woods and the clearings of charcoal-burners. Deer go off between the trees without a sound. By the road stands an old milestone, worn to a stub, with a wheel cut in it and something over the wheel that might once have been a crown. Cattle fill the road from hedge to hedge, going to Lowmouth, and Martin, the drover, is whistling among them. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Meadowsweet grows thick along the wet ground, a froth of cream flowers that smells of almonds and honey. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. Comfrey grows rank by the water, hairy-leaved, its bells hanging: knitbone, the herb-wives call it. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Foxgloves stand tall at the wood’s edge, purple bells speckled inside: they heal, prepared rightly, and kill otherwise. Feverwort grows along the road in the rough grass, bitter-leaved: the herb-wives dry it for a child’s fever. Bamboo grows along the road in a dense clump, its canes knocking together in the wind. Banewort grows along the road, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Celandine grows along the road, yellow-starred in the damp. Cinquefoil runs over the ground along the road, its small yellow flowers five-petalled. Daffodils grow along the road in a bank, their strap-leaves in clumps. Alhuren grows along the road, silver-leaved, its blue flowers pale as a candle-flame. Gentian grows along the road, its blue trumpets open to the sun. Woodbine climbs along the road, its cream and yellow flowers sweet at dusk. Staggerweed grows along the road, tall, with spurred blue flowers. Pennyroyal grows along the road, low and minty, with small purple flowers. Thyme grows along the road in low mats, flowering purple. Tansy grows along the road, its yellow buttons over feathery leaves. Sweetgrass grows along the road, its long blades smelling of hay. A dropberry bush grows along the road, its red berries hanging in strings. Carenfil grows along the road, pale-petalled, its scent heavy on still days. Groundbread grows along the road, broad-leaved, with small white flowers. Ofbit grows along the road on thin stems, its flowers blue. Betony stands in the short grass at the wood’s edge, purple-spiked: the hedge herb, for a cut or a sting.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_s4_way_t)
pages.page: ‘Come in, come in, whoever you are,’ says Martin. ‘Everybody else has.’

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: The scroll-case has not been off your shoulder in eleven days. In it is a letter under the seal of a widow in the town you came from, for Edrick at Mistshaw, into no other hands. Half the fee was paid at the start. The other half, and whatever Edrick thinks it worth, is at the far end of the road. The next town on from Lowmouth is Mistshaw. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Lowmouth: low roofs against the sky, masts at the landing, salt-houses black with tar. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Carry the sealed letter to Edrick at Mistshaw, into no other hands.

pages.label: go(circus__orchard_path_a,circus__orchard_a)
pages.page: Old apple trees in long grass, grey with lichen, and between them the bee-skeps on their stands like a village of straw beehive houses. Three of the skeps are smashed, and the grass round them is torn up, and the bark of the nearest tree is clawed in long pale scores higher than a man. Goody Tarrant, the bee-wife of the orchards, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(circus__tarrant)
pages.page: A woman with a veil pushed up over her hat and a smoker in her hand is sitting on an upturned skep among the wreck of three others. ‘Six skeps,’ she says. ‘In a fortnight. It comes at dusk. It’s as big as a bullock and it’s got a face like an owl, and it eats the comb and the bees and all, and screams.’ She looks at you. ‘If you’re going to kill it, kill it. If you’re not, I don’t want to hear about it.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘A stranger!’ says Eogan, pleased. ‘Sit, if you like. Ask, if you like.’

pages.label: take_healing(region__s1_priest,region__s1_priest_healing)
pages.page: Eogan cleans and dresses every wound in the company.

pages.label: players__priest_players_again
pages.page: Eogan smiles, and then tries not to. ‘They played the Shepherd’s Revenge here on Tuesday, and the clown sat in my place at the front and gave a sermon, and I am still not sure whether I should have minded.’ Then, more soberly: ‘The man who went off with the hat was Lem Coyle, who leads their bear. He was not a bad man at the shrine. I saw him go out along the common toward the old lime-kiln, with the hat under his coat like a hen.’

pages.label: region__s1_priest_coins
pages.page: ‘The faith says nothing of it,’ says Eogan, ‘and the folk have done it since before the faith. A coin at the numbered stone, a coin at the Lady’s bowl wherever one is found, and nobody can say whose lady. I have forbidden nothing. I have not looked closely. Anselm has looked closely, which is why I have not.’

pages.label: change_thing(region__s1_box_look)
pages.page: Somebody on the road, in a road-cloak, who did not mind being seen leaving. Inside: a thread of travelling-cloth caught on the lid’s hinge, the grey of a road-cloak, and a smear where a hand slid in sideways.

pages.label: region__s1_accuse_wrong
pages.page: Brother Anselm Tarr stares. ‘The apprentice? She has never taken a thing in her life that she did not make.’ But he is already thinking about the bell, and the bronze, and the soot on her hands, and you see him decide, against his own judgement. ‘I will have to speak to the priest,’ he says.

pages.label: quarrel__priest_stones
pages.page: ‘They were moved in the spring,’ says Eogan. ‘I married Eamon’s parents in that garden; I know where the stones stood. But Mik gives the most at the shrine, and I have a roof to mend.’

pages.label: region__s1_tie_ask
pages.page: ‘Every spring,’ says Eogan, ‘the children of Lowmouth walk out to Ironkeep, in the fen north-west of Mistshaw, with a heel of bread each, and leave it on a heap of stones. Nobody remembers why. I have never forbidden it. It has been kicked over, and I cannot go. And you must understand that the town does not take that lightly. It is the one thing we do that is not for ourselves. They will find someone to have done it, if it is not mended by the second night, and there is a drover’s boy about who was seen on that hill. I should be sorry for it. But I cannot hold them to nothing.’

pages.label: take_leave(region__s1_anselm)
pages.page: ‘Look after yourself,’ says Brother Anselm Tarr. ‘I mean it.’

pages.label: quarrel__priest_witness
pages.page: Eogan is quiet a long time. Then: ‘The roof can leak.’ You go together to Mik’s, and Eogan says where the stones stood, and who married whom in that garden, and Mik hears it out red to the ears. ‘All right,’ Mik says at last. ‘They go back.’ Wenna makes the persuasion check (d20 12 + charisma 2 = 14 against 13). Wenna gains 300 experience: the boundary stones, seen through.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You have been three years on the other side of the hills, hiring out with the droves. Your mother’s letter took a week to find you. Your father went out on the road with the cart, it said, and did not come home. The road comes out from under the trees, and there is Brightbridge in its clearing. You see the river shining and the crossing over it, timber stacked to season along the road, and smoke from a dozen chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Look along the bridge over the Redwater by Brightbridge for your father, who went out by it with the cart and did not come home.

pages.label: go(region__s2_approach_way,region__s2_green)
pages.page: The road runs down between the houses of Brightbridge and straight into the Redwater, and comes out on the far bank dark with wet. The water is loud over the stones, and the bank smells of mud and trodden weed. Twice this month the Hall’s keeper has driven the town’s pigs off the verge of the old road. At dusk every dog in the town turns its head toward the hill, and the geese go silent. The bell is gone from its frame over the well. ‘Hobs,’ people say, and spit, ‘out of Joygate, where they’ve made their hold.’ Two drovers stand at the edge with sticks in the water, arguing whether it has risen since yesterday. Aldith is going round the cart wheel by wheel, a kick and a look at each. Wulfstan the miser is sorting rags by colour into three small heaps. Leofrun the avenger is running a stone along a blade in long, unhurried strokes. The inn’s dog lies across the doorstep of the Merry Sun with his chin on his paws, and watches who comes. A white cat sits in a window between two pots of herbs, watching the street. Your brother is sitting on a rail with your father’s old spear across his knees, watching the road. He is taller by a head than when you went away. A grey dog lies by the door of the taproom of the Merry Sun with her head on her paws, watching the road. She holds one forefoot off the ground. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. Asters grow in the gardens about the green in clumps, mauve with yellow eyes. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. The spring-head by the green has been running low for a year. The rope comes up with a hand’s depth of brown water in the bucket and a smell of wet stone, and the women who draw it do so in silence, to save breath. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Brightbridge, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. The surveyor’s son, a young man in a good coat, who says the measure was his father’s by gift and means to bring it home before anyone makes a fuss, is here. So is Wilkin Sedge. The grey dog gets up, stretches, and comes over to push her nose into your hand.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_r2)
pages.page: Aldith looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_r7)
pages.page: ‘You’re back, then,’ says Leofrun, as if you had been gone a week and not three years.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_r6)
pages.page: Wulfstan looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_tie_heir)
pages.page: A young man in a coat cut for a better year leans on the well-curb, watching the road. ‘My father’s measure,’ he says, before you have asked. ‘Given, not lent. There is nothing in writing, naturally. There never is, with a gift.’

pages.label: talk_to(drover__son)
pages.page: Wilkin Sedge gets up so fast the stool goes over, and then stands there, not sure what to do with his hands.

pages.label: go(region__s2_drill_gate,region__s2_drill)
pages.page: A square of beaten earth behind the Merry Sun, a rack of blunted blades along one wall and a post hacked pale at the height of a man’s neck. Whoever teaches here will show a technique to anyone who has done enough to be worth the showing, and can pay for it. Beatrix teaches Second Wind, Roundhouse Kick and Feint, 30 coin a lesson: an hour’s work, and only to one who has done enough out in the world to have earned it. On the rack by the gate, for sale and not for practice, are a fine scimitar, a fine shortsword and a fine shortbow. Beatrix, a master-at-arms, who teaches for 30 coin a lesson, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s2_drill_master)
pages.page: ‘You’re back, then,’ says Beatrix, as if you had been gone a week and not three years.

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s2_drill_master,region__s2_drill_master_fine_shortbow_1)
pages.page: Beatrix thinks it over, and names a lower price for a fine shortbow. Wenna Sedge makes the persuasion check (d20 17 + charisma -1 = 16 against 13).

pages.label: take_item(region__party_1__candle,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take a candle.

The inn’s dog lies across the doorstep of the Merry Sun with his chin on his paws, and watches who comes. A white cat sits in a window between two pots of herbs, watching the street.
