A hard wind is banging every shutter in the place. The wardens have stopped paying. A hayrick at Windscar has burned in the night, and the bailiff has put up a new notice: SIX CROWNS, AND A FINE FOR THE FIRE. The surveyor’s son has set out a table at the head of the market with a brass-bound measure on it, filled with water, and a small crowd in front, and a notice in a clerk’s hand: HONEST BY THE TOWN’S OWN MEASURE.

pages.label: go(region__s2_stones_way,region__s2_stones_top)
pages.page: The path comes out on the top of the hill among fallen stones. An arch stands on its own against the sky, and beyond it the broken wall of something long and high. Below, Brightbridge is all roofs and smoke. From up here the country lies open. Far off to the east you can make out a smooth doorway in a crag in Lonecrag.

pages.label: go(region__s2_stones_round,region__s2_stones_tree)
pages.page: A tree older than the stones, its trunk wider than a cart is long, its roots heaving up the turf. Strips of cloth are tied to its lowest branches, old and new: the folk of Brightbridge still come up here. There is room on the low branches for another strip of cloth.

pages.label: search(region__s2_stones_tree)
pages.page: You search the old tree with care, a little at a time. Where a root has heaved up the turf there is a gap, and in it, green with age, a bronze bracelet: an offering of somebody’s, before there was a Brightbridge.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__scale)
pages.page: You set scale mail down.

pages.label: change_thing(region__s2_stones_rags_tie)
pages.page: A strip of your own cloth hangs among the others on the old tree, and moves in the wind with them.

pages.label: go(region__s1_stones_up,region__s1_stones_top)
pages.page: The path comes out on the top of the hill among fallen stones.

pages.label: go(region__s2_stones_up,region__s2_stones_hall)
pages.page: A long hall with no roof. Steps go up at the far end to a dais, and on it stand figures cut from the stone, taller than men, their faces worn smooth. Grass grows between the floor-slabs. Letters are cut along the edge of the dais, deep and square, in no hand anyone in Brightbridge could read.

pages.label: go(region__s1_stones_arch,region__s1_stones_dome)
pages.page: A dome of stone as wide as a church, open to the sky in its crown, so that a round of light moves slowly over the floor through the day. Round the walls are low slabs, each with a hollow in it the length of a body, and nothing in any of them. Owls nest in the crown of the dome, and their pellets lie in the empty graves. Whatever the folk say comes up here after dark, it is only owls.

pages.label: search(region__s2_stones_dome)
pages.page: You search the dome with care, a little at a time. One slab among the graves has a bright edge where hands have shifted it. Under it, a stair goes down, steep and narrow; the slab is too heavy for hands that are not used to labour, and wants a strong back or a bar.

pages.label: go(region__s2_stones_arch,region__s2_stones_dome)
pages.page: A dome of stone as wide as a church, open to the sky in its crown, so that a round of light moves slowly over the floor through the day.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__longsword)
pages.page: You set a longsword down.

pages.label: go(region__s2_stones_arch,region__s2_stones_hall)
pages.page: A long hall with no roof. Letters are cut along the edge of the dais, deep and square, in no hand anyone in Brightbridge could read.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You have the letter inside your coat, from the brothers of your order to the priestess of Lugh at Newmeet. It asks that Wenna, who reads the old script, be given a bed and shown the way to Joygate. There is writing there that the order has heard of for a hundred years and never seen copied. Newmeet is smaller than the brothers made it sound, after so many days on the road. The first person you ask points the way to the priestess of Lugh, and you go in. The brothers want the old writing at Joygate read and set down: who made the place, or how its makers ended. Their letter is for Carmine, priestess of Lugh at Newmeet, who will show you the way.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_priest)
pages.page: Carmine takes in the road on your boots, and that you have come straight to her, and waits to hear what you have brought.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word6__h1_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘A child at the market-place of Newmeet has a fever that will not break, and the herbs have run out,’ says Carmine.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word11__h2_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘Tree Keep: a walled keep on its rise in the woods north of Newmeet,’ says Carmine. ‘The lord of Tree Keep has not been seen in eleven days,’ says Carmine. ‘His castellan signs for him.’ Tree Keep is the name of the walled keep on its rise they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word3__h2_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘Elmspire: a lone tower in the woods north-west of Brockfield,’ says Carmine. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “elm spire”.’ ‘Graves have been opened in the churchyard and the dead taken,’ says Carmine. ‘An acolyte who left the shrine of Lugh years ago lives in Elmspire now.’ Elmspire is the name of the lone tower they speak of.

pages.label: go(region__s1_approach_way,region__s1_green)
pages.page: A stone market cross stands in the middle of the square at Newmeet, its steps worn into dips. Shutters bang open along the houses, and carts grind over the cobbles. The Redwater runs by below the houses. Twice this month the Hall’s keeper has driven the town’s pigs off the verge of the old road. The geese are kept in a bunch at the well, hissing at the lane to the Hall, and three hens have gone from the inn’s yard since Tuesday. The shutters of one house are drawn in daylight, and a woman stands in its door, watching the road. A notice is nailed to the clerk’s trestle by the well, under the shire-reeve’s mark: THE TALLY OF IRON AND GOLD IS TO BE MADE UP BY MIDWINTER. FOR THE WEIGHT OF IRON AND GOLD WANTING, SEE THE CLERK. The gangway is drawn in. Above the roofs, to the east, two columns of smoke stand on the ridge: one thick and black from the digging, one thin and white from the old woman’s fire. A baker’s boy works through the crowd with a tray of loaves on his head. Hild is backing a cart into a yard, one hand on the horse’s bridle. Moll is touching up a painted backcloth of a castle with a small brush. Linden the researcher is copying a page from a borrowed book, a stone on each corner. The inn’s dog sleeps against the wall of the Ancient Lantern with one ear up for the door. Euphrosyne grows in the gardens about the green, low, with small white flowers: eyebright. Hazel grows in the gardens about the green, broad-leaved, its nuts in clusters of three. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. The factor, who keeps the books of the Ísenheald company, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Newmeet, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. So are the old woman in the doorway, Felice Hale, Cecily Hale and Wat. Bess barks twice, then comes to see who you are.

pages.label: talk_to(fever__sister)
pages.page: ‘Lost?’ says Cecily Hale. ‘People usually are, when they come over to me.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r1)
pages.page: Hild grins before you have said anything at all. ‘You look like a person with a question.’

pages.label: talk_to(fever__mother)
pages.page: ‘I don’t know you,’ says Felice Hale, and waits to be told why she should.

pages.label: talk_to(region__w8_head)
pages.page: The factor sighs before you have said a word. ‘Go on, then.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r9)
pages.page: Moll looks you over, and does not like what she sees.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r10)
pages.page: Linden finishes what they were saying to someone else first.

pages.label: go(region__s1_waterside_way,region__s1_waterside)
pages.page: Boats are drawn up on the bank, nets dry on poles, and a plank jetty runs out over the water. The water slaps against its piles, and the mud smells of weed. Sabine is reckoning the week’s takings on a slate.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r8)
pages.page: Sabine lets you speak first, as is plainly her due.

pages.label: take_item(region__party_1__longsword,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take a longsword.

pages.label: go(region__s1_inn_door,region__s1_taproom)
pages.page: A busy room in two parts with a counter between them, and a stair going up to the bedrooms. It smells of roasting meat, and the clatter of the kitchen comes through the back door. Reed-cutters sit at the long table, their hands cut and bound. ‘Caradoc there is looking for work,’ says Sable. ‘Would go anywhere with anyone, for a few coins and their keep.’ Tilda is tying the last of her things into bundles for the handcart, and the children are carrying out the small bundles. A hazel tally-stick lies behind the bar where the innkeeper put it, cut with fine notches in rows, marks on the flat in the wardens’ hand. Sable, the innkeeper, is here. Caradoc, a soldier, is here. Dannel Hobb, a boy of ten with a white streak in his hair, kept indoors, is here. So are Isaure Venn, Osmund Pyle, Arannis, the factor’s hands and Ghokarn.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_innkeeper,word12__h1_s1_innkeeper)
pages.page: ‘The head of the Verderers’ Watch has had no word from one of its halls since the quarter-day, and has sent no one, for want of anyone who can be spared,’ says Sable.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_traveller,word3__h3_s1_traveller)
pages.page: ‘Behind Elmspire, the tower where the green light burns at night, an old well runs down into the cellars,’ says Caradoc. ‘The builders used it.’

pages.label: ask(region__s1_innkeeper,word13__h1_s1_innkeeper)
pages.page: ‘A company of the barefoot is walking the old road from town to town, chalking the milestones and calling out their numbers, and the Bench does not like it,’ says Sable.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_innkeeper,word1__h1_s1_innkeeper)
pages.page: ‘A factor at the inn buys old bronze by the pound and asks no questions: bells, weir-metal, green fittings from the plough,’ says Sable.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_innkeeper)
pages.page: Sable nods to you, and says nothing until you do.

pages.label: search(region__s1_taproom)
pages.page: You search the taproom of the Ancient Lantern with care, a little at a time. Behind the bar of the largest inn in the country a hatch opens on the Exchange’s cellar, where the cellar-men keep the lots.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_traveller)
pages.page: ‘Well now,’ says Caradoc, brightening at the sight of a new face. ‘What brings you?’

pages.label: ask(region__s1_innkeeper,word3__h1_s1_innkeeper)
pages.page: ‘A green light burns at night at the top of Elmspire, and something walks the lane below it,’ says Sable.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_traveller,word8__h1_s1_traveller)
pages.page: ‘Wapshott’s Grand Peregrine Circus is going round the country, three days in a town: Newmeet, then Brockfield, then Windscar, and back,’ says Caradoc. ‘It plays nightly at seven, a coin a head.’

pages.label: examine(region__gate_pentrice_notice_s5)
pages.page: A bill in red and black, much handled and rained on: THE TRIAL OF THE WHEEL AT PENTRICE. THREE COMPANIES OF PLAYERS. THREE NIGHTS. THE PATENT OF THE WHEEL TO BE GIVEN BY THE BENCH. BY LEAVE OF THE OFFICE OF PLAIN SPEECH. Under it someone has written in pencil: west road, a day; and drawn a bear.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_pilgrim)
pages.page: An old man puts a coin on the table by the door and does not look up from it. ‘I am going,’ says Osmund Pyle. ‘I will go slowly, and I will go alone if I must, and I would rather not.’

pages.label: talk_to(factors__factor)
pages.page: Arannis looks up from a ledger and weighs you with a look before weighing anything else. ‘Founders’ Exchange,’ says Arannis. ‘Bells, fittings, weir-metal, anything green. Fourteen to the pound for good bronze, nine for scrap, and no questions. I do not ask where a thing was, only what it weighs.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_iv)
pages.page: A young woman with ink on both cuffs rises from a table covered with paper, knocks over a candle, catches it, and says, ‘You look as if you can read or, failing that, walk. Which?’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_u_hobb)
pages.page: Dannel Hobb looks at you for longer than is comfortable. ‘Well?’

pages.label: talk_to(factors__carter)
pages.page: At the end of the bench Ghokarn looks at your boots, and then at a cup. That is the carter, someone says, who goes south on the first fine day of the week with whatever the factor has bought, and comes back with the money.

pages.label: talk_to(factors__hands)
pages.page: ‘A stranger!’ say the factor’s hands, pleased. ‘Sit, if you like. Ask, if you like.’

pages.label: go(factors__cellar_hatch,factors__cellar)
pages.page: The cellar runs back under the whole yard: barrels on their sides, sacks stencilled NORTH, a bell with its clapper wrapped in felt, a trestle with a scale and a stamp. Every sack has a key and a ring pressed into its lead seal. The cellar-men, who keep the Exchange’s lots, are here. Three or four men in leather aprons turn from the barrels with the unhurried look of men who are paid by the week to be looked at. ‘Cellar’s private,’ says the biggest. ‘Six coin to have not seen it, or the word of the one upstairs. Or the stairs.’ The cellar-men will give you a few minutes, no more.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You owe Falkor fifty coin, for a load of reed that went into the river at the ford last spring. The oxen went too. Falkor has been patient, and wrote to say so. Patient until market day, ten days from now: not a day longer. Newmeet has not changed. You come in off the road with your head down, past faces that knew you once. You go straight to Falkor’s door: better it is done at once. 50 coin by market day, owed to Falkor, herb-wife at Newmeet.

pages.page: ‘A company of the barefoot is walking the old road from town to town, chalking the milestones and calling out their numbers, and the Bench does not like it,’ says Falkor.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word11__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Tree Keep: a walled keep on its rise in the woods north of Newmeet,’ says Falkor. ‘A crier in the castellan’s colours has read a levy on the green: spears and grain, to be at the keep on the twelfth day, for the king’s muster,’ says Falkor. Tree Keep is the name of the walled keep on its rise they speak of.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_merchant)
pages.page: Falkor looks at your hands before your face, to see whether there is anything in them.

pages.label: talk_to(region__w8_head)
pages.page: The factor looks you up and down. ‘Whatever it is, the answer’s probably no. Go on.’

pages.label: talk_to(fever__mother)
pages.page: Felice Hale lets you speak first, as is plainly her due.

pages.label: talk_to(fever__sister)
pages.page: ‘Let me guess,’ says Cecily Hale. ‘You want something.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r9)
pages.page: Moll looks at you for longer than is comfortable. ‘Well?’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r10)
pages.page: ‘I don’t know you,’ says Linden, and waits to be told why they should.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r1)
pages.page: ‘Well now,’ says Hild, brightening at the sight of a new face. ‘What brings you?’

pages.label: go(region__s1_fields_way,region__s1_fields)
pages.page: Strips of field run out from the houses to the hedges, with a trodden track between them. Rooks rise and settle behind whoever is working, and the turned earth smells raw. Orm is carrying a lamb under each arm across the yard, the ewe following.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r7)
pages.page: Orm nods to you, and says nothing until you do.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_pit_path,region__s1_u_pit)
pages.page: A bowl of grey stone cut out of the hill long ago, ivy over its faces. At the bottom a square adit goes back into the rock behind a barred gate. A board on the gate says KEEP OUT in three hands.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_pit_path,region__s1_green)
pages.page: A stone market cross stands in the middle of the square at Newmeet, its steps worn into dips. The inn’s dog sleeps against the wall of the Ancient Lantern with one ear up for the door. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. The factor, who keeps the books of the Ísenheald company, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Newmeet, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. So are the old woman in the doorway, Felice Hale, Cecily Hale and Wat. The bailiff’s men have been through again. The price is five crowns a hearth now, and the reeve has been seen reading the receipt by the well and putting it in his pocket.

pages.label: go(region__edge_south_road,region__edge_south)
pages.page: You leave Newmeet late, with the light already going yellow. The road runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. Night comes on while you are still on the road, and you walk the last of it in the dark. Where the road leaves Acornweald a wooden post carved with faces stands in a clearing, grey as stone, the faces on the far side different from these. Beyond it the road goes on south into Highfells, upland country, the folk say. Few of them have been.

pages.label: go(region__tw35_55,region__t55)
pages.page: Birch and rowan on a slope, the light coming white through the leaves. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw251_252,region__t251)
pages.page: A strong wind blows across the open country the whole way. The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw236_237,region__t236)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Pine wood, the ground soft with needles and the smell of resin heavy in the still air.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: The herb-wife at Brightbridge wrapped the feverwort in a cloth and put it in your hands. ‘The child at Newmeet has had the fever three days, and they have nothing left there,’ she said. ‘Don’t dawdle.’ The road comes out from under the trees, and there is Newmeet in its clearing. You see the market cross and the roofs of the stalls, reed drying in ricks, and smoke from a dozen chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Take the feverwort you carry to the child at the market-place of Newmeet: its mother is waiting, three days into the fever.

pages.label: talk_to(fever__mother)
pages.page: Felice Hale takes in the road on your boots, and that you have come straight to her, and waits to hear what you have brought.

pages.label: go(region__s1_jewelry_door,region__s1_jewelry)
pages.page: A small bright room with one window and everything turned toward it. The rings lie in a tray under glass and throw small sparks across the ceiling. Letice, a jeweller, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_jewelry_keeper)
pages.page: Letice looks up and smiles broadly. ‘Hello! What can I do?’

pages.label: search(region__s1_jewelry)
pages.page: You search Letice’s jewel-shop with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__feverwort)
pages.page: You set a feverwort down.

pages.label: take_item(region__party_1__feverwort,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take a feverwort.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__herbs)
pages.page: You set healing herbs down.

pages.label: take_leave(region__s1_jewelry_keeper)
pages.page: ‘Come back and tell me how it goes!’ calls Letice after you.

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_jewelry_keeper,region__s1_jewelry_keeper_wardstone_1)
pages.page: Letice will not be argued with, and a wardstone is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 10 + charisma -1 = 9 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_jewelry_keeper,region__s1_jewelry_keeper_carnelian_1)
pages.page: Letice will not be argued with, and a carnelian is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 4 + charisma -1 = 3 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_jewelry_keeper,region__s1_jewelry_keeper_ring_of_strength_1)
pages.page: Letice will not be argued with, and a ring of strength is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 3 + charisma -1 = 2 against 13).

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__antidote)
pages.page: You set an antidote down.

pages.label: take_item(region__party_1__antidote,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take an antidote.

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_jewelry_keeper,region__s1_jewelry_keeper_amulet_of_health_1)
pages.page: Letice will not be argued with, and an amulet of health is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 4 + charisma -1 = 3 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_jewelry_keeper,region__s1_jewelry_keeper_carnelian_2)
pages.page: Letice thinks it over, and names a lower price for a carnelian. Wenna makes the persuasion check (d20 19 + charisma -1 = 18 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_jewelry_keeper,region__s1_jewelry_keeper_ring_of_protection_1)
pages.page: Letice thinks it over, and names a lower price for a ring of protection. Wenna makes the persuasion check (d20 16 + charisma -1 = 15 against 13).

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You have come over the hills into Acornweald with your trade and not much else. There is work in any country for someone who will do what others will not. The place to hear of it is the inn. The road comes out from under the trees, and there is Newmeet in its clearing. You see the market cross and the roofs of the stalls, reed drying in ricks, and smoke from a dozen chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Find herbs for a child with a fever at the market-place of Newmeet, or willow bark from where willows grow by water.

pages.label: talk_to(fever__mother)
pages.page: Felice Hale finishes what she was saying to someone else first.

pages.label: go(region__s1_fabrics_door,region__s1_fabrics)
pages.page: Bolts of cloth stand on end along the walls, and cured hides hang from the beams. Isot, a clothier, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_fabrics_keeper)
pages.page: Isot looks up, and puts her hands still, and waits for you to say what you want.

pages.label: search(region__s1_fabrics)
pages.page: You search Isot’s cloth-hall with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_leather_1)
pages.page: Isot will not be argued with, and leather armor is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 9 + charisma -1 = 8 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_cloth_1)
pages.page: Isot thinks it over, and names a lower price for clothing. Wenna makes the persuasion check (d20 16 + charisma -1 = 15 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_studded_2)
pages.page: Isot thinks it over, and names a lower price for studded leather armor. Wenna makes the persuasion check (d20 18 + charisma -1 = 17 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_cloth_2)
pages.page: Isot will not be argued with, and clothing is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 2 + charisma -1 = 1 against 13).

pages.label: take_leave(region__s1_fabrics_keeper)
pages.page: Isot lifts a hand, once.

pages.label: buy_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper_cloth_1,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: Isot is paid, and you take clothing.

pages.label: put_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper_cloth_1)
pages.page: You set clothing down.

pages.label: go(region__s1_scriv_door,region__s1_green)
pages.page: A stone market cross stands in the middle of the square at Newmeet, its steps worn into dips. Fog lies over the place; the far houses are shapes. Lambs cry in the home fields, and the ground is soft from the thaw. Hild is backing a cart into a yard, one hand on the horse’s bridle. Moll is touching up a painted backcloth of a castle with a small brush. Linden the researcher is copying a page from a borrowed book, a stone on each corner. The inn’s dog sleeps against the wall of the Ancient Lantern with one ear up for the door. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. The factor, who keeps the books of the Ísenheald company, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Newmeet, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. So are the old woman in the doorway, Felice Hale, Cecily Hale and Wat.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r8)
pages.page: Sabine looks at you a long moment before speaking.

pages.label: equip_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper_cloth_2,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You ready clothing.

pages.label: take_leave(region__s1_r8)
pages.page: Sabine turns away before you have finished.

pages.label: equip_item(region__party_1__scale,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You ready scale mail.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: The map is inside your shirt, where it has been since the night you won it. It is a square of greased hide with the hills drawn on it in soot. On it are Palelake out in Birchwood, and a cross at its door. The drover you won it from laughed when he lost it. In the morning he was dead in the straw, and nobody in the inn would say of what. The road comes out from under the trees, and there is Newmeet in its clearing. You see the market cross and the roofs of the stalls, reed drying in ricks, and smoke from a dozen chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. The dead man’s map marks Palelake, out in Birchwood, with a cross at its door. Search there.

pages.label: go(region__s1_byre_way,region__s1_byre)
pages.page: A byre of black timber, warm, with a row of broad backs in the gloom and a smell of hay and dung. Robin is walking the cows down the lane with a hazel stick. Robin’s cow is never far away. Bluebell turns her great head to look at you, and goes on chewing.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r5)
pages.page: ‘A stranger!’ says Robin, pleased. ‘Sit, if you like. Ask, if you like.’

pages.label: search(region__s1_byre)
pages.page: You search the byre with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_yard_gate,region__s1_u_yard)
pages.page: Old stones lean in the grass. In the corner by the wall, a low stone door goes into the ground. Its iron ring is bright where someone has pulled at it lately. Three graves by the wall have been dug into and filled again badly. The grass is trodden flat from them to the stone door.

pages.label: listen(region__s1_u_crypt_lock)
pages.page: You put an ear to the lock of the stone door, and hold your breath. There is nothing to hear from it.

pages.label: change_thing(region__s1_u_crypt_lock_force)
pages.page: You set your shoulder to it and heave. Wood groans and iron shrieks, and the noise of it goes further than you would like. The stone door into the ground stands unlocked.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_bone_arch,region__s1_u_ossuary)
pages.page: It is pitch dark. Without a light you can see nothing here, and do nothing that needs seeing. In the dark you can hear the hungry dead of the ossuary and the man with the black candle close by. A man in a muddy coat stands up behind a burning black candle, among the bones. ‘Go back up,’ he says. ‘This is not yours.’ The man with the black candle will give you a few minutes, no more.

pages.label: light_item(region__party_1__candle)
pages.page: You light a candle. A vaulted crypt under the churchyard, its shelves of coffins pushed askew. The dust on the floor is scuffed through in a dozen places by feet that dragged. On the crypt floor is a ring of chalk with marks round it. Inside it, the ends of black candles are burned to the floor. The stone door into the ground stands unlocked.

pages.label: search(region__s1_u_crypt)
pages.page: You search the crypt with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: go(region__s1_u_bone_arch,region__s1_u_ossuary)
pages.page: Bones are stacked to the roof in patient courses, with skulls in rows along the top like a frieze. There are gaps in the courses where some have lately been taken down. A black candle burns on a skull in the middle of the bone-heaps, with a flame that does not move. The man with the black candle stands over it, and the dead are his while it burns. The hungry dead of the ossuary, a dead things raised out of the bone-heaps, hungry, is here. The man with the black candle, a grave-robber who has read a book he should not have, and is trying what it says, is here. A man in a muddy coat stands up behind a burning black candle, among the bones. ‘Go back up,’ he says. ‘This is not yours.’ The man with the black candle will give you 8 minutes, no more.

pages.label: search(region__s1_u_ossuary)
pages.page: The man with the black candle comes at you! The man with the black candle come at you to drive you off. Wenna takes 1 slashing damage (0 HP left). Wenna falls. The fight is lost.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: Her last letter is in your coat, read so often it has come apart at the folds. She was going out to Palelake, in Birchwood, with two men from Newmeet who swore there was silver in it. She would write when she was rich. The two men came back at the end of the summer. She did not, and they will not say why. The road comes out from under the trees, and there is Newmeet in its clearing. You see the market cross and the roofs of the stalls, reed drying in ricks, and smoke from a dozen chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Your sister went into Palelake, out in Birchwood, and did not come out. Search there for any sign of her.

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_studded_1)
pages.page: Isot will not be argued with, and studded leather armor is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 7 + charisma -1 = 6 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_hide_armor_1)
pages.page: Isot will not be argued with, and hide armor is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 2 + charisma -1 = 1 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_hide_armor_2)
pages.page: Isot thinks it over, and names a lower price for hide armor. Wenna makes the persuasion check (d20 16 + charisma -1 = 15 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_studded_2)
pages.page: Isot will not be argued with, and studded leather armor is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 8 + charisma -1 = 7 against 13).

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__shovel)
pages.page: You set a shovel down.

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_leather_1)
pages.page: Isot thinks it over, and names a lower price for leather armor. Wenna makes the persuasion check (d20 20 + charisma -1 = 19 against 13).

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s1_fabrics_keeper,region__s1_fabrics_keeper_leather_2)
pages.page: Isot thinks it over, and names a lower price for leather armor. Wenna makes the persuasion check (d20 17 + charisma -1 = 16 against 13).

pages.label: take_item(region__party_1__shovel,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take a shovel.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: The scroll-case has not been off your shoulder in eleven days. In it is a letter under the seal of a widow in the town you came from, for Lothar at Brockfield, into no other hands. Half the fee was paid at the start. The other half, and whatever Lothar thinks it worth, is at the far end of the road. The next town on from Newmeet is Brockfield. The road comes out from under the trees, and there is Newmeet in its clearing. You see the market cross and the roofs of the stalls, reed drying in ricks, and smoke from a dozen chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Carry the sealed letter to Lothar at Brockfield, into no other hands.

pages.label: go(region__s1_shrine_door,region__s1_shrine)
pages.page: A long stone under a roof of shingles: the altar of Lugh, God of Storms. Drovers leave a stone before it when they go up into the hills, and take one away when they come down. Offerings of reed lie before it. Under the lamp at the back, a young acolyte in a grey habit is copying the offering-book’s yearly sums onto a slate. A stair goes up inside the tower wall, worn hollow in the middle of every step, to where the bell hangs. A man lies on the shrine’s bier under a grey cloth, his boots still on. A wood-warden’s mark is tied at his belt. The offering-box by the lamp is shut, its lock whole, and light in the hand: the little bronze things that were left in it have gone, and the coppers have not. Carmine, the priestess of Lugh, is here. Brother Anselm Tarr, the priest’s acolyte, who has read everything the shrine owns and wants to know what it leaves out, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘A stranger!’ says Carmine, pleased. ‘Sit, if you like. Ask, if you like.’

pages.label: wait_hour
pages.page: Sabine is reckoning the week’s takings on a slate. An hour passes.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r8)
pages.page: Sabine acknowledges you with the smallest movement of the chin.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__scrollcase)
pages.page: You set a scrollcase down.

pages.label: wait_for_dark
pages.page: Out across the gulf, a chain tightens, and a weight the size of a bell goes up the cliff-face through a slot in the glass, slowly. The far capstan turns under its pawl, grunting, and out in the gulf a second weight begins to climb.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You have been three years on the other side of the hills, hiring out with the droves. Your mother’s letter took a week to find you. Your father went out on the road with the cart, it said, and did not come home. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Sedgeminster: low roofs against the sky, the long wall of the brothers’ house, and a bell-cote over the gate, eel-traps stacked against the walls. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Look along the road between Fairholt and Sedgeminster for your father, who went out by it with the cart and did not come home.

pages.label: go(region__s5_approach_way,region__s5_green)
pages.page: The gate-yard of Sedgeminster is swept clean to the cobbles, and smells of wet stone and beeswax from the chapel door. The brothers’ house stands at the back of it behind a low wall, and the village crowds round the front. The Broadwater runs by below the houses. Twice this month the Hall’s keeper has driven the town’s pigs off the verge of the old road. A plank door in the wall, barred on the outside: the lord’s lockup. A brother sells small beer and honey at the gate, counting the coins into a wooden bowl. Letice is sitting on a log by the door, mending a strap and watching the treeline. The brothers’ dog sleeps against the wall of the guest-hall with one ear up for the door. A grey cat sits on a wall-top with her eyes half shut and her tail hanging down the stones. A goat with a broken tether is cropping the verge, with her whole attention. Your brother is sitting on a rail with your father’s old spear across his knees, watching the road. He is taller by a head than when you went away. A grey dog lies by the door of the guest-hall of Sedgeminster with her head on her paws, watching the road. She holds one forefoot off the ground. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. Asters grow in the gardens about the green in clumps, mauve with yellow eyes. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. Perrin, a salter, selling from the house door, is here. The prior, who keeps the rule of the brothers of Reodweard, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Sedgeminster, is here. So are the surveyor’s son and Jankin Reeve. The grey dog thumps her tail on the ground without getting up.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s5_r4)
pages.page: Letice looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: talk_to(drover__son)
pages.page: ‘You came,’ says Jankin Reeve. ‘I said you would. Nobody believed me.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__w8_head)
pages.page: ‘You’re back, then,’ says the prior, as if you had been gone a week and not three years.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s5_merchant)
pages.page: Perrin looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: ask(region__s5_merchant,word6__h1_s5_merchant)
pages.page: ‘A child at the ford at Broadford has a fever that will not break, and the herbs have run out,’ says Perrin.

pages.label: go(region__s5_inn_door,region__s5_taproom)
pages.page: Plain benches stand round a scrubbed table and a fire of small logs. On the whitewash above the hearth the rule of the house is written out in a careful hand, and its first line says that no one is turned away. Everyone here is grumbling about the toll on the road: food is dearer for it, and there is less of it. ‘Alton there is looking for work,’ says Emrys. ‘Would go anywhere with anyone, for a few coins and their keep.’ Elfred the carrier is at the table with his coat on, eating fast: the horse is put to, and the road is waiting. Your mother is at the hearth with her back to the room. Emrys, a guest-master of the brothers’ house, is here. Alton, a pedlar, is here. Dannel Hobb, a boy of ten with a white streak in his hair, kept indoors, is here. So are Olive Reeve and the hedger.

pages.label: talk_to(drover__wife)
pages.page: Your mother gets up so fast the stool goes over, and then stands there, not sure what to do with her hands.

pages.label: examine(region__gate_ombra_notice_s5)
pages.page: A square of grey paper stamped with a bare white oval, nailed up where travellers will see it: THE MASKED WATCH OF OMBRA WILL HIRE ONE STRANGER UNDER THE SEVENTY-FIRST ARTICLE OF THE CONCORD. NO NAME, NO MASK, NO STANDING REQUIRED. APPLY AT THE GATE OF STRANGERS ON THE FIRST DAY OF THE NOVENA, AT THE THIRD BELL. The bottom has been torn off, and in pencil, in a different hand: Nine days. It is always raining.

pages.label: search(region__s5_taproom)
pages.page: You search the guest-hall of Sedgeminster with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s5_s3_way_t)
pages.page: ‘You’re back, then,’ says Elfred, as if you had been gone a week and not three years.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s5_u_hobb)
pages.page: Dannel Hobb looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: examine(region__gate_sennet_notice_s1)
pages.page: A printed sheet in four colours under a seal of a door: BY THE RECTOR OF THE HOUSE OF DOORS AT SENNET. THE GRAND TOUR IS PROCLAIMED, THE FIRST IN TWO HUNDRED YEARS. WHOSOEVER BRINGS TO THE HOUSE THE FOUR PETALS OF THE ROSE OF THE WINDS SHALL GO FIRST THROUGH THE DOOR OF DOORS. I. QUANCE, RECTOR. Under it, in pencil: east, down the coast road; and someone has drawn a little door, and beside it a little figure falling out of the sky.

pages.label: examine(region__gate_longman_notice_s5)
pages.page: A notice in a clerk’s hand, carried down from Merrowdale and nailed up where travellers will see it: WHOEVER LAYS THE MOWER THAT WALKS THE LONG MAN SHALL HAVE FORTY CROWNS OF THE STEWARD. A. VENN, FOR THE LORD. Under it someone has written: up the north road, three days at most.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s5_traveller)
pages.page: ‘Come in, come in, whoever you are,’ says Alton. ‘Everybody else has.’

pages.label: ask(region__s5_innkeeper,raidersWord1Teller2__asked)
pages.page: ‘Stonehill: a smooth doorway in a crag in Cloudfell,’ says Emrys. ‘Sir Hamo Ashdown’s outlaws take road-money on the road by day, and a tithe from the market when they please,’ says Emrys. ‘They hold out at Stonehill.’ Hereabouts the place has a name, and whoever speaks of it uses it.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s5_innkeeper)
pages.page: Emrys looks twice, and then a third time. ‘Well. Look who it is.’

pages.label: region__s5_u_spiders_job_ask
pages.page: ‘Nobody goes in the old quarry now,’ says Emrys. ‘There’s webs across the adit thick as sailcloth. The Hobb boy went in after a ferret and came out white. We put a gate on it.’ A small key, put down on the counter. ‘Twelve coin from the house to whoever burns them out, and a pot of the salve the firemen use. Talk to the boy first. He saw more than he says.’ A stoppered phial follows it, the cork waxed. ‘Hobb’s mother made that, for the bite. Drink it the moment one has you, not after.’ Emrys looks you over. ‘Not on your own, you won’t. Arlen at the taproom of the Laughing Flame is looking for work: take someone with you.’ You take the key to the quarry gate. Wenna Reeve gains 1 Antidote.

pages.label: region__gate_lull_beyond_told_s5
pages.page: ‘Up in the north of the country there’s a hamlet called Sixways,’ says Emrys, ‘and above it a stone, and past the stone a valley you can only walk into one day in seven. The other six the road goes round a hill and back. The Lull, they call it. They don’t work in there: whatever’s done there without meaning it comes apart at sunset, bread and money and all. And if you sleep a night in it, you lose a week out here.’ ‘Misthythe is where the road to the Lull goes out from,’ Emrys adds.

pages.label: take_leave(region__s5_traveller)
pages.page: ‘Off you go, then,’ says Alton, ‘and don’t do anything I’d be ashamed to hear about. Or do, and tell me.’

pages.label: region__gate_tolleth_beyond_told_s5
pages.page: ‘Down the coast, at Tolleth, there’s a ketch called the Dorothea,’ says Emrys, ‘that sails for an island nobody goes to. Skerrow. A night and a morning out, past a reef they call the Combs. There’s a lamp on it, older than the roads. The captain’s short of hands, and short of money, and sails on the noon ebb whether you’re aboard or no.’ ‘Broadford is where the road to Tolleth and the Skerrow passage goes out from,’ Emrys adds.

pages.label: region__s5_th_plaque_ask
pages.page: ‘That?’ says Emrys. ‘A shepherd brought it down from the high grazing and swapped it for a night’s bed. Smooth, black, cold in summer. It has little marks on it in columns. A scholar came through, looked at it for an hour, and went white. She said they were sums, and that the sums were true: every column came out to a number, and the numbers came out to another number, and so on up, and it did not matter which way she added it. She said it was older than anything. Older than the road.’ They scratch their head. ‘It is a very good doorstop.’

pages.label: put_item(quarry_key_given1)
pages.page: You set the key to the quarry gate down.

pages.label: region__gate_larum_beyond_told_s5
pages.page: ‘West, up the country, at the head of a long valley, there’s a hamlet called Larum under a high pass,’ says Emrys. ‘For nine hundred years, on a still day, you could hear the dead fighting up there in the snow: like a smithy the size of the sky, faint, all day, and stopping at dusk. Larum sold their ballads. Forty days ago it stopped. The carters say Larum can’t sleep for the quiet.’ ‘Misthythe is where the road to Larum and the Pass goes out from,’ Emrys adds.

pages.label: region__w4_hook_again
pages.page: ‘The old wells?’ Emrys leans on the bar. ‘A door in the hill out in Ashurst, and a stair going down further than anyone has followed it: Rainpool, we call it. Folk say the kings of old kept their gold down there under the water, where no thief would follow. Folk say a lot of things.’

pages.label: region__gate_pentrice_beyond_told_s5
pages.page: ‘Away in the west of the country, where the Ise falls into the Arle, there’s Pentrice,’ says Emrys. ‘A minster town, very grand, where they license every word said on a stage and fine you for the rest. This week it’s their Trial of the Wheel: three companies of players, three nights in a round playhouse over the river, and the best of them given a house of its own for ever.’ Emrys grins. ‘They say old Absalom Gosse is going back for it, after forty years. They banned him from every stage inside the walls the last time. He started a riot.’ ‘Misthythe is where the road to the vale of the Arle goes out from,’ Emrys adds.

pages.label: wait_for_dark
pages.page: Dunstan and the children have the corner by the fire, the youngest asleep in a heap. Your brother sits by the kitchen fire with your father’s old spear across his knees, not drinking. He is taller by a head than when you went away. The light goes. It is dark.

pages.label: wait_for_light
pages.page: Dunstan is tying the last of his things into bundles for the handcart, and the children are carrying out the small bundles. The sky greys, then lightens. It is morning. It is a long time since you slept. You are weary, and will fight the worse for it until you sleep.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s4_s5_way_t)
pages.page: ‘You’re back, then,’ says Dunstan, as if you had been gone a week and not three years.

pages.label: region__gate_ghessil_beyond_told_s5
pages.page: ‘West, up on the Ghessil Uplands,’ says Emrys, ‘there is a light lies on the glass that slows whatever drinks it. There are people standing in it, they say, that went in last autumn and are standing there yet, alive.’ ‘Misthythe is where the road to the Ghessil Uplands goes out from,’ Emrys adds.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You have the letter inside your coat, from the brothers of your order to the priest of Belenus at Misthythe. It asks that Wenna, who reads the old script, be given a bed and shown the way to Glassarch. There is writing there that the order has heard of for a hundred years and never seen copied. Misthythe is smaller than the brothers made it sound, after so many days on the road. The first person you ask points the way to the priest of Belenus, and you go in. The brothers want the old writing at Glassarch read and set down: who made the place, or how its makers ended. Their letter is for Gizon, priest of Belenus at Misthythe, who will show you the way.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word3__h2_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘The figure of Belenus at Misthythe was set up after the sickness, by those who were left, and the names of the dead are under it,’ says Gizon. ‘Mosswatch: a lone tower in Cloudfell,’ says Gizon. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “moss watch”.’ ‘Graves have been opened in the churchyard and the dead taken,’ says Gizon. ‘An acolyte who left the shrine of Belenus years ago lives in Mosswatch now.’ Mosswatch is the name of the lone tower they speak of.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_priest)
pages.page: Gizon takes in the road on your boots, and that you have come straight to him, and waits to hear what you have brought.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word9__h2_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘Fenstone: the fallen walls in the fen south of Misthythe,’ says Gizon. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “fen stone”.’ ‘Dogs will not go into the hollow beyond Fenstone, and an old priest said the ground there hummed on feast days, a long low note that the monks of the old order tried to sing against, and could not,’ says Gizon. Fenstone is the name of the fallen walls they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word10__h3_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘Wet Howe: a grassed mound in the fen north-west of Merscstede,’ says Gizon. ‘An old woman keeps a fire on the ridge above Wet Howe, in sight of the king’s howe,’ says Gizon. ‘The priest says she is the last who still keeps the dead’s rest.’ Wet Howe is the name of the grassed mound north-west of Merscstede they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_priest,word11__h2_s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘Marsh Garth: a walled keep on its rise in the fen south of Misthythe,’ says Gizon. ‘The lord of Marsh Garth has not been seen in eleven days,’ says Gizon. ‘His castellan signs for him.’ Marsh Garth is the name of the walled keep on its rise they speak of.

pages.label: go(region__s1_approach_way,region__s1_green)
pages.page: Boats lie drawn up keel to keel on the shingle at Misthythe, and the houses come right down to them, nets hung on every fence. The air is salt and tar, and the shingle rattles back with every wave. The Saltbrook runs by below the houses, and beyond the roofs lies the Mistwater. The boat-sheds are short of oak this year: the Hall has chained the road-wood, and the good timber is behind it. At dusk every dog in the town turns its head toward the hill, and the geese go silent. A bear is asleep on the ground by the players’ wagon, with a thin man for a pillow, and a big old man in a faded crimson coat sits on the wagon’s tail-board, squinting up at the sky. The gangway is drawn in. A woman sells mackerel straight off a boat, holding each up by the tail and calling its price. Magot is crying wares along the street: pots mended, knives ground. Hild is darning the hem of a red stage cloak. Isot the bookkeeper is weighing a handful of nails on a small brass scale. Averil the conspirator is shuffling a worn pack of cards one-handed. The inn’s dog lies across the doorstep of the Laughing Flame with his chin on his paws, and watches who comes. A thin brown cat crouches at the foot of a wall, watching a hole in it without a blink. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. Amaranth grows in the gardens about the green, its dark red tassels hanging over the beds. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. A tall wagon, painted with a sun and a moon and the words GOSSE’S COMPANY in red letters gone pink, stands on the landing at Misthythe with its shafts down. A chain runs from its back wheel to a post, and the chain has a padlock on it. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. The spring-head by the green has been running low for a year. The rope comes up with a hand’s depth of brown water in the bucket and a smell of wet stone, and the women who draw it do so in silence, to save breath. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Misthythe, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. The old woman in the doorway, the innkeeper’s mother, who has not been out of her chair since the harvest and who asks, every morning, whether the lamp has been lit, is here. So are Absalom Gosse, Hepzibah Dimmock and Jem Pudding. Patience ambles to the end of her rope to see who you are, and goes through your hands for honey.

pages.label: go(region__w14_track,region__w14)
pages.page: It is cold enough to see your breath, and the ruts are hard with frost. A walled keep stands on a rise above the fields, smoke at its chimneys and a banner over its gate. Reeds hiss in the wind. A lizard watches from a tussock, its throat pulsing. This is Marsh Garth. Below the north wall the ditch has been scythed clean in one place, and a stone outfall there breathes out a thread of cold air that smells of old water. Nothing else on the wall has been tended. A banner hangs over the gate, a tower with a star over it in white on green, and under it, lower, a black cloth the width of a hand that has been there some days. Wenna gains 10 experience: found Marsh Garth.

pages.label: search(region__w14)
pages.page: You search Marsh Garth with care, a little at a time. Pulling the weed back from the outfall, you find the arch behind it is no drain-mouth but a culvert cut for a man to crawl, and the air coming out of it is cold. The air in the culvert is thick and sweetish. A flame held up in it burns blue and leans back toward the outfall.

pages.label: prod(keep__foul_air)
pages.page: You prod the air in the culvert with the pole, from as far off as it allows. Nothing gives, and nothing answers.

pages.label: go(region__tl_w14,region__t102)

pages.label: go(region__tw102_123,region__t123)
pages.page: You walk fast to keep warm, and it does not help much. It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by. Meadow, wet in the hollows and dry on the rises, with a few thorn trees leaning all the same way.

pages.label: go(region__tw123_124,region__t124)
pages.page: Water stands on both sides, and the path between is soft enough to take the print of your boot and keep it. Fen: reeds taller than a man, black water between, and the ground giving underfoot with every step. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw125_126,region__t125)
pages.page: Larks go up out of the grass on either hand, and come down again behind you. Meadow, wet in the hollows and dry on the rises, with a few thorn trees leaning all the same way.

pages.label: go(region__tw84_103,region__t84)
pages.page: Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. Mist lying on the marsh, the reeds standing up out of it and the ground not showing at all. To the north-west the land rises.

One of the wicker traps is fast under a sunk branch in the deep channel, and the eel-catcher has been heaving at it a long while. The eel-catcher, a fisher in a flat boat among wicker traps, with a pole twice their height, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tr48_s1_s2_way,region__s1_s2_way)
pages.page: The road between Misthythe and Merscstede goes through scattered woods and the clearings of charcoal-burners. A stag stands in a clearing, watching, before it turns away. By the road stands an old milestone, worn to a stub, with a wheel cut in it and something over the wheel that might once have been a crown. Cattle fill the road from hedge to hedge, going to Misthythe, and Ralf, the drover, is whistling among them. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Sphagnum moss lies in the wet hollows, red and green, holding water like a sponge: it binds a wound better than linen. Comfrey grows rank by the water, hairy-leaved, its bells hanging: knitbone, the herb-wives call it. Dragonwort grows along the road, a red spike among spearing leaves. Bloodroot grows along the road, broad-leaved, with white flowers low to the ground. Celandine grows along the road, yellow-starred in the damp. Cinquefoil runs over the ground along the road, its small yellow flowers five-petalled. Daffodils grow along the road in a bank, their strap-leaves in clumps. Alhuren grows along the road, silver-leaved, its blue flowers pale as a candle-flame. Rosenoble grows along the road, a briar of deep red roses. Hazel grows along the road, broad-leaved, its nuts in clusters of three. Hyssop grows along the road in spikes of blue, bees working it. Staggerweed grows along the road, tall, with spurred blue flowers. Pennyroyal grows along the road, low and minty, with small purple flowers. Poppies grow along the road, red among the beds. Thistles grow along the road, purple-headed. Tansy grows along the road, its yellow buttons over feathery leaves. A dropberry bush grows along the road, its red berries hanging in strings. Starwort grows along the road, small and white-flowered. Actaea grows along the road, its white flowers in feathery spikes. Bruisewort grows along the road, thick-leaved, with small purple flowers. Betony stands in the short grass at the wood’s edge, purple-spiked: the hedge herb, for a cut or a sting.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_s2_way_t)

pages.label: go(region__w13_track,region__w13)
pages.page: It is cold enough to see your breath, and the ruts are hard with frost. The path runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate. A long grassed mound with a stone-lined entrance. Owl pellets lie on the lintel stone. On the stone across the entrance, in the old script: WET HOWE. A mist lies in the low ground below the ridge and thins as it climbs, so that the howe on the skyline appears and goes in it like something breathing. A drystone wall climbs the slope beside the mound, and the steep path goes up along it, a pale scar in the heather. The steep path climbs the ridge in the clear, a pale scar through heather and scree. Above the mound a long ridge climbs to the east, bare and brown, and along its crest, three times the height of any mound below it, a great howe lies against the sky. This low one at your feet is a marker, set where the Barrow-Kin’s land began. Two columns of smoke stand on the ridge above you: one thick and black, from some digging on the near side, and one thin and white and steady, from higher ground to the north. There is more here than the way you came by, and the place would bear searching. Wenna gains 10 experience: found Wet Howe.

pages.label: search(region__w13)
pages.page: You search Wet Howe with care, a little at a time. Where the wall meets the scree, a sheep-way goes off along the slope, keeping well under the skyline.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You owe Hallon fifty coin, for a cart of smoked eels that went into the river at the ford last spring. The oxen went too. Hallon has been patient, and wrote to say so. Patient until market day, ten days from now: not a day longer. Misthythe has not changed. You come in off the road with your head down, past faces that knew you once. You go straight to Hallon’s door: better it is done at once. 50 coin by market day, owed to Hallon, salter at Misthythe.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word9__h3_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Fenstone: the fallen walls in the fen south of Misthythe,’ says Hallon. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “fen stone”.’ ‘At Fenstone, where the brook goes under the road-wall, the arch is wide enough to crawl in, and the water that comes out of it is warmer than brook water has any right to be,’ says Hallon. Fenstone is the name of the fallen walls they speak of.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_merchant)
pages.page: Hallon looks at your hands before your face, to see whether there is anything in them.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word9__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘The old paved road bends once at Fenstone, eight miles round a hill that has nothing in it to bend for,’ says Hallon. ‘Carters leave a coin at the bend and do not stop. Some say the hill hums.’

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word13__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘A company of the barefoot is walking the old road from town to town, chalking the milestones and calling out their numbers, and the Bench does not like it,’ says Hallon.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word12__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘The head of the Chapter of the Unshuttered Window has had no word from one of its halls since the quarter-day, and has sent no one, for want of anyone who can be spared,’ says Hallon.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word11__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Marsh Garth: a walled keep on its rise in the fen south of Misthythe,’ says Hallon. ‘A crier in the castellan’s colours has read a levy on the green: spears and grain, to be at the keep on the twelfth day, for the king’s muster,’ says Hallon. Marsh Garth is the name of the walled keep on its rise they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word10__h2_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Wet Howe: a grassed mound in the fen north-west of Merscstede,’ says Hallon. ‘The shire-reeve’s clerk is raising a levy and is short of iron and gold,’ says Hallon. ‘He will pay by the weight for the torc of the king of the great howe on the ridge, or for any torc of the Barrow-Kin.’ Wet Howe is the name of the grassed mound north-west of Merscstede they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word3__h3_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Mosswatch: a lone tower in Cloudfell,’ says Hallon. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “moss watch”.’ ‘Behind Mosswatch, the tower where the green light burns at night, an old well runs down into the cellars,’ says Hallon. ‘The builders used it.’ Mosswatch is the name of the lone tower they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word1__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘A factor at the inn buys old bronze by the pound and asks no questions: bells, weir-metal, green fittings from the plough,’ says Hallon.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: The herb-wife at Misthythe wrapped the feverwort in a cloth and put it in your hands. ‘The child at Broadford has had the fever three days, and they have nothing left there,’ she said. ‘Don’t dawdle.’ The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Broadford: low roofs against the sky, the river shining and the crossing over it, slate roofs and slate fences. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Take the feverwort you carry to the child at the ford at Broadford: its mother is waiting, three days into the fever.

pages.label: go(region__s3_approach_way,region__s3_green)
pages.page: At Broadford the houses stand close along the bank where the road goes down into the Broadwater. A rope is strung across the water on posts, green where hands have held it. Beyond the roofs lies the Palewater. The fells rise steeply behind the last houses. Twice this month the Hall’s keeper has driven the town’s pigs off the verge of the old road. At dusk every dog in the town turns its head toward the hill, and the geese go silent. The shutters of one house are drawn in daylight, and a woman stands in its door, watching the road. The Broadwater runs knee-deep and clear over the ford stones. A carter stands thigh-deep in the water with his breeches rolled, hauling at the bridle of a horse that will not come. Wellby is roping down a load of barrels. Garret Greenbottle is soldering a hole in a kettle over a little fire, squinting through the smoke. Bree is reading the evening office from a small book, lips moving. Alton Tosscobble is touching up a painted backcloth of a castle with a small brush. The inn’s dog lies across the doorstep of the Golden Bear with her chin on her paws, and watches who comes. A woman in black sits on the step of a cold house with her hands in her lap, watching the road. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. Amaranth grows in the gardens about the green, its dark red tassels hanging over the beds. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Broadford, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. A drover’s boy of fourteen, seen on the hill the morning after the herd crossed it, is here. So are Garrow Pelt, Fenella Hilltopple, Myrtle Hilltopple and the woman in black. Ghost gets up, stretches, and comes over to push her nose into your hand.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: You have come over the hills into Faennmeós with your trade and not much else. There is work in any country for someone who will do what others will not. The place to hear of it is the inn. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Misthythe: low roofs against the sky, masts at the landing, eel-traps stacked against the walls. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Go to the taproom of the Laughing Flame and ask after work: there is work in Misthythe for someone who will do what others will not.

A hedgehog, a small brown hedgehog with a coat of pale-tipped spines and a pointed, whiskered snout, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw101_121,region__t101)
pages.page: You walk fast to keep warm, and it does not help much. The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Bramble and hazel thick under the trees, and a way through only where the deer have pushed.

pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. A stand of tall trees with little under them, so that you can see a long way between the trunks, and nothing moving.

pages.page: Bramble and hazel thick under the trees, and a way through only where the deer have pushed. A moth, a large moth with soft grey-brown wings marked with eyes, its feathered feelers spread, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw41_61,region__t61)
pages.page: Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. Trampled into the bracken by the rooting lies a pack, its strap broken, as if dropped by someone running. The ground under the oaks is rooted up in raw swathes, the earth in them still dark and wet. Whatever did it is not far off. A boar, an old boar with one tusk broken, rooting for mast, is here. A boar comes out of the holly with its head low, and stands, and blows. It does not mean to go round you. A boar is watching you. In 8 minutes it will be on you.

pages.page: It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by. Meadow, wet in the hollows and dry on the rises, with a few thorn trees leaning all the same way. Misthythe is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tl_w10,region__w10)
pages.page: A long grassed mound with a stone-lined entrance. Crows sit along the ridge of the mound, and do not fly. On the stone across the entrance, in the old script: BLACK BARROW. A cold fire-ring, a crushed bed of bracken, and under a stone a small grey pouch sewn with red letters. Someone slept here once, and meant to be back. Water comes out of the back wall of Black Barrow warm, and runs down a channel worn in the rock to a basin no larger than a bucket. The air round it smells of iron and, faintly, of eggs. Eyes shine at the back of Black Barrow. Bones lie scattered in front of it. The zombies are here. Wenna gains 10 experience: found Black Barrow.

pages.label: go(region__tl_w10,region__t62)
pages.page: Meadow, wet in the hollows and dry on the rises, with a few thorn trees leaning all the same way.

pages.label: go(region__tw62_82,region__t82)
pages.page: You set out from open fields south-west of Misthythe. The path runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate. Open country: rough pasture and old field-strips gone back to grass, a hedge here and there, the sky very big over it. To the south the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw102_122,region__t102)
pages.page: Larks go up out of the grass on either hand, and come down again behind you. Old ridge and furrow under the turf, the plough’s lines still there long after the plough.

pages.label: go(region__tw83_102,region__t83)
pages.page: Flat grazing on close, springy turf, and willows along a ditch you cannot see.

pages.label: go(region__tw63_83,region__t63)

pages.label: go(region__tw63_64,region__t64)
pages.page: Wet ground, sedge and cotton-grass, the pools reflecting the sky, a heron getting up slow and offended. The Swanwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. To the west the land rises. Misthythe is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke. Three stones are set one on another here, where no other stones lie, and the ground at their foot has been dug and trodden flat again: somebody’s mark.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: The map is inside your shirt, where it has been since the night you won it. It is a square of greased hide with the hills drawn on it in soot. On it are High Hold out in the fen north-east of Merscstede, and a cross at its door. The drover you won it from laughed when he lost it. In the morning he was dead in the straw, and nobody in the inn would say of what. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Misthythe: low roofs against the sky, masts at the landing, eel-traps stacked against the walls. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. The dead man’s map marks High Hold, out in the fen north-east of Merscstede, with a cross at its door. Search there.

pages.label: go(region__gate_lull_road,region__gate_lull)
pages.page: It is cold enough to see your breath, and the ruts are hard with frost. For a while the road keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. The last mile is slow going. The road goes on into the Lull. Ahead, a bare green hill with a standing stone on it, and a road that goes round the hill and comes back.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_lull,region__t56)
pages.page: Woodland: oak and ash and holly, the light green and broken, last year’s leaves deep underfoot. To the north-west the land rises. Broadford is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw56_76,region__t76)
pages.page: The path runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. The Swanwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. Broadford is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw57_76,region__t57)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Pine wood, the ground soft with needles and the smell of resin heavy in the still air. To the north-west the land rises. Broadford is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke. A shepherd with a crook and a young dog at heel, looking about as if for something lost, is here. A whistle, and a young dog comes bounding at you through the grass and stops short, and behind it a shepherd, crook in hand, who calls it off and looks you over.

pages.label: talk_to(region__wr97)
pages.page: A shepherd nods to you, and says nothing until you do.

pages.label: go(region__tw57_58,region__t58)
pages.page: You walk fast to keep warm, and it does not help much. Water stands on both sides, and the path between is soft enough to take the print of your boot and keep it. Night comes on while you are still on the path, and you walk the last of it in the dark. Alder carr standing in its own black water, the roots like knuckles. To the north-west the land rises. Broadford is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw38_58,region__t38)
pages.page: You set out from wet ground north-east of Broadford. The path goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it. Reed-beds whispering in the wind, and a bittern in them booming like a blown jar. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw37_38,region__t37)
pages.page: The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw36_37,region__t36)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw17_37,region__t17)
pages.page: Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. Woundwort grows thick in a wet hollow under the trees, purple-flowered and rank-smelling: the herb the hedge-doctors bind on cuts.

pages.label: go(region__tw16_17,region__t16)
pages.page: Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw16_35,region__t35)
pages.page: Sheep stand on the path and move off only when you are close. High ground, rock breaking through the turf, and below, when you turn, the whole country laid out small. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw15_34,region__t15)
pages.page: The path goes up by stony steps and down by rougher ones, and it is windy on every rise. A saddle between two tops, boggy, with the cloud sitting on both of them. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw15_34,region__t34)
pages.page: Up on the tops there is nothing but heather, sky and wind, and a cairn now and then to say you are still on the path. High ground, rock breaking through the turf, and below, when you turn, the whole country laid out small.

pages.label: go(region__tw55_74,region__t74)
