pages.label: go(region__tl_w2,region__w2)
pages.page: A doorway opens in the face of a crag, round-headed and smooth as poured wax, with no mark of a tool anywhere on it. Wind across it makes a low note that comes and goes. Over the doorway, letters flow into the stone rather than being cut in it, in the old script: VITRUMARCUS. The flat stone by the way in has been turned over, not long ago: the grass beneath it is still pressed in the shape of something round, and there are the prints of good boots, going back the way they came. A door of one grey stone fills the way in, without hinge or handle. Words are cut deep across it in the old script, and under them, in a later hand, scratched small, what they say: ‘What goes through cities and fields, but never moves?’ Below is a row of words with a hollow beside each, worn smooth by fingers. This is Glassarch, as the folk call it. Its makers called it Vitrumarcus. Deer go off between the trees without a sound. Cut deep over the way in, in the makers’ letters: VITRUMARCUS. Wenna gains 20 experience: found Glassarch.

pages.label: listen(region__w2_riddle)
pages.page: You put an ear to the speaking door, and hold your breath. There is nothing to hear from it.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: Her last letter is in your coat, read so often it has come apart at the folds. She was going out to Streamfountain, in Hollyholt, with two men from Misthythe who swore there was silver in it. She would write when she was rich. The two men came back at the end of the summer. She did not, and they will not say why. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Misthythe: low roofs against the sky, masts at the landing, eel-traps stacked against the walls. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Your sister went into Streamfountain, out in Hollyholt, and did not come out. Search there for any sign of her.

pages.label: go(region__z2_way5,region__z2_edge)
pages.page: You walk fast to keep warm, and it does not help much. Here Ashurst begins: hazel and thorn at first, then oak, and the light under them goes green. Misthythe is behind you, out in the open. A smell of rain comes from deeper in, though no rain has fallen here for days. Willows lean out over the water here, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Meadowsweet grows thick along the wet ground, a froth of cream flowers that smells of almonds and honey. Comfrey grows rank by the water, hairy-leaved, its bells hanging: knitbone, the herb-wives call it. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Feverwort grows here in the rough grass, bitter-leaved: the herb-wives dry it for a child’s fever. Bamboo grows here in a dense clump, its canes knocking together in the wind. A bay tree grows here, dark and glossy, clipped for its leaves. Banewort grows here, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Celandine grows here, yellow-starred in the damp. Staggerweed grows here, tall, with spurred blue flowers. A cinnamon tree grows here, its bark peeled in strips.

pages.label: go(region__z2_way1,region__s1_s2_way)
pages.page: The path runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. The road between Misthythe and Merscstede goes through scattered woods and the clearings of charcoal-burners. A stag stands in a clearing, watching, before it turns away. By the road stands an old milestone, worn to a stub, with a wheel cut in it and something over the wheel that might once have been a crown. Ralf is standing in the road shouting at a hedge. One of the cattle has gone through it into the field beyond. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Sphagnum moss lies in the wet hollows, red and green, holding water like a sponge: it binds a wound better than linen. Dragonwort grows along the road, a red spike among spearing leaves. Bloodroot grows along the road, broad-leaved, with white flowers low to the ground. Celandine grows along the road, yellow-starred in the damp. Cinquefoil runs over the ground along the road, its small yellow flowers five-petalled. Daffodils grow along the road in a bank, their strap-leaves in clumps. Alhuren grows along the road, silver-leaved, its blue flowers pale as a candle-flame. Rosenoble grows along the road, a briar of deep red roses. Hazel grows along the road, broad-leaved, its nuts in clusters of three. Hyssop grows along the road in spikes of blue, bees working it. Staggerweed grows along the road, tall, with spurred blue flowers. Pennyroyal grows along the road, low and minty, with small purple flowers. Poppies grow along the road, red among the beds. Thistles grow along the road, purple-headed. Tansy grows along the road, its yellow buttons over feathery leaves. A dropberry bush grows along the road, its red berries hanging in strings. Starwort grows along the road, small and white-flowered. Actaea grows along the road, its white flowers in feathery spikes. Bruisewort grows along the road, thick-leaved, with small purple flowers. Betony stands in the short grass at the wood’s edge, purple-spiked: the hedge herb, for a cut or a sting.

pages.label: go(region__z1_way1,region__z1_edge)
pages.page: It is cold enough to see your breath, and the ruts are hard with frost. The path runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate. Where the fields end, Duskmoss begins: black water between tussocks, reed higher than your head, and the smell of it. Misthythe is behind you, on the firm ground. Deeper in, at the edge of sight, there are people at work. Nobody lives out there.

pages.label: go(region__tl_z1_edge,region__t46)
pages.page: Alder carr standing in its own black water, the roots like knuckles. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.page: The path goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it. pages.page: You set out from the woods of Ashurst. A stand of tall trees with little under them, so that you can see a long way between the trunks, and nothing moving. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw69_70,region__t70)
pages.page: Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. To the south-east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw70_90,region__t90)

Merscstede is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw90_109,region__t109)
pages.page: Fen: reeds taller than a man, black water between, and the ground giving underfoot with every step. To the north-east the land rises. Merscstede is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw108_109,region__t108)

pages.page: Alder carr standing in its own black water, the roots like knuckles.

pages.label: go(region__tw107_108,region__t108)
pages.page: Mist lying on the marsh, the reeds standing up out of it and the ground not showing at all.

pages.label: go(region__tw128_129,region__t129)
pages.page: Peat ground cut once into steps, and long since flooded. To the south the land rises. Merscstede is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw149_169,region__t169)
pages.page: Pine wood, the ground soft with needles and the smell of resin heavy in the still air.

pages.label: go(region__tw148_169,region__t148)

pages.page: For a while the path keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. Open water and mud among willow stumps, smelling of rot and mint. The Swanwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. To the east the land rises.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: The scroll-case has not been off your shoulder in eleven days. In it is a letter under the seal of a magistrate who did not give his name, for Lindal at Merscstede, into no other hands. Half the fee was paid at the start. The other half, and whatever Lindal thinks it worth, is at the far end of the road. The next town on from Misthythe is Merscstede. The causeway runs on its piles across the last of the fen. At the end of it is Misthythe: low roofs against the sky, masts at the landing, eel-traps stacked against the walls. Smoke goes straight up from the chimneys. A cart stands canted at the side of the road, one wheel down in the ditch to the hub. The horse is blowing in the shafts, and a sack of meal has burst on the bed. The wagoner is up to his knees in the ditch with his shoulder to the wheel. He looks round when he hears you, and does not ask for help. Carry the sealed letter to Lindal at Merscstede, into no other hands.

pages.page: You walk fast to keep warm, and it does not help much. It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by. Long grass gone to seed, and the wind combing it one way and then the other.

pages.label: go(region__tw102_123,region__t123)
pages.page: The path runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate. Meadow, wet in the hollows and dry on the rises, with a few thorn trees leaning all the same way.

pages.label: go(region__tw83_103,region__t83)
pages.page: Flat grazing on close, springy turf, and willows along a ditch you cannot see. A pedlar with a pack on a frame and a staff, walking the drove-ways between the farms, is here. A pedlar is coming the other way along the sheep-track, bent under a pack on a frame, and lifts his staff to you from a long way off.

pages.label: talk_to(region__wr44)
pages.page: ‘Well now,’ says a pedlar, brightening at the sight of a new face. ‘What brings you?’

pages.label: go(region__tw63_83,region__t63)
pages.page: You set out from open fields south of Misthythe. The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Birch and rowan on a slope, the light coming white through the leaves. Misthythe is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.page: Meadow, wet in the hollows and dry on the rises, with a few thorn trees leaning all the same way. Misthythe is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw61_82,region__t61)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. Trampled into the bracken by the rooting lies a pack, its strap broken, as if dropped by someone running. The ground under the oaks is rooted up in raw swathes, the earth in them still dark and wet. pages.label: go(region__tl_edge_west,region__edge_west)
pages.page: The road comes to the edge of Faennmeós on a causeway of logs, and a tall post stands in the water beside it with a fish-basket hung on it and a mark cut at the top, where the bounds were set. Beyond it the road goes on west into Muzgkatzeh, upland country, the folk say. Few of them have been.

pages.label: go(region__edge_west_road,region__s1_green)
pages.page: It is cold enough to see your breath, and the ruts are hard with frost. Misthythe shows ahead a long while before you reach it: smoke, a roofline, the noise of it on the wind. Boats lie drawn up keel to keel on the shingle at Misthythe, and the houses come right down to them, nets hung on every fence. A board is nailed to the tail-gate of the hiring-man’s cart: WANTED, DIGGERS, FOR THE SPADE-COMPANY’S WORKS ON THE LONG RIDGE, ABOVE A GRASSED MOUND, IN THE HILLS. FOUR A DAY AND FOUND. BY LICENCE OF THE SHIRE-REEVE. Under it, in a child’s chalk: DON’T. The crier’s paper names the lord’s keep, a walled keep on its rise, in the fen south of Misthythe, a day or so along the roads from here, and the tower and star on his breast are the keep’s. Magot is crying wares along the street: pots mended, knives ground. Hild is darning the hem of a red stage cloak. Isot the bookkeeper is weighing a handful of nails on a small brass scale. Averil the conspirator is shuffling a worn pack of cards one-handed. The inn’s dog lies across the doorstep of the Laughing Flame with his chin on his paws, and watches who comes. A thin brown cat crouches at the foot of a wall, watching a hole in it without a blink. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. A tall wagon, painted with a sun and a moon and the words GOSSE’S COMPANY in red letters gone pink, stands on the landing at Misthythe with its shafts down. A chain runs from its back wheel to a post, and the chain has a padlock on it. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. The spring-head by the green has been running low for a year. The rope comes up with a hand’s depth of brown water in the bucket and a smell of wet stone, and the women who draw it do so in silence, to save breath. A paper is nailed to the post under the crier’s bell-rope: THE LORD OF THE KEEP CALLS HIS MARCH TO THE KING’S MUSTER. TWENTY SPEARS AND A HUNDRED BUSHELS TO THE KEEP ON THE TWELFTH DAY. Underneath, in another hand, scratched with a nail: AND WHO IS TO SOW? Somebody has chalked a number on the well-stone, large and fresh, and under it a small neat wheel with a wing on it. A few barefoot prints go in and out of the inn’s door. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Misthythe, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. The old woman in the doorway, the innkeeper’s mother, who has not been out of her chair since the harvest and who asks, every morning, whether the lamp has been lit, is here. So are Absalom Gosse, Hepzibah Dimmock, Jem Pudding, Ulf, Aldred, Alfric, the Dunning lads, Tilda and the walkers. The wardens have stopped paying. A hayrick at Merscstede has burned in the night, and the bailiff has put up a new notice: SIX CROWNS, AND A FINE FOR THE FIRE. A board is nailed to the tail-gate of the hiring-man’s cart: WANTED, DIGGERS, FOR THE SPADE-COMPANY’S WORKS ON THE LONG RIDGE, ABOVE A GRASSED MOUND, IN THE HILLS. FOUR A DAY AND FOUND. BY LICENCE OF THE SHIRE-REEVE. Under it, in a child’s chalk: DON’T. The crier’s paper names the lord’s keep, a walled keep on its rise, in the fen south of Misthythe, a day or so along the roads from here, and the tower and star on his breast are the keep’s. A string of barefoot strangers has taken the well-steps and is chalking the stone: a number, and a little wheel with a wing. They are singing something with no tune to speak of and a great deal of will. Somewhere behind the singing a man is selling something, with the voice of a man who has sold it before.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: Bran went with them without a word, only putting his tally-stick into your hand as they took him. The drove is in the pens behind the customs-house, thirty-six head and nobody’s but yours to mind. Owain is at your elbow on the landing. He is your cousin, fourteen, and frightened. The customs clerk says four beasts were hidden from the toll. Eleven days down from the fells, and the last mile the worst. In the dark the Black Rhyne’s bank went out from under the tail of the drove. You heard them in the water. Bran said leave them. Then Porthalen at first light, salt-houses and masts, the customs-men waiting at the march-stone with their staves. They counted. They took Bran. Ask Owain how many head came down: the customs clerk says four were hidden from the toll.

pages.label: talk_to(region__w8_head)
pages.page: The factor looks you up and down. ‘Whatever it is, the answer’s probably no. Go on.’ Patch barks twice, then comes to see who you are. You take Bran’s tally-stick.

pages.label: read_item(origin__stick)
pages.page: Bran’s tally-stick has thirty-six notches for the drove, and four more cut through at the Black Rhyne.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r7)
pages.page: Sabine looks you over, and does not like what she sees.

pages.label: talk_to(drove__owain)
pages.page: Owain gets up so fast the stool goes over, and then stands there, not sure what to do with his hands.

pages.label: talk_to(gate__wright)
pages.page: Gwil Pryce looks up and smiles broadly. ‘Hello! What can I do?’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r9)
pages.page: Aldred waits for you to speak, and does nothing to help.

pages.label: talk_to(pricePatron__widow)
pages.page: ‘Yes?’ says the woman in black, without hurry.

pages.label: talk_to(gate__reeve)
pages.page: Reeve Annis Talfryn looks at you for longer than is comfortable. ‘Well?’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r10)
pages.page: Baldric does not look up. ‘Say it, then.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r8)
pages.page: Thurstan looks up, and puts his hands still, and waits for you to say what you want.

pages.label: go(drove__rhyne_bank,drove__pens)
pages.page: Thirty-six black bullocks of the fells, rough-coated and restless, crowd the rails, bawling to be watered.

pages.label: go(drove__rhyne_bank,drove__rhyne)
pages.page: A dyke of black water between steep banks, the far bank slumped into it where the sea came over in the winter. The smell reaches you before the sight does.

pages.label: search(drove__rhyne)
pages.page: You search the Black Rhyne, behind the pens with care, a little at a time. Down where the bank has slumped, under the black water, something big and dark: a bullock, and another beyond it, four in all, the brand of a Brynach drove burnt into each flank. They have been there days.

pages.label: put_item(origin__stick)
pages.page: You set Bran’s tally-stick down.

pages.label: go(drove__pens_gate,region__s1_green)
pages.page: A quay of grey stone runs out into the water at Porthalen, its edge worn round and green with weed, and the town climbs behind it. The inn’s dog lies across the doorstep of the Stone Horn with his chin on his paws, and watches who comes. Owain stands at the edge of the quay with his hands in his armpits, watching the customs-house door. A woman in black sits on the step of a cold house with her hands in her lap, watching the road. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. A notice in a clerk’s hand is nailed to the post by the well: THE SEA-GATE AT GATESEND IS TO BE MENDED BEFORE THE SPRING TIDE. THIRTY CROWNS OF THE REEVE TO WHOEVER MENDS IT. A. TALFRYN, REEVE. The spring-head by the green has been running low for a year. The rope comes up with a hand’s depth of brown water in the bucket and a smell of wet stone, and the women who draw it do so in silence, to save breath. The factor, who keeps the books of the Guldríce company, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Porthalen, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. So are Reeve Annis Talfryn, Gwil Pryce and the woman in black. The bailiff’s men have been through again. The price is five crowns a hearth now, and the reeve has been seen reading the receipt by the well and putting it in his pocket. The surveyor’s son has gone: his mule is not at the rail, and the boy at the stable says he was gone before light, with a spade. The merchant keeps looking up the road with the face of a person doing sums.

pages.label: go(region__gate_skerrow_road,region__gate_skerrow)
pages.page: You leave Porthalen late, in rain, with the light going early under the cloud. The road goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the road. The road goes on into Scarth Holm. Ahead, a white tower on a grey flat, with posts going out to it. It is a long time since you slept. You are weary, and will fight the worse for it until you sleep.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_skerrow,region__t16)
pages.page: Wet ground, sedge and cotton-grass, the pools reflecting the sky, a heron getting up slow and offended. To the south-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw16_36,region__t36)
pages.page: It rains on and off the whole way, a fine rain that soaks through your clothes. An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. To the south the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw36_56,region__t56)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Woodland: oak and ash and holly, the light green and broken, last year’s leaves deep underfoot.

pages.label: go(region__tw56_57,region__t57)
pages.page: Birch and rowan on a slope, the light coming white through the leaves. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw100_121,region__t100)
pages.page: A stand of tall trees with little under them, so that you can see a long way between the trunks, and nothing moving.

pages.label: go(region__tw107_128,region__t128)
pages.page: Water stands on both sides, and the path between is soft enough to take the print of your boot and keep it. Wet ground, sedge and cotton-grass, the pools reflecting the sky, a heron getting up slow and offended. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw78_98,region__t78)
pages.page: The path goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it. Wet ground, sedge and cotton-grass, the pools reflecting the sky, a heron getting up slow and offended. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw58_78,region__t58)
pages.page: Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. Peat ground cut once into steps, and long since flooded. To the west the land rises. Tracks cross the ground here, heavy and fresh and all going the one way, west, and the same tracks older under them: something uses this way often.

pages.label: go(region__tw37_58,region__t37)
pages.page: Mist lying on the marsh, the reeds standing up out of it and the ground not showing at all. To the south the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_tessary,region__gate_tessary)
pages.page: The road goes on into the Ossel delta. Ahead, the smoke of a town where the marsh meets the sea.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: Holgar stands at the door looking up the river toward Reedbridge, as Holgar has every hour since the day before yesterday. ‘Two days late,’ Holgar says, without turning. ‘Three days cold and the brine goes off. Then the season is lost, and your wage with it.’ Then, turning: ‘I can’t leave the pans. You can.’ Grey light through the salt-house door at Porthalen, and your breath smoking. All night you fed the last hearth with barrel-staves and broken crates. It was not enough. By dawn two of the three pans had a skin of salt on them like ice on a pond. Find out what has become of Holgar’s fuel boat at Reedbridge: the salt-pans at Porthalen go cold in three days without it.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word4__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘The last of the Water-Wardens’ sea-gates, at Gatesend, no longer shuts: at the spring tide, six days off, the sea will come over into the fen,’ says Holgar. ‘The reeve at Porthalen pays thirty crowns to have it mended.’

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word8__h3_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Merekeep: the fallen walls in the fen south of Reedbridge,’ says Holgar. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “wet keep”.’ ‘At Merekeep, where the brook goes under the road-wall, the arch is wide enough to crawl in, and the water that comes out of it is warmer than brook water has any right to be,’ says Holgar. Merekeep is the name of the fallen walls they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word8__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘The old paved road bends once at Merekeep, eight miles round a hill that has nothing in it to bend for,’ says Holgar. ‘Carters leave a coin at the bend and do not stop. Some say the hill hums.’

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word2__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘The customs-men at Porthalen hold Bran, the Brynach lead-drover, for cheating the Rì’s toll: four head short, their clerk says,’ says Holgar.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_merchant)
pages.page: Holgar takes in the state of you: the road dust, the tiredness. ‘You’ve come a way. What do you need?’

pages.label: ask(region__s1_merchant,word1__h1_s1_merchant)
pages.page: ‘A factor at the inn buys old bronze by the pound and asks no questions: bells, weir-metal, green fittings from the plough,’ says Holgar.

pages.label: go(region__s1_shop_door,region__s1_green)
pages.page: A quay of grey stone runs out into the water at Porthalen, its edge worn round and green with weed, and the town climbs behind it. Gulls sit along it in a row, facing the wind, over the slap of water on stone. The Whitewater runs by below the houses. Twice this month the Hall’s keeper has driven the town’s pigs off the verge of the old road. The geese are kept in a bunch at the well, hissing at the lane to the Hall, and three hens have gone from the inn’s yard since Tuesday. Across the green the customs-house door stands open, and a customs-man in the Rì’s blue leans on the jamb with his staff. From the pens beyond comes the bawling of cattle nobody has fed. Over the salt-houses only one chimney is smoking, thin and grey. A salter stands in a doorway looking up the river with his arms folded. A boat is coming in under half its sail, and a man waits on the quay with a coil of rope over his arm. On the landing a man is caulking the seams of a flat-bottomed boat no longer than a cart, and three more stand finished on trestles with a chalked price on each: thirty. Sabine is crying wares along the street: pots mended, knives ground. Thurstan is showing a boy how to hold a staff, and correcting his feet without a word. Aldred stands by the door with a cudgel at his belt, watching the street. Baldric the painting master is weighing a handful of nails on a small brass scale. The inn’s dog lies across the doorstep of the Stone Horn with his chin on his paws, and watches who comes. Owain stands at the edge of the quay with his hands in his armpits, watching the customs-house door. A woman in black sits on the step of a cold house with her hands in her lap, watching the road. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. A bay tree grows in the gardens about the green, dark and glossy, clipped for its leaves. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. A notice in a clerk’s hand is nailed to the post by the well: THE SEA-GATE AT GATESEND IS TO BE MENDED BEFORE THE SPRING TIDE. THIRTY CROWNS OF THE REEVE TO WHOEVER MENDS IT. A. TALFRYN, REEVE. The spring-head by the green has been running low for a year. The rope comes up with a hand’s depth of brown water in the bucket and a smell of wet stone, and the women who draw it do so in silence, to save breath. The factor, who keeps the books of the Guldríce company, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Porthalen, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. So are the surveyor’s son, Reeve Annis Talfryn, Gwil Pryce and the woman in black. Patch thumps his tail on the ground without getting up.

pages.label: talk_to(drove__owain)
pages.page: Owain slaps the nearest flat surface by way of welcome. ‘Well? Out with it!’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r7)
pages.page: ‘If it’s trouble,’ says Sabine, ‘I have enough of my own.’

pages.label: talk_to(gate__wright)
pages.page: ‘Well now,’ says Gwil Pryce, brightening at the sight of a new face. ‘What brings you?’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r8)
pages.page: Thurstan hears you come, and finishes what he was doing before he looks round.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r10)
pages.page: Baldric looks at you for longer than is comfortable. ‘Well?’

pages.label: talk_to(region__w8_head)
pages.page: ‘Lost?’ says the factor. ‘People usually are, when they come over to me.’

pages.label: talk_to(gate__reeve)
pages.page: Reeve Annis Talfryn does not look up. ‘Say it, then.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r9)
pages.page: Aldred looks you over, and does not like what he sees.

pages.label: go(region__z1_way5,region__z1_heart)
pages.page: Showers come over one after another, and between them the sun comes out on the wet country. A landing of piled faggots where the reed-cutters bring their bundles out. Cut reed is stacked here in ricks, waiting for a boat. One of the stakes here has a twist of rag tied round it, faded to no colour, and leans off the line of the others: someone marked a way off from here. Reed-buntings sit on the ricks. Ricks of cut reed stand on the staithe. Willows lean out over the water here, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Sphagnum moss lies in the wet hollows, red and green, holding water like a sponge: it binds a wound better than linen. Comfrey grows rank by the water, hairy-leaved, its bells hanging: knitbone, the herb-wives call it.

pages.label: search(region__z1_heart)
pages.page: You search the reed landing with care, a little at a time. A track you had not seen goes off from here: the way to a great long mound with a door of stone.

pages.label: look_closely(region__z1_heart_ricks)
pages.page: You look closely at the reed ricks. The reed is tied in bundles a fathom round, the way thatchers buy it. Chalked on the end of the nearest rick is a tally, and a mark like a bird’s foot.

pages.label: go(region__tw277_278,region__t278)
pages.page: Open water and mud among willow stumps, smelling of rot and mint. The Whitewater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. To the north the land rises. Porthalen is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tl_edge_south,region__edge_south)
pages.page: At the edge of Iscoed a beacon stands on stilts above the reeds, a fire-basket rusted open at the top, so that the bounds could be found in fog. Beyond it the road goes on south into Cloudwold, frozen country, the folk say. Few of them have been.

pages.label: go(region__tl_edge_south,region__t278)
pages.page: Open water and mud among willow stumps, smelling of rot and mint.

pages.label: go(region__tw277_278,region__t277)
pages.page: It rains on and off the whole way, a fine rain that soaks through your clothes. For a while the path keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. Alder carr standing in its own black water, the roots like knuckles. The Whitewater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. To the north the land rises. Porthalen is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw258_277,region__t258)
pages.page: The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Bramble and hazel thick under the trees, and a way through only where the deer have pushed. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight.

pages.label: go(region__tw237_258,region__t237)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Birch and rowan on a slope, the light coming white through the leaves. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. Porthalen is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw237_238,region__t238)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Birch and rowan on a slope, the light coming white through the leaves. To the west the land rises. Porthalen is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw218_238,region__t218)
pages.page: Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. Wet ground, sedge and cotton-grass, the pools reflecting the sky, a heron getting up slow and offended. To the north-west the land rises. Tracks cross the ground here, heavy and fresh and all going the one way, north-west, and the same tracks older under them: something uses this way often.

pages.label: go(region__tw197_218,region__t197)
pages.page: Larks go up out of the grass on either hand, and come down again behind you. Fields let go to thistle and dock, the larks going up out of them as you pass. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight.

pages.label: go(region__tw197_198,region__t198)
pages.page: Water stands on both sides, and the path between is soft enough to take the print of your boot and keep it. Mist lying on the marsh, the reeds standing up out of it and the ground not showing at all. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw178_198,region__t178)
pages.page: The path goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it. Open water and mud among willow stumps, smelling of rot and mint. To the south-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw177_178,region__t177)
pages.page: It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by. Old ridge and furrow under the turf, the plough’s lines still there long after the plough. To the south the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw156_177,region__t156)
pages.page: The path runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate. Night comes on while you are still on the path, and you walk the last of it in the dark. Meadow, wet in the hollows and dry on the rises, with a few thorn trees leaning all the same way. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: the opening
pages.page: ‘You’ll be Tegwen’s,’ says the woman at the next door, and looks you over. ‘Nest. I kept her weir going since the burying. The traps want lifting every morning or the eels rot in them.’ She nods up at the gatehouse. ‘And the gate’s not shut since the new moon. Spring tide’s in six days. When the sea comes over, there’s no weir, and no Gatesend either.’ Your aunt’s door in Gatesend has a wreath of dried rushes on it, and her nets are still on the fence. Below the last houses the fen goes away green and flat. Above the hamlet, where the river meets the sea-bank, stands a squat stone gatehouse. From under it comes a sound you do not remember from when you were a child. It is the sea, running in. Find out why the sea-gate at Gatesend will not shut, before the spring tide.

pages.label: listen(region__s4_u_store_lock)
pages.page: You put an ear to the corn-store padlock, and hold your breath. Pudding comes to wind once round your ankles, and goes back to her place. You take Tegwen’s lease.

pages.label: ask(region__s4_merchant,word9__h2_s4_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Black Howe: a grassed mound in the fen south of Gatesend,’ says Gek. ‘The shire-reeve’s clerk is raising a levy and is short of iron and gold,’ says Gek. ‘He will pay by the weight for the torc of the king of the great howe on the ridge, or for any torc of the Barrow-Kin.’ Black Howe is the name of the grassed mound south of Gatesend they speak of.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s4_merchant)
pages.page: Gek finishes what she was saying to someone else first.

pages.label: ask(region__s4_merchant,word5__h3_s4_merchant)
pages.page: ‘Mosstower: a lone tower in the fen north-west of Edderwick,’ says Gek. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “moss tower”.’ ‘Behind Mosstower, the tower where the green light burns at night, an old well runs down into the cellars,’ says Gek. ‘The builders used it.’ Mosstower is the name of the lone tower they speak of.

pages.label: talk_to(origin__nest)
pages.page: Nest sighs before you have said a word. ‘Go on, then.’

pages.label: talk_to(region__s4_r4)
pages.page: Wat does not look up. ‘Say it, then.’

pages.label: read_item(origin__lease_scroll)
pages.page: The weir at Gatesend is yours on the reeve’s lease. Five coin is owed to the reeve of Porthalen at the quarter-day, a month off.

pages.label: go(region__s4_drill_gate,region__s4_drill)
pages.page: A square of beaten earth behind the Golden Horse, a rack of blunted blades along one wall and a post hacked pale at the height of a man’s neck. Whoever teaches here will show a technique to anyone who has done enough to be worth the showing, and can pay for it. Emmot teaches Whirlwind Attack, Rapid Strike and Shield Bash, 35 coin a lesson: an hour’s work, and only to one who has done enough out in the world to have earned it. On the rack by the gate, for sale and not for practice, are a fine battleaxe, a fine greatsword and a fine scimitar. Emmot, a master-at-arms, who teaches for 35 coin a lesson, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s4_drill_master)
pages.page: ‘Yes?’ says Emmot, without hurry.

pages.label: haggle_item(region__s4_drill_master,region__s4_drill_master_fine_scimitar_1)
pages.page: Emmot will not be argued with, and a fine scimitar is dearer for the asking. Wenna fails the persuasion check (d20 1 + charisma 1 = 2 against 13).

pages.label: region__s4_drill_unearned
pages.page: Emmot looks you over. ‘Come back when you have done something out there: a nest cleared, a debt paid, the dead laid. Then 35 coin, and I will show you.’

pages.label: go(region__s4_drill_gate,region__s4_green)
pages.page: The gate-yard of Gatesend is swept clean to the cobbles, and smells of wet stone and beeswax from the chapel door. Wat the collier is knocking dried clay from a pick, a careful blow at a time. The brothers’ dog lies across the doorstep of the guest-hall with his chin on his paws, and watches who comes. A thin brown cat crouches at the foot of a wall, watching a hole in it without a blink. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. Gek, a herb-wife, selling from the house door, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Gatesend, is here. The old woman in the doorway, the innkeeper’s mother, who has not been out of her chair since the harvest and who asks, every morning, whether the lamp has been lit, is here. So are Simkin and Nest.

pages.label: go(region__s4_cloister_way,region__s4_cloister)
pages.page: A square of grass lies inside a covered walk, with a well in the middle. The walk smells of cold stone and candle-smoke, and water drips far down the well. Edric is hoeing between rows of cabbages, saying the hours under his breath. A book lies face down and open on the bench in the cloister walk.

pages.label: look_closely(region__s4_cloister_book)
pages.page: You look closely at the book left open on the bench. It is the house’s own chronicle, in many hands. The last entry is a week old, and stops in the middle of a word.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s4_r1)
pages.page: Edric looks up, and puts his hands still, and waits for you to say what you want.

pages.label: region__s4_r1_work_again
pages.page: ‘We’re to be silent before the noon bell,’ says Edric, ‘which it isn’t, quite, so I’ll be quick.’

pages.label: wait_hour
pages.page: Edric is hoeing between rows of cabbages, saying the hours under his breath. An hour passes.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s4_r1)
pages.page: ‘Again,’ says Edric, as a thing noted, not a complaint.

pages.label: region__s4_r1_wants
pages.page: ‘I need a bundle of herbs and I’ve no time to go for one,’ says Edric. ‘If you can get one, I’d pay you back and a bit over.’

pages.label: put_item(origin__lease_scroll)
pages.page: You set Tegwen’s lease down.

pages.label: take_leave(region__s4_r1)
pages.page: Edric lifts a hand, once.

pages.label: put_item(region__party_1__rope)
pages.page: You set a coil of rope down.

pages.label: go(region__s2_drill_gate,region__s2_drill)
pages.page: A square of beaten earth behind the Ancient Boar, a rack of blunted blades along one wall and a post hacked pale at the height of a man’s neck. Whoever teaches here will show a technique to anyone who has done enough to be worth the showing, and can pay for it. Lyle teaches Roundhouse Kick, Reckless Attack and Feint, 30 coin a lesson: an hour’s work, and only to one who has done enough out in the world to have earned it. On the rack by the gate, for sale and not for practice, are a fine battleaxe, a fine shortsword and a fine greatsword. Lyle, a master-at-arms, who teaches for 30 coin a lesson, is here.

pages.label: go(region__s2_u_pit_path,region__s2_u_pit)
pages.page: A bowl of grey stone cut out of the hill long ago, ivy over its faces. At the bottom a square adit goes back into the rock behind a barred gate. A board on the gate says KEEP OUT in three hands. Runs worn to bare earth go in under the ivy at the foot of the east face. The smell of fox is on them.

pages.label: go(region__road_s4_s2_on,region__s4_s2_way)
pages.page: It is hot on the road, and you walk slower than you meant to. The road runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate. A drove road, broad and rutted, between Mistshaw and Millholm, with thorn hedges and the odd byre. Rooks walk the new-ploughed furrows for grubs. A milestone leans in the grass at the roadside, half sunk: on its face a worn wheel, and over it, if you look closely, the points of a crown. Lyle Goodbarrel, a pedlar, is sitting on a milestone on the road to Millholm, laying out a tray of ribbons, buttons and needles. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Meadowsweet grows thick along the wet ground, a froth of cream flowers that smells of almonds and honey. Comfrey grows rank by the water, hairy-leaved, its bells hanging: knitbone, the herb-wives call it. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Foxgloves stand tall at the wood’s edge, purple bells speckled inside: they heal, prepared rightly, and kill otherwise. Asters grow along the road in clumps, mauve with yellow eyes. Bamboo grows along the road in a dense clump, its canes knocking together in the wind. Banewort grows along the road, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Daffodils grow along the road in a bank, their strap-leaves in clumps. Rosenoble grows along the road, a briar of deep red roses. Gentian grows along the road, its blue trumpets open to the sun. Woodbine climbs along the road, its cream and yellow flowers sweet at dusk. Poppies grow along the road, red among the beds. Rue grows along the road, blue-green and bitter-smelling. Sweetgrass grows along the road, its long blades smelling of hay. A dropberry bush grows along the road, its red berries hanging in strings. A cherry tree grows along the road, its bark banded and glossy. Starwort grows along the road, small and white-flowered. Groundbread grows along the road, broad-leaved, with small white flowers. Ofbit grows along the road on thin stems, its flowers blue. Fresh ruts run off the edge of the road here, where the bank drops away.

pages.label: go(region__z4_way1,region__z4_side1)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Here Elmholt begins: hazel and thorn at first, then oak, and the light under them goes green. Millholm is behind you, out in the open. Yarrow grows in the grass at the wayside, flat white heads over feathery leaves: a soldier’s herb, for cuts. Feverwort grows here in the rough grass, bitter-leaved: the herb-wives dry it for a child’s fever. Bamboo grows here in a dense clump, its canes knocking together in the wind. Dragonwort grows here, a red spike among spearing leaves. Celandine grows here, yellow-starred in the damp. Cinquefoil runs over the ground here, its small yellow flowers five-petalled. Woodbine climbs here, its cream and yellow flowers sweet at dusk. Staggerweed grows here, tall, with spurred blue flowers. Actaea grows here, its white flowers in feathery spikes. Bruisewort grows here, thick-leaved, with small purple flowers.

pages.label: gather(region__z4_side1_staggerweed_1,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You gather a sprig of staggerweed.

pages.label: go(region__z4_trail1,region__z4_edge)
pages.page: You set out from the edge of Elmholt by Millholm. The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Here Elmholt begins: hazel and thorn at first, then oak, and the light under them goes green. Mossminster is behind you, out in the open. A bay tree grows here, dark and glossy, clipped for its leaves. A cinnamon tree grows here, its bark peeled in strips. Betony stands in the short grass at the wood’s edge, purple-spiked: the hedge herb, for a cut or a sting.

pages.label: go(region__tl_z4_edge,region__t31)
pages.page: Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the west the land rises. Mossminster is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tr31_s4_s5_way,region__s4_s5_way)
pages.page: Larks go up out of the grass on either hand, and come down again behind you. Open farmland on either hand: strip-fields, a mill-pond, cattle that lift their heads as you pass. A fox crosses the road ahead, unhurried, and goes through the hedge. A family is moving house along the road to Mossminster: Cade Underbough pushing a handcart with everything they own on it, and three children walking beside it carrying the rest. Gilliflowers grow along the road, pink and white, smelling of cloves. Celandine grows along the road, yellow-starred in the damp. Euphrosyne grows along the road, low, with small white flowers: eyebright. Hazel grows along the road, broad-leaved, its nuts in clusters of three. Hyssop grows along the road in spikes of blue, bees working it. Staggerweed grows along the road, tall, with spurred blue flowers. Cedron grows along the road, its leaves smelling of lemon when brushed. Pennyroyal grows along the road, low and minty, with small purple flowers. Thistles grow along the road, purple-headed. Thyme grows along the road in low mats, flowering purple. A cinnamon tree grows along the road, its bark peeled in strips. Carenfil grows along the road, pale-petalled, its scent heavy on still days.

pages.label: go(region__e1_track,region__e1)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. The road comes out of the fen north-east of Millholm as a strip of kerbed stone, straighter than anything the folk have built. It runs through a gate-arch into a walled yard. Thirty paces short of the arch stands a squat numbered post, a worn dish on its top. Over the arch, in letters a hand high, is the name and office: FLUMENPORTA. Under it is the mark of the Posts, a wheel with a wing. The gate leaves lie flat on the cobbles inside the arch, long since fallen outward, and moss has grown over them. The road runs in over them as it ran in under them. This is Rivergate, as the folk call it. Its makers called it Flumenporta. An owl roosts where a roof-beam was. Cut deep over the way in, in the makers’ letters: FLUMENPORTA. A squat stone post stands by the kerb with a count cut in it in the old numerals. The dish worn into its top holds rainwater, and in the water, three small coins. Three small coins lie in the dish on top of the post, green with weather: a toll paid against robbery on the road. Wenna Holt gains 20 experience: found Rivergate.

pages.label: go(region__e1_front,region__e1_gate)
pages.page: A vaulted passage wide enough for a post-wagon, its floor paved in stone and grooved by two hundred years of wheels. A guard’s niche on either side. Chalked in the plaster of one, in a crowd of hands, are the distances to places that have no names now. A beam of oak as thick as a man’s thigh, black with age and bound in iron, sits across the inner arch in its brackets.

pages.label: go(region__e1_front,region__e1)

pages.page: Open country: rough pasture and old field-strips gone back to grass, a hedge here and there, the sky very big over it. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight.

pages.label: go(region__tr69_s2_s5_way,region__s2_s5_way)
pages.page: It is hot on the path, and you walk slower than you meant to. The road between Millholm and Mossminster goes through scattered woods and the clearings of charcoal-burners. Deer go off between the trees without a sound. Wheel-ruts, fresh today and deep with a load, go along the road toward Mossminster. Feverwort grows along the road in the rough grass, bitter-leaved: the herb-wives dry it for a child’s fever. Amaranth grows along the road, its dark red tassels hanging over the beds. A bay tree grows along the road, dark and glossy, clipped for its leaves. Bloodroot grows along the road, broad-leaved, with white flowers low to the ground. Rosemary grows along the road, grey-green, with small blue flowers. Tansy grows along the road, its yellow buttons over feathery leaves. Actaea grows along the road, its white flowers in feathery spikes.

pages.label: go(region__z2_way2,region__z2_edge)
pages.page: The shadows are long when you leave the road between Millholm and Mossminster, and getting longer. Here Bearwood begins: hazel and thorn at first, then oak, and the light under them goes green. Mossminster is behind you, out in the open. From deeper in comes a thin ringing when the wind gets up. The notes make no tune. Willows lean out over the water here, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Banewort grows here, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells.

pages.label: go(region__z2_way3,region__s5_green)
pages.page: Mossminster is a handful of roofs at the end of the road, and a dog that comes out to see who you are. A wall runs round the brothers’ house at Mossminster, with the village built against the outside of it. The gate stands open by day, and the bell over it stirs in the wind. The Broadbourne runs by below the houses. Inside the brothers’ house a voice is practising a chant, the same four notes over and over. The brothers’ dog noses along the foot of the wall of the guest-hall, following a smell from stone to stone. A ginger cat sits in the middle of the way, and people step round her. Sabin, a salter, selling from the house door, is here. The prior, who keeps the rule of the brothers of Aergodríce, is here. A drover’s boy of fourteen, seen on the hill the morning after the herd crossed it, is here. So is Garrow Pelt. Soot comes to wind once round your ankles, and goes back to her place.

pages.label: go(region__gate_thrume_road,region__gate_thrume)
pages.page: For a while the road keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the road. By the end of it you are footsore and tired. The road goes on into Thrume. Ahead, smoke going up from salt-pans under the fells. It is a long time since you slept. You are weary, and will fight the worse for it until you sleep.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_priest)
pages.page: ‘You’ve come a long way to find somebody,’ says Eogan. ‘Is it me?’

pages.label: go(region__gate_pentrice_road,region__gate_pentrice)
pages.page: It is hot on the road, and you walk slower than you meant to. The road goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. The road goes on into the vale of the Arle. Ahead, a minster tower over a river town, where one river falls into another.

pages.label: go(region__tw85_105,region__t105)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Birch and rowan on a slope, the light coming white through the leaves. A fox, a red fox with a white throat, black legs and a full brush, looking back over its shoulder, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw105_106,region__t106)
pages.page: You set out from the woods of Oakhurst. A stand of tall trees with little under them, so that you can see a long way between the trunks, and nothing moving. To the west the land rises. A monkey, a small brown long-tailed monkey with a wizened black face, hanging by one hand and staring, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw106_107,region__t107)
pages.page: It is hot on the path, and you walk slower than you meant to. Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw127_128,region__t127)
pages.page: Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. Wet ground, sedge and cotton-grass, the pools reflecting the sky, a heron getting up slow and offended. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw126_127,region__t126)
pages.page: Bramble and hazel thick under the trees, and a way through only where the deer have pushed. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw126_146,region__t146)
pages.page: The path goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it. Fen: reeds taller than a man, black water between, and the ground giving underfoot with every step. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw146_167,region__t167)
pages.page: You leave the fen of Duskcarr late, with the light already going yellow. The path runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. Reed-beds whispering in the wind, and a bittern in them booming like a blown jar. The Deepwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. A snake, an adder, grey-brown with a dark zigzag down its back, coiled with its head raised, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw166_167,region__t166)
pages.page: For a while the path keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. Night comes on while you are still on the path, and you walk the last of it in the dark. A causey of old turves across the marsh, and on either side of it water that does not show how deep it is. The Deepwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round.

pages.label: go(region__tw256_257,region__t257)

pages.label: go(region__tw103_124,region__t124)
pages.page: Peat ground cut once into steps, and long since flooded. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw102_123,region__t123)

pages.label: go(region__tw2_21,region__t2)
pages.page: Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg.

pages.label: go(region__tw21_42,region__t21)
pages.page: Water stands on both sides, and the path between is soft enough to take the print of your boot and keep it. Mist lying on the marsh, the reeds standing up out of it and the ground not showing at all. To the east the land rises. Lowmouth is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tl_edge_west,region__edge_west)
pages.page: At the edge of Merscfaenn a beacon stands on stilts above the reeds, a fire-basket rusted open at the top, so that the bounds could be found in fog. Beyond it the road goes on west into Fencarr, fen country, the folk say. Few of them have been.

pages.label: go(region__tl_z3_edge_2,region__z3_edge_2)
pages.page: A clearing where charcoal has been burned for years: rings of black earth, a turf hut with its door off, cordwood stacked under bark. The smell of old smoke hangs over all of it. A woodpecker is at work somewhere close. The turf hut’s door lies in the nettles beside it. The burning-rings lie black in the grass. Yarrow grows in the grass at the wayside, flat white heads over feathery leaves: a soldier’s herb, for cuts. pages.label: go(region__z3_trail2,region__z3_heart)
pages.page: A hollow full of holly, dark even at noon, the ground dry underneath and littered with prickled leaves. A good place to keep out of the rain, and to keep out of sight. Off to one side the undergrowth is broken in a line at the height of a man’s shoulder, not a deer’s: someone goes off this way now and then. A blackbird scuffles away under the holly. Under the holly the ground is dry as a floor. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Foxgloves stand tall at the wood’s edge, purple bells speckled inside: they heal, prepared rightly, and kill otherwise. Banewort grows here, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Rosenoble grows here, a briar of deep red roses. A cinnamon tree grows here, its bark peeled in strips.

pages.label: go(region__tw86_105,region__t86)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. To the south-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw65_85,region__t65)
pages.page: The path runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate. A long low field, buttercups to the knee, and the smell of hay on the air. To the north-east the land rises. Mistshaw is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: camp(region__t7)
pages.page: You find what shelter there is, and sleep as well as you can, with one ear open.

pages.label: go(region__tw65_66,region__t66)
pages.page: It is hot on the path, and you walk slower than you meant to. It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by. Old ridge and furrow under the turf, the plough’s lines still there long after the plough. To the north-east the land rises. Mistshaw is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke. A red heifer has broken through the hedge and stands in the next field eating what is not hers, and will not be driven by one. The hayward, a bounds-keeper walking the common, with a hazel switch, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw47_66,region__t47)
pages.page: Larks go up out of the grass on either hand, and come down again behind you. Grassland, rolling a little, cropped short by sheep you cannot see. A wall of fieldstone runs along nowhere in particular. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the north the land rises. Mistshaw is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: wait_hour
pages.page: A pedlar is coming the other way along the sheep-track, bent under a pack on a frame, and lifts her staff to you from a long way off.

pages.label: go(region__tw46_47,region__t46)
pages.page: It is hot on the path, and you walk slower than you meant to. Grassland, rolling a little, cropped short by sheep you cannot see. A wall of fieldstone runs along nowhere in particular. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw25_46,region__t25)
pages.page: You leave the country about Mistshaw late, with the light already going yellow. Open country: rough pasture and old field-strips gone back to grass, a hedge here and there, the sky very big over it. Mistshaw is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tl_w6,region__w6)
pages.page: A square keep of grey stone stands on the rise above the road, its corners rounded by weather and its top broken like a bad tooth. A curtain wall ran round it once; some of it still does. The gate faces the road. Over the gate a shield is cut in the stone, a tower with a star over it, and under the shield the keep’s name in the kingdom’s letters, which anyone who reads at all can read: ÍSENCEPAN. The flat stone by the way in has been turned over, not long ago: the grass beneath it is still pressed in the shape of something round, and there are the prints of good boots, going back the way they came. This is Ironkeep, as the folk call it. Its makers called it Ísencepan. A snake suns itself on a fallen stone. Cut deep over the way in, in the makers’ letters: ÍSENCEPAN. A cairn of stones lies tumbled at the foot of the way in, with scraps of old bread, a bead, a knotted cord and a child’s clay bird among the stones: a place where somebody has come every year, and somebody has kicked it over. Wenna gains 20 experience: found Ironkeep.

pages.label: go(region__w6_track,region__s1_s4_way)
pages.page: The road between Lowmouth and Mistshaw goes through scattered woods and the clearings of charcoal-burners. Deer go off between the trees without a sound. By the road stands an old milestone, worn to a stub, with a wheel cut in it and something over the wheel that might once have been a crown. The road is churned by cattle, all going toward Lowmouth, and not long since: some of it is still warm. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Meadowsweet grows thick along the wet ground, a froth of cream flowers that smells of almonds and honey. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. Comfrey grows rank by the water, hairy-leaved, its bells hanging: knitbone, the herb-wives call it. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Foxgloves stand tall at the wood’s edge, purple bells speckled inside: they heal, prepared rightly, and kill otherwise. Feverwort grows along the road in the rough grass, bitter-leaved: the herb-wives dry it for a child’s fever. Bamboo grows along the road in a dense clump, its canes knocking together in the wind. Banewort grows along the road, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Celandine grows along the road, yellow-starred in the damp. Cinquefoil runs over the ground along the road, its small yellow flowers five-petalled. Daffodils grow along the road in a bank, their strap-leaves in clumps. Alhuren grows along the road, silver-leaved, its blue flowers pale as a candle-flame. Gentian grows along the road, its blue trumpets open to the sun. Woodbine climbs along the road, its cream and yellow flowers sweet at dusk. Staggerweed grows along the road, tall, with spurred blue flowers. Pennyroyal grows along the road, low and minty, with small purple flowers. Thyme grows along the road in low mats, flowering purple. Tansy grows along the road, its yellow buttons over feathery leaves. Sweetgrass grows along the road, its long blades smelling of hay. A dropberry bush grows along the road, its red berries hanging in strings. Carenfil grows along the road, pale-petalled, its scent heavy on still days. Groundbread grows along the road, broad-leaved, with small white flowers. Ofbit grows along the road on thin stems, its flowers blue. Betony stands in the short grass at the wood’s edge, purple-spiked: the hedge herb, for a cut or a sting.

pages.label: go(region__road_s1_s4_on,region__s4_green)
pages.page: The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the road. Mistshaw is a handful of roofs at the end of the road, and a dog that comes out to see who you are. Mistshaw is dark, and smells of cold hearths. A dog barks once, then is quiet. By the track stands the wayside shrine of Nodens, a small weathered altar. Offerings of reed lie before it. Everyone here is grumbling about the toll on the road: food is dearer for it, and there is less of it. A trestle table under the well, a ledger open on it, a lead seal on a cord, and, as the light goes, a queue of villagers with their dues in cloth, not speaking. A hayrick stands blackened at the edge of the town, and a woman is sweeping the ash from a doorstep into the road without looking up. The surveyor’s son has set out a table at the head of the market with a brass-bound measure on it, filled with water, and a small crowd in front, and a notice in a clerk’s hand: HONEST BY THE TOWN’S OWN MEASURE. Osborn’s dog noses along the foot of the wall of Osborn’s house, following a smell from stone to stone. Lyle Goodbarrel, the pedlar, has his tray of ribbons and needles open on a bench. Cade Underbough is mending a handcart wheel while the children explain to strangers where they are moving to. A woman in black sits on the step of a cold house with her hands in her lap, watching the road. Daffodils grow in the gardens about the green in a bank, their strap-leaves in clumps. Euphrosyne grows in the gardens about the green, low, with small white flowers: eyebright. A strip of vellum is pinned to the lintel of the inn at Mistshaw, with a lead seal in wax. A faded Wapshott’s bill from the last round is peeling off the wall, the Colonel’s face half gone. Across it someone has chalked the round: Lowmouth, Mistshaw, Millholm, THREE DAYS EACH. The green’s post has nothing on it today but a bill about a lost cow. Osborn, who speaks for Mistshaw, is here. Tolman, a keeper of the wayside shrine, is here. Edrick, a herb-wife, selling from the house door, is here. So are Roscoe, Maudlin Rooke, the surveyor’s son, Jos Haverhill and the woman in black. Bess lifts his head, looks at you, and puts it down again.

pages.label: wait_for_light
pages.page: The merchant’s stall is shuttered at midday. The surveyor’s son has the head of the market, and the brass-bound measure, and a following, and a way of saying ‘mine’ that has gone from a claim to a custom. Sir Hamo’s men rode into the market at noon and took a tithe of everything on the stalls, with the reeve standing by because there was nothing he could do. Hereabouts the place has a name, and whoever speaks of it uses it. In the market the merchant’s weights are being weighed against the other measure by a woman with a basket and a hard face, and are found to be short, as they are, by a thimble; and nobody is laughing, but nobody is looking at the merchant either.

pages.label: wait_for_light
pages.page: Mistshaw is one farm grown into four, their yards running together, with reed drying in ricks behind the houses. A cow lows behind a wall. A man goes by with a bundle of reed on his back as big as himself. The air is close and wet, and the flies are bad. The hay stands in cocks in the meadows, and swallows hunt low over the grass. Lyle Goodbarrel the pedlar is packing the tray away for the road, everything in its own place. Cade Underbough is tying the last of his things into bundles for the handcart, and the children are carrying out the small bundles. The sky greys, then lightens. It is morning.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_libdoor,region__s1_manor_hall)
pages.page: A house of the grey stone of the hill, long and gabled, its windows set in rows, smoke going up from three chimneys. Wystan Hale, the gamekeeper of the Hall, once a castellan’s spearman, who has been told to stand at the road-wood chain and let nobody cut, is here. The steward looks at what you have in your hands, and then at you, for a long moment. ‘I shall have to ask you to go,’ the steward says, ‘and not to come back.’ And opens the front door, and stands by it until you do. The front door of the Hall is shut, and stays shut to you. The door in the garden wall is bolted on the far side.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_kdoor,region__s1_manor_kitchen)
pages.page: A flagged kitchen with a hearth you could stable a horse in, a table scarred by a century of cleavers, copper pans in rows, and a dresser with a missing plate. Everything in it is clean, and nothing is where you would put it; the room is arranged to the convenience of one person only. A horn lantern hangs on a nail by the kitchen door with a flask of oil beneath it, and beyond the dresser the cellar steps go down into a dark that no kitchen fire reaches. Whoever goes down wants a light that will last, and a torch is only an hour. A boy of ten or so sits on the settle by the hearth turning the same potato over and over in his hands. Every so often he hums, three notes down and one up, and stops, and looks surprised. Orla Pennick, the cook of the Hall, who feeds forty on a budget for ten, is here. Wimble, the kitchen boy, who went up to the dome and came back not knowing his name, is here.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_cellar_steps,region__s1_manor_cellar)
pages.page: It is pitch dark. Without a light you can see nothing here, and do nothing that needs seeing. In the dark you can hear rats in the cellar close by. The racks shiver. Three brown rats the length of your forearm come out of the dark behind the barrels and do not run. Rats in the cellar are watching you. In 10 minutes they will be on you.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_cellar_steps,region__s1_manor_kitchen)
pages.page: A flagged kitchen with a hearth you could stable a horse in, a table scarred by a century of cleavers, copper pans in rows, and a dresser with a missing plate. Orla Pennick, the cook of the Hall, who feeds forty on a budget for ten, is here. Wimble, the kitchen boy, who went up to the dome and came back not knowing his name, is here.

pages.label: take_item(region__s1_manor_lantern,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take a horn lantern.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_kdoor,region__s1_manor_front)
pages.page: A house of the grey stone of the hill, long and gabled, its windows set in rows, smoke going up from three chimneys. Wystan Hale, the gamekeeper of the Hall, once a castellan’s spearman, who has been told to stand at the road-wood chain and let nobody cut, is here.

pages.label: search(region__s1_manor_kitchen)
pages.page: You search the Hall kitchen with care, a little at a time. Nothing is put away or hidden here. You have been over the whole of it, and nothing is hidden here.

pages.label: take_item(region__s1_manor_lamp_oil,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take a flask of lamp oil.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_cellar_steps,region__s1_manor_cellar)
pages.page: It is pitch dark. Without a light you can see nothing here, and do nothing that needs seeing. In the dark you can hear rats in the cellar close by. The racks shiver. Three brown rats the length of your forearm come out of the dark behind the barrels and do not run. Rats in the cellar are watching you. In a few minutes they will be on you.

pages.label: go(region__s1_manor_cellar_steps,region__s1_manor_cellar)
pages.page: It is pitch dark. Without a light you can see nothing here, and do nothing that needs seeing. In the dark you can hear rats in the cellar close by. The racks shiver. Three brown rats the length of your forearm come out of the dark behind the barrels and do not run. Rats in the cellar are watching you. In 8 minutes they will be on you.

pages.label: attack(region__s1_manor_rats)
pages.page: Wenna hits Rat 1. Rat 1 takes 2 slashing damage. Rat 1 falls. Wenna hits Rat 2. Rat 2 takes 2 slashing damage. Rat 2 falls. Rat 3 takes 2 slashing damage. Rat 3 falls. The fight is won. Wenna gains 50 experience.

pages.label: go(region__s1_inn_door,region__s1_taproom)
pages.page: A busy room in two parts with a counter between them, and a stair going up to the bedrooms. It smells of roasting meat, and the clatter of the kitchen comes through the back door. Salt-boilers sit at the long table, still white to the elbow. ‘Cyril there is looking for work,’ says Eamon. ‘Would go anywhere with anyone, for a few coins and their keep.’ Martin the drover is at the window, counting the cattle in the pens before the road. A hazel tally-stick lies behind the bar where the innkeeper put it, cut with fine notches in rows, marks on the flat in the wardens’ hand. Eamon, the innkeeper, is here. Cyril, a pedlar, is here. Dannel Hobb, a boy of ten with a white streak in his hair, kept indoors, is here. So are Isaure Venn, Osmund Pyle, Naillil, the factor’s hands and Marina.

pages.label: go(factors__yard_gate,region__s1_taproom)
pages.page: A busy room in two parts with a counter between them, and a stair going up to the bedrooms. The air in here is close, and the flies have found it. Martin the drover is at the window, counting the cattle in the pens before the road. A hazel tally-stick lies behind the bar where the innkeeper put it, cut with fine notches in rows, marks on the flat in the wardens’ hand. Eamon, the innkeeper, is here. Cyril, a pedlar, is here. Dannel Hobb, a boy of ten with a white streak in his hair, kept indoors, is here. So are Isaure Venn, Osmund Pyle, Naillil, the factor’s hands and Marina.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_innkeeper,word9__h1_s1_innkeeper)
pages.page: ‘Fengate: the fallen walls in the fen north of Mistshaw,’ says Eamon. ‘The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “fen gate”.’ ‘The old paved road bends once at Fengate, eight miles round a hill that has nothing in it to bend for,’ says Eamon. ‘Carters leave a coin at the bend and do not stop. Some say the hill hums.’ Fengate is the name of the fallen walls they speak of.

pages.label: go(quarrel__back_door,quarrel__garden)
pages.page: Cabbages, a hen-house, a washing line. A row of white stones runs across the bottom of the garden, freshly set, a stride inside the hedge.

pages.label: search(quarrel__garden)
pages.page: You search the inn’s back garden with care, a little at a time. Under the grass along the hedge, your heel finds the old holes: square, stone-sided, a stride outside the new row. The stones were moved.

pages.label: go(quarrel__back_door,region__s1_taproom)
pages.page: A busy room in two parts with a counter between them, and a stair going up to the bedrooms. Martin the drover is at the window, counting the cattle in the pens before the road. A hazel tally-stick lies behind the bar where the innkeeper put it, cut with fine notches in rows, marks on the flat in the wardens’ hand. Eamon, the innkeeper, is here. Cyril, a pedlar, is here. Dannel Hobb, a boy of ten with a white streak in his hair, kept indoors, is here. So are Isaure Venn, Osmund Pyle, Naillil, the factor’s hands and Marina.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_traveller,word10__h1_s1_traveller)
pages.page: ‘Black Barrow: a grassed mound in the fen east of Mistshaw,’ says Cyril. ‘A salvage crew, the Spade-Company, has made a camp on the ridge above Black Barrow and is digging into the flank of a great howe, under the shire-reeve’s licence,’ says Cyril. ‘They keep a watch on the steep path, and they have lost men under the hill.’ Black Barrow is the name of the grassed mound east of Mistshaw they speak of.

pages.label: ask(region__s1_traveller,word9__h3_s1_traveller)
pages.page: ‘At Fengate, where the brook goes under the road-wall, the arch is wide enough to crawl in, and the water that comes out of it is warmer than brook water has any right to be,’ says Cyril.

pages.label: go(fellowship__door_a,fellowship__hall_a)
pages.page: A long low room with a table down the middle and benches either side. On the end wall hangs the roll: the brothers and sisters in four columns, one to a hall, each column in its keeper’s hand and each hand different. The table has been cleared at one end and a single sheet squared up on it. Three columns of the roll are ticked to the quarter-day in a thin brown ink. The fourth is ticked as far as the last quarter, and after that there is only the white of the wall. Tilda, the head of the fellowship, is here.

pages.label: go(region__s1_herbs_door,region__s1_herbs)
pages.page: Bunches of drying herbs hang from every beam, so that you walk in stooping, and the air is thick with sage, mint and wormwood. Aldred, a herbalist, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw42_43,region__t43)
pages.page: It is hot on the path, and you walk slower than you meant to. For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Pine wood, the ground soft with needles and the smell of resin heavy in the still air. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the north-west the land rises. Lowmouth is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: region__survey(party,region__t81)
pages.page: You stand a while on the highest ground to hand and look out over the country, learning the lie of it: where the land rises and falls, where the water runs, what stands on it.

pages.label: go(walk__gate_d,region__s2_green)
pages.page: The road runs down between the houses of Brightbridge and straight into the Redwater, and comes out on the far bank dark with wet. The water is loud over the stones, and the bank smells of mud and trodden weed. Twice this month the Hall’s keeper has driven the town’s pigs off the verge of the old road. At dusk every dog in the town turns its head toward the hill, and the geese go silent. The bell is gone from its frame over the well. ‘Hobs,’ people say, and spit, ‘out of Joygate, where they’ve made their hold.’ Aldith is going round the cart wheel by wheel, a kick and a look at each. Wulfstan the miser is sorting rags by colour into three small heaps. Leofrun the avenger is running a stone along a blade in long, unhurried strokes. The inn’s dog lies across the doorstep of the Merry Sun with his chin on his paws, and watches who comes. A white cat sits in a window between two pots of herbs, watching the street. Your brother is sitting on a rail with your father’s old spear across his knees, watching the road. He is taller by a head than when you went away. A grey dog lies by the door of the taproom of the Merry Sun with her head on her paws, watching the road. She holds one forefoot off the ground. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. The spring-head by the green has been running low for a year. The rope comes up with a hand’s depth of brown water in the bucket and a smell of wet stone, and the women who draw it do so in silence, to save breath. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Brightbridge, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. The surveyor’s son, a young man in a good coat, who says the measure was his father’s by gift and means to bring it home before anyone makes a fuss, is here. So is Wilkin Sedge.

pages.label: go(region__s2_crossing_way,region__s2_crossing)
pages.page: Flat stones step across the Redwater, slick and green below the waterline. Spray wets the shins of anyone crossing. Piers is bailing out the ferry with a wooden scoop. The notched post leans a little downstream.

pages.label: go(region__s2_crossing_way,region__s2_green)
