The surveyor’s son, a young man in a good coat, who says the measure was his father’s by gift and means to bring it home before anyone makes a fuss, is here. So is Wilkin Sedge.

pages.label: talk_to(drover__son)
pages.page: ‘You came,’ says Wilkin Sedge. ‘I said you would. Nobody believed me.’

pages.label: go(region__edge_north_road,region__edge_north)
pages.page: You leave Brightbridge in a thick white fog. At ten paces the hedges are hard to make out. The road runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. A milestone stands by the road at the edge of Acornweald, cut with the merchant-princes’ ship and the distances to places whose names have worn away. Beyond it the road goes on north into Blóstmawudu, forest country, the folk say. Few of them have been.

pages.label: go(region__tl_edge_north,region__t10)
pages.page: A stand of tall trees with little under them, so that you can see a long way between the trunks, and nothing moving. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. To the south-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw9_10,region__t9)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Bramble and hazel thick under the trees, and a way through only where the deer have pushed. To the south-west the land rises. A beetle as big as a hand, its black shell glossed green, jaws like pincers and legs fringed with spines, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw9_29,region__t29)
pages.page: Fog lies on the path, and things come out of it one at a time: a gate, a tree, a stone. The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. To the west the land rises. Brightbridge is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw29_50,region__t50)
pages.page: For a while the path keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. Birch and rowan on a slope, the light coming white through the leaves. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: take_item(region__party_1__torch,region__member_party_1)
pages.page: You take a torch.

pages.label: go(region__tw50_70,region__t70)
pages.page: You set out from the country about Brightbridge. Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the west the land rises. Brightbridge is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tr70_s2_s3_way,region__s2_s3_way)
pages.page: In Birchwood the road narrows to a cart’s width. Woodcutters have stacked cordwood along it, and left. Deer go off between the trees without a sound. A tin button lies in the road, the kind pedlars sell by the card. A goat with a broken tether is cropping the verge, with her whole attention. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Meadowsweet grows thick along the wet ground, a froth of cream flowers that smells of almonds and honey. Comfrey grows rank by the water, hairy-leaved, its bells hanging: knitbone, the herb-wives call it. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Foxgloves stand tall at the wood’s edge, purple bells speckled inside: they heal, prepared rightly, and kill otherwise. Asters grow along the road in clumps, mauve with yellow eyes. A bay tree grows along the road, dark and glossy, clipped for its leaves. Banewort grows along the road, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Dragonwort grows along the road, a red spike among spearing leaves. Bloodroot grows along the road, broad-leaved, with white flowers low to the ground. Euphrosyne grows along the road, low, with small white flowers: eyebright. Rosenoble grows along the road, a briar of deep red roses. Gentian grows along the road, its blue trumpets open to the sun. Woodbine climbs along the road, its cream and yellow flowers sweet at dusk. Hyssop grows along the road in spikes of blue, bees working it. Purslane grows along the road, low, with small fleshy leaves. Rosemary grows along the road, grey-green, with small blue flowers. Rue grows along the road, blue-green and bitter-smelling. Thyme grows along the road in low mats, flowering purple. Tansy grows along the road, its yellow buttons over feathery leaves. Carenfil grows along the road, pale-petalled, its scent heavy on still days. Actaea grows along the road, its white flowers in feathery spikes. Groundbread grows along the road, broad-leaved, with small white flowers. Ofbit grows along the road on thin stems, its flowers blue.

pages.label: go(region__tr89_s2_s3_way,region__t89)
pages.page: Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw89_90,region__t90)
pages.page: Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the north-west the land rises. A squirrel, a red squirrel with tufted ears and a bushy tail, sitting up with a nut in its paws, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw90_109,region__t109)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. To the west the land rises. A moth, a large moth with soft grey-brown wings marked with eyes, its feathered feelers spread, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw109_130,region__t130)
pages.page: The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the path. Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. To the east the land rises. A squirrel, a red squirrel with tufted ears and a bushy tail, sitting up with a nut in its paws, is here.

pages.label: take_healing(region__s1_priest,region__s1_priest_healing)
pages.page: Carmine cleans and dresses every wound in the company.

pages.label: go(region__gate_sennet_road,region__gate_sennet)
pages.page: You leave Newmeet in a thick white fog. At ten paces the hedges are hard to make out. For a while the road keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. The road goes on into Sennet. Ahead, far off over the sea, a hill hanging in the sky with houses on it, and a chain coming down from it.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_sennet,region__t235)
pages.page: Fen: reeds taller than a man, black water between, and the ground giving underfoot with every step. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. To the north-east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw215_235,region__t215)
pages.page: The path runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. Woodland: oak and ash and holly, the light green and broken, last year’s leaves deep underfoot. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw215_216,region__t216)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw216_236,region__t236)
pages.page: Fog lies on the path, and things come out of it one at a time: a gate, a tree, a stone. The path goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it. Wet ground, sedge and cotton-grass, the pools reflecting the sky, a heron getting up slow and offended. To the north-east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw236_237,region__t237)
pages.page: You set out from the fen of Saltmoss. Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. Peat ground cut once into steps, and long since flooded. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw218_238,region__t238)
pages.page: Water stands on both sides, and the path between is soft enough to take the print of your boot and keep it. Mist lying on the marsh, the reeds standing up out of it and the ground not showing at all. To the north-east the land rises.

pages.label: camp(region__t238)
pages.page: A whistle, and a young dog comes bounding at you through the grass and stops short, and behind it a shepherd, crook in hand, who calls it off and looks you over.

pages.label: go(region__tw238_239,region__t239)
pages.page: The shadows are long when you leave the fen of Saltmoss, and getting longer. A causey of old turves across the marsh, and on either side of it water that does not show how deep it is. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw219_239,region__t219)
pages.page: You leave the fen of Saltmoss late, with the light already going yellow. For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the path. Bramble and hazel thick under the trees, and a way through only where the deer have pushed. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw198_219,region__t198)
pages.page: A strong wind blows across the open country the whole way. The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Pine wood, the ground soft with needles and the smell of resin heavy in the still air. To the north-east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw198_199,region__t199)
pages.page: Bramble and hazel thick under the trees, and a way through only where the deer have pushed. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw179_199,region__t179)
pages.page: It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by. Fields let go to thistle and dock, the larks going up out of them as you pass.

pages.label: go(region__tw159_179,region__t159)
pages.page: Larks go up out of the grass on either hand, and come down again behind you. Meadow, wet in the hollows and dry on the rises, with a few thorn trees leaning all the same way. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw158_159,region__t158)
pages.page: A strong wind blows across the open country the whole way. The path runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate. Long grass gone to seed, and the wind combing it one way and then the other. To the north-east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_hume,region__gate_hume)
pages.page: The road goes on into the Wold of Hume. Ahead, a long grey brow of rock on the hills, and under it a glow like a lamp behind a curtain.

pages.label: go(region__gate_hume_road,region__s1_green)
pages.page: For a while the road runs along a shore, and birds get up off the water as you pass. Newmeet shows ahead a long while before you reach it: smoke, a roofline, the noise of it on the wind. A stone market cross stands in the middle of the square at Newmeet, its steps worn into dips. The crier’s paper names the lord’s keep, a walled keep on its rise, in the woods north of Newmeet, a day or so along the roads from here, and the tower and star on his breast are the keep’s. Hild is backing a cart into a yard, one hand on the horse’s bridle. Moll is touching up a painted backcloth of a castle with a small brush. Linden the researcher is copying a page from a borrowed book, a stone on each corner. The inn’s dog sleeps against the wall of the Ancient Lantern with one ear up for the door. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. A paper is nailed to the post under the crier’s bell-rope: THE LORD OF THE KEEP CALLS HIS MARCH TO THE KING’S MUSTER. TWENTY SPEARS AND A HUNDRED BUSHELS TO THE KEEP ON THE TWELFTH DAY. Underneath, in another hand, scratched with a nail: AND WHO IS TO SOW? Somebody has chalked a number on the well-stone, large and fresh, and under it a small neat wheel with a wing on it. A few barefoot prints go in and out of the inn’s door. The factor, who keeps the books of the Ísenheald company, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Newmeet, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. So are the old woman in the doorway, Felice Hale, Cecily Hale, Wat, Alfric, Bartle the younger, Lambert, the Dunning lads, Maud the younger and the walkers. A hard wind is banging every shutter in the place. The wardens have stopped paying. A hayrick at Brockfield has burned in the night, and the bailiff has put up a new notice: SIX CROWNS, AND A FINE FOR THE FIRE. The crier’s paper names the lord’s keep, a walled keep on its rise, in the woods north of Newmeet, a day or so along the roads from here, and the tower and star on his breast are the keep’s. A string of barefoot strangers has taken the well-steps and is chalking the stone: a number, and a little wheel with a wing. They are singing something with no tune to speak of and a great deal of will. Somewhere behind the singing a man is selling something, with the voice of a man who has sold it before.

pages.label: go(region__s1_stones_way,region__s1_stones_top)
pages.page: The path comes out on the top of the hill among fallen stones. An arch stands on its own against the sky, and beyond it the broken wall of something long and high. Below, Newmeet is all roofs and smoke. From up here the country lies open. Far off to the north-west you can make out a square doorway in a hillside in Birchwood.

pages.label: go(region__s1_stones_round,region__s1_stones_tree)
pages.page: A tree older than the stones, its trunk wider than a cart is long, its roots heaving up the turf. Strips of cloth are tied to its lowest branches, old and new: the folk of Newmeet still come up here. There is room on the low branches for another strip of cloth.

pages.label: go(region__s1_stones_up,region__s1_stones_hall)
pages.page: A long hall with no roof. Steps go up at the far end to a dais, and on it stand figures cut from the stone, taller than men, their faces worn smooth. Grass grows between the floor-slabs. Letters are cut along the edge of the dais, deep and square, in no hand anyone in Newmeet could read.

pages.label: go(region__s1_stones_arch,region__s1_stones_hall)
pages.page: A long hall with no roof. Letters are cut along the edge of the dais, deep and square, in no hand anyone in Newmeet could read.

pages.label: go(region__s1_stones_round,region__s1_stones_tree)
pages.page: A tree older than the stones, its trunk wider than a cart is long, its roots heaving up the turf. There is room on the low branches for another strip of cloth.

pages.label: search(region__s1_stones_tree)
pages.page: You search the old tree with care, a little at a time. Where a root has heaved up the turf there is a gap, and in it, green with age, a bronze bracelet: an offering of somebody’s, before there was a Newmeet.

pages.label: go(walk__moot_door,walk__moot_a)
pages.page: A tall chair with the Hundred’s ash-and-keys carved on its back, pushed square to the table. It is not comfortable and was not meant to be.

pages.label: go(region__s1_chandlery_door,region__s1_chandlery)
pages.page: Shelves to the ceiling: coils of rope, lamps and lamp-oil, candles in bundles, sacks of meal; everything a traveller forgets, and the smell of tallow over it all. Thurstan, a chandler, is here.

pages.label: go(factors__yard_gate,region__s1_taproom)
pages.page: A busy room in two parts with a counter between them, and a stair going up to the bedrooms. Tilda is tying the last of her things into bundles for the handcart, and the children are carrying out the small bundles. A hazel tally-stick lies behind the bar where the innkeeper put it, cut with fine notches in rows, marks on the flat in the wardens’ hand. Sable, the innkeeper, is here. Caradoc, a soldier, is here. Dannel Hobb, a boy of ten with a white streak in his hair, kept indoors, is here. So are Isaure Venn, Osmund Pyle, Arannis, the factor’s hands and Ghokarn.

pages.label: take_lodging(region__s1_innkeeper_lodging,region__s1_innkeeper)
pages.page: You eat what is put in front of you, and sleep long, under a roof.

pages.label: go(factors__yard_gate,region__s1_taproom)
pages.page: A busy room in two parts with a counter between them, and a stair going up to the bedrooms. A hazel tally-stick lies behind the bar where the innkeeper put it, cut with fine notches in rows, marks on the flat in the wardens’ hand. Sable, the innkeeper, is here. Caradoc, a soldier, is here. Dannel Hobb, a boy of ten with a white streak in his hair, kept indoors, is here. So are Isaure Venn, Osmund Pyle, Arannis, the factor’s hands and Ghokarn.

pages.label: go(region__s1_inn_door,region__s1_green)
pages.page: A stone market cross stands in the middle of the square at Newmeet, its steps worn into dips. Fog lies over the place; the far houses are shapes. Lambs cry in the home fields, and the ground is soft from the thaw. Hild is backing a cart into a yard, one hand on the horse’s bridle. Moll is touching up a painted backcloth of a castle with a small brush. Linden the researcher is copying a page from a borrowed book, a stone on each corner. The inn’s dog sleeps against the wall of the Ancient Lantern with one ear up for the door. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. The factor, who keeps the books of the Ísenheald company, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Newmeet, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. So are the old woman in the doorway, Felice Hale, Cecily Hale, Colonel Florian Wapshott, Mumchance, Pip Gallant, Honoria Bulstrode, Signor Cornelius Fipps and Wat. The bailiff’s men have been through again. The price is five crowns a hearth now, and the reeve has been seen reading the receipt by the well and putting it in his pocket. ‘You’ve not eaten,’ Honoria says to Mumchance. ‘I’ve eaten,’ says Mumchance. ‘You’ve not eaten properly,’ says Honoria, and gives him a bowl, and he eats it, and neither of them says anything else, and it is the most married thing you have ever seen. Bucephalus looks at you down the length of his nose, decides you have no apples, and looks at the horizon instead.

pages.label: go(region__gate_tolleth_road,region__gate_tolleth)
pages.page: Fog lies on the road, and things come out of it one at a time: a gate, a tree, a stone. An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. By the end of it you are footsore and tired. The road goes on into Tolleth and the Skerrow passage. Ahead, masts, close as reeds, in a harbour the colour of slate.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_tolleth,region__t118)
pages.page: Long grass gone to seed, and the wind combing it one way and then the other. A pedlar with a pack on a frame and a staff, walking the drove-ways between the farms, is here. A pedlar is coming the other way along the sheep-track, bent under a pack on a frame, and lifts her staff to you from a long way off.

pages.label: go(region__tw98_118,region__t98)
pages.page: The path runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate. Flat grazing on close, springy turf, and willows along a ditch you cannot see. To the south-west the land rises.

pages.label: make_remedy(region__member_party_1,minor_healing_potion,region__party_1__herbs,region__party_1__herbs)
pages.page: It boils over, or goes to a brown sludge: healing herbs is spoiled. Wenna fails the mending check (d20 8 + wisdom 2 + mending 2 = 12 against 13).

pages.label: go(region__tw98_117,region__t117)
pages.page: You leave open fields south-east of Windscar late, with the light already going yellow. Sheep stand on the path and move off only when you are close. Night comes on while you are still on the path, and you walk the last of it in the dark. Heather and broom, and a grouse going off underfoot with a noise like a rattle.

pages.label: go(region__tw116_117,region__t116)
pages.page: A strong wind blows across the open country the whole way. The path climbs onto open moor, and the country falls away behind you in long brown folds. High open heath: ling and bilberry, a scatter of grey stones, a lark going up and up. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight.

pages.label: region__survey(party,region__t116)
pages.page: You stand a while on the highest ground to hand and look out over the country, learning the lie of it: where the land rises and falls, where the water runs, what stands on it. To the south-east, not far off: a walled keep on its rise. To the south-west, some way off: Brockfield. To the west, some way off: a lone tower.

pages.label: go(region__tw116_136,region__t136)
pages.page: You set out from open heath south of Windscar. Larks go up out of the grass on either hand, and come down again behind you. Long grass gone to seed, and the wind combing it one way and then the other. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw136_137,region__t137)
pages.page: It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by. A long low field, buttercups to the knee, and the smell of hay on the air. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw116_137,region__t116)
pages.page: Up on the tops there is nothing but heather, sky and wind, and a cairn now and then to say you are still on the path. High open heath: ling and bilberry, a scatter of grey stones, a lark going up and up.

pages.label: go(region__tr116_s4_s5_way,region__s4_s5_way)
pages.page: Open farmland on either hand: strip-fields, a mill-pond, cattle that lift their heads as you pass. A fox crosses the road ahead, unhurried, and goes through the hedge. A milestone leans in the grass at the roadside, half sunk: on its face a worn wheel, and over it, if you look closely, the points of a crown. Avice the carrier is walking at the head of a cart-horse, a cart of sacks and barrels behind, on her way to Brockfield. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Meadowsweet grows thick along the wet ground, a froth of cream flowers that smells of almonds and honey. Heather covers the ground along the road, low and wiry, purple with its small bells: steeped, it eases an ache. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Foxgloves stand tall at the wood’s edge, purple bells speckled inside: they heal, prepared rightly, and kill otherwise. Asters grow along the road in clumps, mauve with yellow eyes. Gilliflowers grow along the road, pink and white, smelling of cloves. Celandine grows along the road, yellow-starred in the damp. Euphrosyne grows along the road, low, with small white flowers: eyebright. Rosenoble grows along the road, a briar of deep red roses. Hazel grows along the road, broad-leaved, its nuts in clusters of three. Hyssop grows along the road in spikes of blue, bees working it. Staggerweed grows along the road, tall, with spurred blue flowers. Cedron grows along the road, its leaves smelling of lemon when brushed. Pennyroyal grows along the road, low and minty, with small purple flowers. Rue grows along the road, blue-green and bitter-smelling. Thistles grow along the road, purple-headed. Thyme grows along the road in low mats, flowering purple. Starwort grows along the road, small and white-flowered. Carenfil grows along the road, pale-petalled, its scent heavy on still days. Groundbread grows along the road, broad-leaved, with small white flowers.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s4_s5_way_t)
pages.page: ‘If it’s trouble,’ says Avice, ‘I have enough of my own.’

pages.label: go(region__tr96_s4_s5_way,region__t96)
pages.page: A strong wind blows across the open country the whole way. The path goes up by stony steps and down by rougher ones, and it is windy on every rise. Heather and broom, and a grouse going off underfoot with a noise like a rattle. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. Windscar is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke. It is a long time since you slept. You are weary, and will fight the worse for it until you sleep.

pages.label: go(region__s1_reedbeds_way,region__s1_reedbeds)
pages.page: The reed comes right up to the last houses, with paths cut into it and bundles stacked in ricks on the hard ground. Roger is up to the knees in water, cutting reed with a sickle.

pages.label: go(region__s1_shop_door,region__s1_shop)
pages.page: Bunches of herbs hang drying from every beam, and the jars along the wall are labelled in a cramped brown hand. A pot of wormwood simmers at the back. Falkor, a herb-wife, is here.

pages.label: go(region__road_s1_s4,region__s1_s4_way)
pages.page: You leave Newmeet in a thick white fog. At ten paces the hedges are hard to make out. For an hour the road runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. The road between Newmeet and Brockfield goes through scattered woods and the clearings of charcoal-burners. Deer go off between the trees without a sound. By the road stands an old milestone, worn to a stub, with a wheel cut in it and something over the wheel that might once have been a crown. Tilda’s handcart has stopped on the road to Brockfield while the children are counted. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Meadowsweet grows thick along the wet ground, a froth of cream flowers that smells of almonds and honey. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. Comfrey grows rank by the water, hairy-leaved, its bells hanging: knitbone, the herb-wives call it. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Foxgloves stand tall at the wood’s edge, purple bells speckled inside: they heal, prepared rightly, and kill otherwise. Feverwort grows along the road in the rough grass, bitter-leaved: the herb-wives dry it for a child’s fever. Banewort grows along the road, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Celandine grows along the road, yellow-starred in the damp. Cinquefoil runs over the ground along the road, its small yellow flowers five-petalled. Daffodils grow along the road in a bank, their strap-leaves in clumps. Alhuren grows along the road, silver-leaved, its blue flowers pale as a candle-flame. Gentian grows along the road, its blue trumpets open to the sun. Woodbine climbs along the road, its cream and yellow flowers sweet at dusk. Staggerweed grows along the road, tall, with spurred blue flowers. Pennyroyal grows along the road, low and minty, with small purple flowers. Thyme grows along the road in low mats, flowering purple. Tansy grows along the road, its yellow buttons over feathery leaves. Sweetgrass grows along the road, its long blades smelling of hay. A dropberry bush grows along the road, its red berries hanging in strings. Carenfil grows along the road, pale-petalled, its scent heavy on still days. Groundbread grows along the road, broad-leaved, with small white flowers. Ofbit grows along the road on thin stems, its flowers blue. Betony stands in the short grass at the wood’s edge, purple-spiked: the hedge herb, for a cut or a sting.

pages.label: go(region__tr176_s1_s4_way,region__t176)
pages.page: It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by. A stand of tall trees with little under them, so that you can see a long way between the trunks, and nothing moving. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight. To the north-west the land rises. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw175_176,region__t175)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Bramble and hazel thick under the trees, and a way through only where the deer have pushed. To the north the land rises. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tl_w3,region__w3)
pages.page: A square doorway goes into the hillside under a lintel of a single dressed stone. Cold air comes out of it, smelling of water. Letters are cut deep in the lintel, in a script older than the folk’s: PALLIDUSLACUS. A cold fire-ring, a crushed bed of bracken, and under a stone a small grey pouch sewn with red letters. Someone slept here once, and meant to be back. Under a flat stone by the way in lies a dented, brass-bound measure, put there with care. A door of one grey stone fills the way in, without hinge or handle. Words are cut deep across it in the old script, and under them, in a later hand, scratched small, what they say: ‘What has a head, a tail, is brown, and has no legs?’ Below is a row of words with a hollow beside each, worn smooth by fingers. This is Palelake, as the folk call it. Its makers called it Palliduslacus. A stag stands in a clearing, watching, before it turns away. Cut deep over the way in, in the makers’ letters: PALLIDUSLACUS. Letters are cut in the lintel stone in the old script. Someone who reads it could say what they mean. Wenna gains 20 experience: found Palelake.

pages.label: go(region__tw175_195,region__t195)
pages.page: For a while the path keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke. A shepherd with a crook and a young dog at heel, looking about as if for something lost, is here. A whistle, and a young dog comes bounding at you through the grass and stops short, and behind it a shepherd, crook in hand, who calls it off and looks you over.

pages.label: talk_to(region__wr198)
pages.page: A shepherd looks up, and puts her hands still, and waits for you to say what you want.

pages.label: take_leave(region__wr198)
pages.page: A shepherd lifts a hand, once.

pages.label: go(region__tw195_215,region__t215)
pages.page: Fog lies on the path, and things come out of it one at a time: a gate, a tree, a stone. The path runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. Woodland: oak and ash and holly, the light green and broken, last year’s leaves deep underfoot. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw215_216,region__t216)
pages.page: The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw216_217,region__t217)
pages.page: Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke. A stack of cordwood under turf smokes in the clearing, and on one side the turf has slipped and flame shows through it. The charcoal-burner, a collier black to the elbows, minding a smoking stack in a clearing, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__wm217_burner)
pages.page: The charcoal-burner nods to you, and says nothing until you do.

pages.label: go(region__tw217_237,region__t237)
pages.page: You set out from the woods of Birchwood. Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. Peat ground cut once into steps, and long since flooded. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__s1_lanes_way,region__s1_lanes)
pages.page: The lanes behind the houses run between yards and workshops: the ring of a hammer, a smell of bread or tallow, a door open on somebody’s work, a cat asleep on a sill. Edric is up a ladder against a roof, beating reed into place with a wooden bat. Orabel is winding yarn off a skein held between two chair backs.

pages.label: go(region__gate_strewnfield_road,region__gate_strewnfield)
pages.page: You leave Newmeet in a thick white fog. At ten paces the hedges are hard to make out. The road runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. It is a long walk, and your feet are sore by the end. The road goes on into the Strewnfield. Ahead, a flash in the fields, like a window where no house stands.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_ghessil,region__t142)
pages.page: Wet ground, sedge and cotton-grass, the pools reflecting the sky, a heron getting up slow and offended. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw233_234,region__t234)
pages.page: Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. Peat ground cut once into steps, and long since flooded. To the north the land rises. One of the wicker traps is fast under a sunk branch in the deep channel, and the eel-catcher has been heaving at it a long while. The eel-catcher, a fisher in a flat boat among wicker traps, with a pole twice their height, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw215_234,region__t215)
pages.page: For a while the path keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. Woodland: oak and ash and holly, the light green and broken, last year’s leaves deep underfoot. The Redwater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw215_216,region__t216)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw216_236,region__t236)
pages.page: The path goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it. Wet ground, sedge and cotton-grass, the pools reflecting the sky, a heron getting up slow and offended. To the north-east the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw217_236,region__t217)
pages.page: The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. Newmeet is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke. A stack of cordwood under turf smokes in the clearing, and on one side the turf has slipped and flame shows through it. The charcoal-burner, a collier black to the elbows, minding a smoking stack in a clearing, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw15_16,region__t16)
pages.page: An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. Close wood, old and mossy, the paths between the trunks made by animals and going where animals go. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw237_238,region__t237)
pages.page: The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the path. Peat ground cut once into steps, and long since flooded. To the north the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tl_gate_calamy,region__gate_calamy)
pages.page: The road goes on into Calamy. Ahead, the sails of tide-mills turning along a coast of reeds.

pages.label: go(region__gate_calamy_road,region__s1_green)
pages.page: A strong wind blows across the open country the whole way. Newmeet shows ahead a long while before you reach it: smoke, a roofline, the noise of it on the wind. A stone market cross stands in the middle of the square at Newmeet, its steps worn into dips. Hild is backing a cart into a yard, one hand on the horse’s bridle. Moll is touching up a painted backcloth of a castle with a small brush. Linden the researcher is copying a page from a borrowed book, a stone on each corner. The inn’s dog sleeps against the wall of the Ancient Lantern with one ear up for the door. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. A strip of vellum is nailed to the post by the well, in a fair clerk’s hand, with a lead seal pressed in a blob of wax. Wapshott’s bill on the wall says NOW PLAYING, NIGHTLY AT SEVEN, ADMISSION ONE COIN, CHILDREN AND DOGS HALF, on a strip pasted over the word COMING. A paper is nailed to the post under the crier’s bell-rope: THE LORD OF THE KEEP CALLS HIS MARCH TO THE KING’S MUSTER. TWENTY SPEARS AND A HUNDRED BUSHELS TO THE KEEP ON THE TWELFTH DAY. Underneath, in another hand, scratched with a nail: AND WHO IS TO SOW? Somebody has chalked a number on the well-stone, large and fresh, and under it a small neat wheel with a wing on it. A few barefoot prints go in and out of the inn’s door. The factor, who keeps the books of the Ísenheald company, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Newmeet, is here. Hesper Lowe, a boat-wright’s apprentice with a drawing of a bell, is here. So are the old woman in the doorway, Felice Hale, Cecily Hale, Wat, Alfric, Bartle the younger, Lambert, the Dunning lads, Maud the younger and the walkers. A hard wind is banging every shutter in the place. The wardens have stopped paying. A hayrick at Brockfield has burned in the night, and the bailiff has put up a new notice: SIX CROWNS, AND A FINE FOR THE FIRE. A string of barefoot strangers has taken the well-steps and is chalking the stone: a number, and a little wheel with a wing. They are singing something with no tune to speak of and a great deal of will. Somewhere behind the singing a man is selling something, with the voice of a man who has sold it before.

pages.label: talk_to(walk__pettifer)
pages.page: A round man in a coat with too many pockets has stood a barrel on end by the well and laid out on it, in a row, fifteen stubs of chalk. ‘My friend, my friend,’ says Lambert. ‘You have the face of someone who has been wondering where to put a mile. Here. A stub of the true chalk, one penny, from the very hand of the Mile-Keeper’s first mile, or near enough, and if it is not near enough I have another, and that one is nearer.’

pages.label: go(circus__orchard_path_a,region__s1_green)
pages.page: A stone market cross stands in the middle of the square at Newmeet, its steps worn into dips. Hild is backing a cart into a yard, one hand on the horse’s bridle. Moll is touching up a painted backcloth of a castle with a small brush. Linden the researcher is copying a page from a borrowed book, a stone on each corner. Underneath, in another hand, scratched with a nail: AND WHO IS TO SOW? Somebody has chalked a number on the well-stone, large and fresh, and under it a small neat wheel with a wing on it.
