pages.label: go(region__s1_chandlery_door,region__s1_chandlery)
pages.page: Shelves to the ceiling: coils of rope, lamps and lamp-oil, candles in bundles, sacks of meal; everything a traveller forgets, and the smell of tallow over it all. Mabel, a chandler, is here.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s1_r10)
pages.page: Baldric looks you over, and does not like what he sees.

pages.label: go(region__s1_sheds_way,region__s1_sheds)
pages.page: Long low sheds stand open to the water, with boats inside in every stage of being built or mended: ribs like a whale’s, an oar with a split blade. Shavings and tar lie thick underfoot, and an adze knocks at the back. Maud is steaming a plank in a long box to bend it. A hull stands half planked in the nearest shed, its ribs bare at the stern.

pages.label: go(region__z1_trail2,region__z1_heart_2)
pages.page: It rains on and off the whole way, a fine rain that soaks through your clothes. The path runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. The last mile is slow going. A sluice of squared timbers stands half in the water, its gate gone, a channel running straight as a rule away from it into the reed. Somebody drained this fen once, or meant to. Water talks in the broken gate. The sluice-post is cut all over with marks.

pages.label: go(region__z1_trail1,region__z1_edge)
pages.page: Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. It is a long walk, and your feet are sore by the end. Where the fields end, Addermoss begins: black water between tussocks, reed higher than your head, and the smell of it. Reedbridge is behind you, on the firm ground. A smell of rain comes from deeper in, though no rain has fallen here for days.

pages.label: go(region__z1_way2,region__s5_s2_way)
pages.page: Partway, the path comes down to the river and goes over it by the bridge, and the water runs deep and quick under your feet. The road crosses the Whitewater by a bridge of old grey stone, three arches green with moss; the river runs deep and quick beneath. An otter’s head breaks the water downstream and is gone. The road is churned by cattle, all going toward Wrackham, and not long since: some of it is still warm. Willows lean out over the water along the road, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Foxgloves stand tall at the wood’s edge, purple bells speckled inside: they heal, prepared rightly, and kill otherwise. Banewort grows along the road, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Dragonwort grows along the road, a red spike among spearing leaves. Cinquefoil runs over the ground along the road, its small yellow flowers five-petalled. Alhuren grows along the road, silver-leaved, its blue flowers pale as a candle-flame. Rosenoble grows along the road, a briar of deep red roses. Betony stands in the short grass at the wood’s edge, purple-spiked: the hedge herb, for a cut or a sting.

pages.label: go(region__road_s5_s2,region__s5_green)
pages.page: The road follows the river a while, close enough to hear it, and crosses at the bridge, where it runs too deep to wade. Reedbridge is a handful of roofs at the end of the road, and a dog that comes out to see who you are. Reedbridge is a crossing with houses at each end of it, the near end the larger, and the Whitewater between them, brown and quick. On this side the mud is churned by hooves and cartwheels down to the water’s edge. By the track stands the wayside shrine of Coventina, a small weathered well-head. Offerings of reed lie before it. A trestle table under the well, a ledger open on it, a lead seal on a cord, and, as the light goes, a queue of villagers with their dues in cloth, not speaking. A carter stands thigh-deep in the water with his breeches rolled, hauling at the bridle of a horse that will not come. The alehouse dog noses along the foot of the wall of Afran’s alehouse, following a smell from stone to stone. A ginger cat sits in the middle of the way, and people step round her. A goat with a broken tether is cropping the verge, with her whole attention. Asters grow in the gardens about the green in clumps, mauve with yellow eyes. A strip of vellum is pinned to the lintel of the inn at Reedbridge, with a lead seal in wax. Errich, a keeper of the wayside shrine, is here. Luthor, a herb-wife, selling from the house door, is here. Maudlin Rooke, the Road’s bailiff, who collects dues for the keeping of the old road in the name of the Office of the Road, over a seal that is nearly right, is here. So are a drover’s boy and Garrow Pelt. Smut watches you from a high ledge, unblinking, and does not come down.

pages.label: go(region__road_s1_s5_on,region__s1_s5_way)
pages.page: The road goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the road. The road between Porthalen and Reedbridge goes through scattered woods and the clearings of charcoal-burners. A stag stands in a clearing, watching, before it turns away. A tin button lies in the road, the kind pedlars sell by the card. Meadowsweet grows thick along the wet ground, a froth of cream flowers that smells of almonds and honey. Feverwort grows along the road in the rough grass, bitter-leaved: the herb-wives dry it for a child’s fever. Bloodroot grows along the road, broad-leaved, with white flowers low to the ground. Hazel grows along the road, broad-leaved, its nuts in clusters of three. Woodbine climbs along the road, its cream and yellow flowers sweet at dusk. Purslane grows along the road, low, with small fleshy leaves. Thistles grow along the road, purple-headed. Tansy grows along the road, its yellow buttons over feathery leaves. Sweetgrass grows along the road, its long blades smelling of hay. A cherry tree grows along the road, its bark banded and glossy. Bruisewort grows along the road, thick-leaved, with small purple flowers. Ofbit grows along the road on thin stems, its flowers blue.

pages.label: wait_for_light
pages.page: Rain drives across in grey sheets, and every rut is a stream. The sky greys, then lightens. It is morning. It is a long time since you slept. You are weary, and will fight the worse for it until you sleep.

pages.label: go(region__z6_way1,region__z6_edge)
pages.page: You leave the road between Porthalen and Reedbridge with your hood up and the rain in your face. It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by. Here Thornwood begins: hazel and thorn at first, then oak, and the light under them goes green. Porthalen is behind you, out in the open. Yarrow grows in the grass at the wayside, flat white heads over feathery leaves: a soldier’s herb, for cuts. A bay tree grows here, dark and glossy, clipped for its leaves. Bloodroot grows here, broad-leaved, with white flowers low to the ground. Celandine grows here, yellow-starred in the damp. Cinquefoil runs over the ground here, its small yellow flowers five-petalled. Staggerweed grows here, tall, with spurred blue flowers. Actaea grows here, its white flowers in feathery spikes. Ofbit grows here on thin stems, its flowers blue.

pages.label: go(region__tl_z6_edge,region__t217)
pages.page: Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight.

pages.label: go(region__tw216_217,region__t216)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Woodland: oak and ash and holly, the light green and broken, last year’s leaves deep underfoot. A fox, a red fox with a white throat, black legs and a full brush, looking back over its shoulder, is here.

pages.label: go(region__s4_lanes_way,region__s4_lanes)
pages.page: The lanes behind the houses run between yards and workshops: the ring of a hammer, a smell of bread or tallow, a door open on somebody’s work, a cat asleep on a sill. Averil is grinding willow bark in a stone mortar. You take Tegwen’s lease.

pages.label: go(region__s4_lanes_way,region__s4_green)
pages.page: The gate-yard of Gatesend is swept clean to the cobbles, and smells of wet stone and beeswax from the chapel door. The brothers’ house stands at the back of it behind a low wall, and the village crowds round the front. Beyond the roofs lies the Starmere. The fells rise steeply behind the last houses. Twice this month the Hall’s keeper has driven the town’s pigs off the verge of the old road. A notice is nailed to the clerk’s trestle by the well, under the shire-reeve’s mark: THE TALLY OF IRON AND GOLD IS TO BE MADE UP BY MIDWINTER. FOR THE WEIGHT OF IRON AND GOLD WANTING, SEE THE CLERK. Above the roofs, to the east, two columns of smoke stand on the ridge: one thick and black from the digging, one thin and white from the old woman’s fire. Inside the brothers’ house a voice is practising a chant, the same four notes over and over. Wat the collier is knocking dried clay from a pick, a careful blow at a time. The brothers’ dog lies across the doorstep of the guest-hall with his chin on his paws, and watches who comes. A thin brown cat crouches at the foot of a wall, watching a hole in it without a blink. Dandelions stand in the grass, yellow and seeding: a tea of them cleans the blood. Daffodils grow in the gardens about the green in a bank, their strap-leaves in clumps. A notice is nailed to the post by the well, written over in several hands. Gek, a herb-wife, selling from the house door, is here. Aldous Fenn, the reeve of the wood-wardens, who license the cutting in the woods round Gatesend, is here. The old woman in the doorway, the innkeeper’s mother, who has not been out of her chair since the harvest and who asks, every morning, whether the lamp has been lit, is here. So are Simkin and Nest. Pudding watches you from a high ledge, unblinking, and does not come down.

pages.label: talk_to(region__s4_r4)
pages.page: Wat looks at you for longer than is comfortable. ‘Well?’

pages.label: go(region__z2_way6,region__z2_deep)
pages.page: Showers come over one after another, and between them the sun comes out on the wet country. A hollow full of holly, dark even at noon, the ground dry underneath and littered with prickled leaves. A good place to keep out of the rain, and to keep out of sight. A tune comes from nowhere you can find, low and sad, played on something with strings. It stops when you stop walking. A blackbird scuffles away under the holly. Under the holly the ground is dry as a floor. Willows lean out over the water here, grey-green, their roots in the bank and their long shoots trailing in the current. Meadowsweet grows thick along the wet ground, a froth of cream flowers that smells of almonds and honey. Feverwort grows here in the rough grass, bitter-leaved: the herb-wives dry it for a child’s fever. A bay tree grows here, dark and glossy, clipped for its leaves. Hazel grows here, broad-leaved, its nuts in clusters of three. Betony stands in the short grass at the wood’s edge, purple-spiked: the hedge herb, for a cut or a sting.

pages.label: go(region__z2_trail3,region__z2_side1)
pages.page: For an hour the path runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves. Here Ashwood begins: hazel and thorn at first, then oak, and the light under them goes green. Gatesend is behind you, out in the open. A bramble of goodberries grows along the edge of the trees, the berries small and red. Ofbit grows here on thin stems, its flowers blue.

pages.label: go(region__z2_trail4,region__z2_water)
pages.page: The path runs along a river for a mile, with alders on the bank and the water loud over the stones. The Broadwater comes through the wood here over gravel and is shallow enough to wade. Deer have trodden the banks to mud. A kingfisher goes downstream like a thrown stone. A bar of gravel runs out into the Broadwater below the ford. Banewort grows here, dark-leaved, with dull purple bells. Woodbine climbs here, its cream and yellow flowers sweet at dusk. Staggerweed grows here, tall, with spurred blue flowers.

pages.label: look_closely(region__z2_water_gravel)
pages.page: You look closely at the gravel bar. The water has sorted the gravel into bands, coarse to fine, and in the finest something glints: a brass button, green at the edges, with a badge on it.

pages.label: go(region__z2_trail5,region__z2_heart)
pages.page: You set out from the ford over the Broadwater in the middle of the afternoon, in the rain. An axe is going in the wood, a long way off, and you never see the woodman. A long bank and ditch run through the wood, grown over with trees as old as any around them. It was dug long before anyone now living. Off to one side the undergrowth is broken in a line at the height of a man’s shoulder, not a deer’s: someone goes off this way now and then. A badger’s path runs along the top of the bank. A ditch full of leaves runs along the foot of the bank. Bloodroot grows here, broad-leaved, with white flowers low to the ground. Celandine grows here, yellow-starred in the damp.

pages.label: go(region__tl_z2_heart,region__t126)
pages.page: Beech wood, grey trunks over a floor of copper leaves, and very little sound. To the west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw125_145,region__t145)
pages.page: The path goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend. Woodland: oak and ash and holly, the light green and broken, last year’s leaves deep underfoot. Wrackham is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke. A pedlar with a pack on a frame and a staff, walking the drove-ways between the farms, is here. A pedlar is coming the other way along the sheep-track, bent under a pack on a frame, and lifts her staff to you from a long way off.

pages.label: go(region__tw145_166,region__t166)
pages.page: For a while the path keeps company with a river, close enough to hear it. Old coppice gone wild, each stool grown into a clump of stems as thick as a leg. The Whitewater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. A road crosses it, the only straight thing in sight.

pages.label: go(region__tw146_166,region__t146)
pages.page: You leave the country about Wrackham late, in rain, with the light going early under the cloud. Bramble and hazel thick under the trees, and a way through only where the deer have pushed. The Whitewater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. Wrackham is close by: you can hear it, and smell its smoke.

pages.label: go(region__tw127_146,region__t127)
pages.page: Water stands on both sides, and the path between is soft enough to take the print of your boot and keep it. The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the path. Reed-beds whispering in the wind, and a bittern in them booming like a blown jar. To the south-west the land rises.

pages.label: go(region__tw127_128,region__t128)
pages.page: It rains on and off the whole way, a fine rain that soaks through your clothes. Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron. Mist lying on the marsh, the reeds standing up out of it and the ground not showing at all. To the south-west the land rises. The light comes nearer over the water, and is not a candle, and there is no one holding it. The reeds hiss. A will-o’-the-wisp will give you 6 minutes, no more.

pages.label: go(region__tw107_128,region__t107)
pages.page: The path goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it. Reed-beds whispering in the wind, and a bittern in them booming like a blown jar. To the west the land rises. An otter, a sleek brown otter with a pale throat and a thick tapering tail, rising from the river, is here.

pages.label: go(region__tw88_108,region__t88)
pages.page: Mist lying on the marsh, the reeds standing up out of it and the ground not showing at all. The Whitewater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round.

pages.label: go(region__tw87_88,region__t87)
pages.page: Alder carr standing in its own black water, the roots like knuckles. The Whitewater runs through it, and has to be waded or gone round. To the north-west the land rises.

pages.label: region__survey_haze(party,region__t87)
pages.page: You look out over the country, but the weather has closed in: the nearer land is plain enough, and nothing past it.

pages.label: go(region__tw67_87,region__t67)
pages.page: You leave the fen of Addermoss with your hood up and the rain in your face. Fen: reeds taller than a man, black water between, and the ground giving underfoot with every step. To the north the land rises.
